events.title: ‘Unwelcome and unsafe’: Why Japanese companies are retreating from China at a historic rate
events.summary: The number of Japanese companies operating in China fell to the lowest level on record: report. The exodus is likely to intensify amid the diplomatic feud between Asia's top two economies. Tariff risks, growing labour and manufacturing costs, and cutthroat local competition also weighed on profit margins. Japanese companies are leaving China in record numbers, as a slowing Chinese economy and a diplomatic freeze force businesses to reassess their presence in the world's second-largest economy. The number of Japanese companies operating in China fell to a historic low, standing at 10,118 as of June, according to Teikoku Databank , a corporate credit research firm in Japan. That's down 22% from the previous survey held in June 2024 and about 30% below the 2012 peak, and the lowest since Teikoku began tracking the data in 2010. Japanese firms, which were already planning to reduce their footprint in China, are considering withdrawing from the market with greater urgency since China-Japan ties went into a tailspin, said Jeremy Chan, an analyst at political consultancy firm Eurasia Group. The exodus is likely to intensify as the diplomatic feud between Asia's top two economies forces Japanese companies — already grappling with shrinking profitability strained by tariff risks, growing labor and manufacturing costs, cutthroat local competition — to shrink or shut their operation in China, Teikoku said in its report last week. Some firms have reduced dependence on China without fully decoupling from it, it added. China-Japan relations have come under heavy strain since Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told parliament in November last year that Japan could get militarily involved in the event of a Chinese invasion of Taiwan. Beijing has responded by curbing exports of critical minerals to Japanese companies and urged citizens to refrain from traveling to Japan. Factors such as U.S. tariffs and a growing public resistance to Chinese goods and a growing Indian market have also further incentivised Japanese businesses' push to diversify away from Beijing, said Martin Schulz, chief policy economist at Fujitsu Research Institute. "Investment in China is weathering the perfect storm," he said. In the past two years, a record number of 4,137 Japanese companies fully withdrew from China, according to Teikoku's data. Only 1,221 entered over the same period, through subsidiaries, factories or representative offices, the fewest on record outside the Covid-19 pandemic. Japanese firms have grown increasingly reliant on the U.S. market while shifting away from China, what was once a key market, said Jesper Koll, expert director at Monex Group. Topix-listed companies saw the share of profits derived in China dwindle to less than 15% so far this year, down from 23% in 2020, while those from the U.S. rose to 35% compared with 25% over the same period, according to Koll's estimates. Washington is "openly courting" Japanese players to aid its re-industrialization efforts while Beijing has shifted towards a "made in and made by China" model, Koll said. Cases of Japanese nationals being detained by Beijing this year have further added to businesses' concerns about sending personnel to China, analysts say. Several Japanese nationals, including executives at top Japanese firms, were reportedly detained in August over alleged violations of dual-use goods export restrictions. "Japanese firms and their employees increasingly feel unwelcome and unsafe in China," Chan said. An April report from Japan External Trade Organization showed that companies are increasingly reluctant to expand their business in China. On Tuesday, a day after the Teikoku report, Chinese vice premier He Lifeng said China "always welcomes" Japanese enterprises to develop business and share market opportunities in the country. He told a delegation from the Japanese Association for the Promotion of International Trade to "keep to the right course on historical issues … and play a greater role in advancing China-Japan economic and trade cooperation." Automakers, parts suppliers and export-oriented manufacturers are the most likely to scale back in China, said Kei Koga, a professor at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore. Companies that have localized and can compete with Chinese rivals, particularly medical and precision equipment makers, are more likely to stay, he added.

events.title: Why surging Treasury yields don’t signal a U.S. 'fiscal apocalypse' — yet
events.summary: Treasury yields above 5% are raising fears that higher borrowing costs could fuel a debt spiral. Analysts say a fiscal crisis is not imminent, with higher rates feeding into debt costs gradually. Strategists say strong economic growth, not just fiscal fears, is driving the surge in Treasury yields. U.S. government borrowing costs have risen to their highest levels in decades, stoking concerns that the country's growing debt burden could eventually trigger a fiscal crisis. Will it? The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield is now firmly above 5%, while the government's net interest costs estimated at about $1.05 trillion in the first 11 months of fiscal year 2026. Experts are voicing concerns over the vicious cycle of rising debt and higher yields. Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a U.S. policy think tank, has warned that higher borrowing costs risk becoming self-reinforcing as mounting interest expenses force the government to borrow still more. "The real threat is the debt spiral. If interest begets debt, and debt begets interest, eventually debt will spin out of control. A fiscal crisis, once unthinkable, is now a distinct possibility," MacGuineas said in a statement last month after the 10-year Treasury yield crossed 5%. The nightmare scenario is relatively straightforward: investors demand higher yields to lend to a heavily indebted government; those higher rates push up Washington's interest bill; the government has to borrow more to service its debt obligations; and investors demand even higher yields in response. Some bond market experts, however, say the U.S. is some distance from a fiscal breaking point, and that the latest surge in yields may have as much to do with a surprisingly resilient economy as fears over government debt. "A fiscal apocalypse is not upon us just yet," TD Securities strategists Gennadiy Goldberg and Molly Brooks said in a recent note. The bank estimates U.S. interest expenses in fiscal year 2026 to be around $1.1 trillion and continue rising if rates remain elevated. Its projections show financing costs reaching $1.4 trillion in fiscal 2027, $1.5 trillion in 2028 and $1.6 trillion in 2029, if yields stay around current levels. An important buffer is that Washington does not have to refinance its entire debt pile at today's higher rates immediately, the investment bank's analysts said. The weighted-average maturity of U.S. government debt is about 5.9 years, meaning higher borrowing costs feed through gradually as existing bonds mature and new debt is issued. The average coupon on Treasury securities excluding bills is still just 3.1%, according to TD Securities. Perhaps more importantly, the average interest rate on U.S. debt, at about 3.4%, remains below the rate at which the economy is growing in nominal terms. Nominal U.S. GDP grew at an annualized rate of 8.5% in the second quarter, according to the latest Bureau of Economic Analysis estimate. That helps keep the debt burden manageable even as deficits remain large, TD said. Matthew Reese, head of global bond strategies at L&G Asset Management, also said fears of an imminent U.S. fiscal crisis were "exaggerated." "There are valid concerns that the U.S., along with many other developed economies, will suffer from the negative feedback loop caused by higher yield costs increasing their fiscal burden as they refinance their debt and fund their fiscal deficit," he told CNBC in an e-mail. "However, the US still retains much of the 'exorbitant privilege' of the US dollar and its role as the most liquid and still highly rated economy. Therefore, we are some way away from a fiscal crisis." The negative feedback loop becomes more dangerous when nominal economic growth falls to low levels, causing debt relative to the size of the economy to rise persistently, Reese said. Still, high debt alone does not necessarily trigger a crisis. "It is important to note that countries such as Japan have coped with significantly higher debt levels than the U.S., with very low nominal growth, without suffering a fiscal crisis," Reese said. Federal debt held by the public is projected to stand at about 101% of GDP in fiscal 2026 , according to the Congressional Budget Office. While that trajectory is enough to keep investors concerned, TD Securities does not see a fiscal crisis as imminent. And government finances may not even be the main reason Treasury yields have risen so sharply. TD pointed to stronger economic growth, expectations for Federal Reserve rate hikes, higher oil prices, corporate bond issuance and repositioning by fast-money investors alongside fiscal concerns, as factors driving yields higher. Ian Lyngen, head of U.S. rates strategy at BMO Capital Markets, also pointed to the resilience of the U.S. economy as an important driver of higher Treasury yields.

events.title: Trump unveils 'Super Intelligence Force' to oversee AI policy
events.summary: Published 5 October 2026, 02:33 BST US President Donald Trump says he has created a new task force focused on artificial intelligence, which will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton. The "Super Intelligence Force" will work to ensure that the US continues to lead in the technology's development and will coordinate the government's engagement with the public, Trump posted on Sunday. Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson and Undersecretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael will also be part of the task force. Trump said last week that he would set up a board to oversee AI safety after top tech bosses signed what he described as a "morally binding" pact to regulate the technology. "The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies," Trump wrote. The taskforce's announcement follows growing pressure from prominent figures in the industry to tighten regulation of the technology. Trump has dismissed calls for stronger oversight and largely left it to AI companies to regulate themselves. The pact signed on 29 September includes the signatures of executives from top tech firms like OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX and Google. US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton On the same day, the president also signed an executive order to rename AI as "super intelligence", after previously saying the word artificial made the technology sound "fake". Some experts have questioned the logic of the rebranding , arguing that the use of "super intelligence" could cause confusion as it refers to more advanced systems. Some top tech leaders have already started to use the new name, including multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who said on social media on Sunday that he will rename his firm's AI platform SpaceXAI as SpaceXSI. "SpaceX is a super intelligence company", Musk wrote. The Tesla boss has recently been brought back into the US government to be part of a project to study the future of war. Musk previously served in the Trump administration, heading the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, before his tenure ended in a public spat with Trump . events.title: SoftBank’s Masayoshi Son Has Rare Cautionary Note on AI Safety
events.summary: Speaking at a tech forum in Kyoto, Masayoshi Son called for global cooperation on AI safeguards, warning that superintelligence could pose a greater threat than conflict between humans if misused. Bloomberg tech editor Mayumi Negishi said the caution marks a notable shift in tone from the longtime technology optimist, though Son remains strongly bullish on AI. He estimates AI machines could account for at least 20% of global GDP—about $46 trillion—by 2040, and suggested investors could see 50-fold returns over roughly 15 years. Negishi also noted that SoftBank has committed about $65 billion to OpenAI. Son continues to describe AI as a potential source of hope and greater happiness, while emphasizing that its capabilities and associated risks are growing rapidly. events.title: Far East Orchard crosses $3 billion AUM target with higher stakes in business trust managers
events.summary: Alan Tang, group chief executive of Far East Orchard, noted that the accretive acquisition is a significant step towards scaling a fully integrated lodging platform. Far East Orchard is acquiring an additional 42% stake in Far East Hospitality Trust managers, raising its ownership to 75% and increasing its core assets under management to S$3.9 billion. This acquisition accelerates Far East Orchard’s "FEOR30" roadmap and supports a new core AUM target of at least S$5 billion by FY2030. The S$28.3 million cash deal strengthens recurring income, enhances growth flexibility, and expands capital-efficient channels alongside its private fund platform. SINGAPORE – Far East Orchard is acquiring an additional 42% stake in the managers of Far East Hospitality Trust (FEHT) , a transaction that will propel its core assets under management (AUM) past its $3 billion goal to $3.9 billion, four years earlier than targeted. Far East Orchard announced on the morning of Oct 5 that the $28.3 million deal will raise its ownership in the managers from its current 33% to 75%. The remaining 25% will continue to be held by the seller, FEO Asset Management, a wholly owned subsidiary of Far East Organization Centre. The acquisition involves shares in both FEO Hospitality Asset Management, the manager of Far East Hospitality Real Estate Investment Trust (FEH-Reit), and FEO Hospitality Trust Management, the trustee-manager of Far East Hospitality Business Trust (FEH-BT). FEHT is a hospitality stapled group with a market capitalisation of $1.25 billion. It comprises FEH-Reit and FEH-BT and holds a portfolio of 13 properties, comprising 12 properties in Singapore and one hotel in Japan. Far East Orchard said in its statement that the deal with its associates is a strategic move to accelerate Far East Orchard’s “FEOR30” business road map . By gaining effective control of the FEHT managers, Far East Orchard’s core assets under management (AUM) will scale by about 86%, jumping from $2.1 billion to $3.9 billion. This exceeds the company’s previously announced core AUM target of $3 billion, and supports a new core AUM target of “at least $5 billion” by financial year 2030, Far East Orchard said. “By strengthening our alignment with FEHT, we are expanding our recurring income base and broadening the channels through which we can grow in a capital efficient manner, including capital recycling and capital-light AUM growth alongside our existing private fund platform,” he said. “This gives us greater flexibility to grow faster, build more resilient earnings, and capture value and maximise returns across the full asset lifecycle,” he added. The $28.3 million consideration will be paid entirely in cash, funded by Far East Orchard’s internal resources. As part of the transaction’s conditions, FEO Hospitality Asset Management will distribute a dividend in specie of roughly 165.2 million FEHT stapled securities to its shareholders.

events.title: Temu took the world by storm – but has the shopping app lost its thunder?
events.summary: In Focus Temu took the world by storm – but has the shopping app lost its thunder? Temu is quickly losing its shine in the face of a wave of global regulation. Can the platform reinvent itself? In February 2023, the budget shopping platform Temu announced itself on the world stage in the brashest way possible: becoming one of the youngest ever brands to buy a Super Bowl advertising spot. “Download the Temu app and shop like a billionaire,” a voice proclaimed in the 30-second commercial, as a woman danced on screen and ordered a series of outlandishly cheap items: from a US$8.99 dress to a US$4.99 wig. The commercial – which aired twice during the game, costing Temu an estimated US$14 million – was part of a marketing blitz by the platform, as it tried to introduce American consumers to a marketplace built on ultra-low prices, a wide array of products, and a gamified shopping experience. That expense paid off: Temu’s downloads jumped 45 per cent on the day of the Super Bowl campaign compared with a day earlier, according to a report by trade outlet ModernRetail, citing Sensor Tower data.

events.title: Brazil’s presidential race: Three key takeaways from the first round
events.summary: Flavio Bolsonaro beat polling expectations as Brazil’s right gained ground, setting up October 25 run-off with Lula. Brazil’s closely watched presidential election is heading to a second round between leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, prolonging a deeply polarised race with major implications for the country and the wider region. Brazil’s electoral court confirmed on Sunday that the two candidates will advance to a run-off on October 25 after neither won the majority needed to secure the presidency outright, with Bolsonaro leading at 55.8 million votes to Lula’s almost 53.2 million. list 1 of 4 Brazil’s Lula and Bolsonaro close campaigns ahead of critical election list 2 of 4 Will Brazil’s Lula halt the right-wing wave sweeping Latin America? list 3 of 4 Polls close in Brazil’s polarised election pitting Lula against Bolsonaro list 4 of 4 Lula and Bolsonaro vote in Brazil’s polarised presidential election Lula, 80, is seeking a fourth, non-consecutive term after a political career spanning nearly five decades. Bolsonaro, 45, is the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro and is trying to return his father’s right-wing movement to power, even as the former president serves a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election. The election comes at a pivotal time for Latin America’s largest economy. Brazilians are grappling with concerns over crime and the cost of living, while the country faces an increasingly tense relationship with the United States. The vote is also being closely watched across a region that has shifted sharply to the right in a series of recent elections. While a second round was widely expected, the first-round result did not play out quite as pollsters had predicted. Here are some of the key takeaways from the election so far. Brazil is heading for another Lula-Bolsonaro run-off With nearly 99 percent of votes reported, Bolsonaro had about 47 percent of valid votes, compared with 44.9 percent for Lula. Neither reached the 50 percent threshold needed to win in the first round. That sets up another Lula-Bolsonaro showdown, four years after Lula narrowly defeated former President Jair Bolsonaro. This time, he will face the former president’s eldest son. The race could be extremely close, as polling ahead of Sunday’s vote suggested Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro were roughly tied in a potential run-off. That puts voters who backed one of the other 10 candidates in the first round at the centre of the fight for the presidency over the next three weeks. Ronaldo Caiado and Renan Santos, who together received about 5.3 million votes, have previously said they will not endorse either candidate in the run-off. Flavio Bolsonaro did better than polls suggested Most polls leading up to election day predicted the race would be pushed into the second round, but had Lula finishing the first round ahead of Bolsonaro. Instead, Bolsonaro emerged with a lead of two percentage points, raising questions about why the final polls underestimated his support. On Sunday, Bolsonaro said the results showed that Brazilians want change. Analysts told the Reuters news agency that Bolsonaro may have benefitted from “protest votes” from people who may have preferred another candidate but saw defeating Lula as the priority. Many had been expected to shift their support to Bolsonaro only in a second round, meaning this could have consequences for his support in three weeks. “The protest vote foreshadows what is to come in the run-off,” political analyst Rafael Favetti told Reuters. “While this should benefit Flavio Bolsonaro now, his growth potential in the second round drops precisely because that support has already been front-loaded.” After the results came in, Lula said the votes were “unexpected” but that he would come back stronger in the run-off. “I admit, I was convinced I would win in the first round. The game is about to start. We are in extra time. In extra time, we will win over the Brazilian people,” the 80-year-old said. The right had a strong night in Congress, too Bolsonaro’s surprising performance in the first round was part of a broader show of strength for Brazil’s right. Right-wing parties, led by Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL), were performing strongly in both houses of Congress, with the PL on track to emerge as the largest force in the Chamber of Deputies and making gains in the Senate. This included victories for other members of the Bolsonaro family , including former First Lady Michelle Bolsonaro, Flavio’s stepmother, who won a Senate seat in the Federal District, her first elected office. His brother, Carlos Bolsonaro, was elected to the Senate in Santa Catarina. The results show that the political movement built around former President Jair Bolsonaro – known as “bolsonarista” – remains a powerful electoral force, even with the former president barred from running himself.

events.title: AkzoNobel to sell South-east Asia paints business to Nippon Paint for US$1.35 billion
events.summary: Dulux paint maker AkzoNobel earlier divested its decorative paints operations in India and Pakistan for US$1.6 billion and €50 million respectively. AkzoNobel agreed to sell its Southeast Asian decorative paints business to Nippon Paint for US$1.35 billion, covering operations in eight countries. The deal is expected to close by mid-2027, except Indonesia's sale, which will close in late 2026, with net cash proceeds around US$1 billion. AkzoNobel aims to focus on its merger with US coatings maker Axalta and has no current plans to sell more assets, while Nippon Paint remains interested in larger acquisitions. AkzoNobel said on Oct 5 it has agreed to sell its South-east Asian decorative paints business to Nippon Paint for US$1.35 billion (S$1.72 billion), completing a review of its Asian decorative paints portfolio. The sale covers decorative paints operations in Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore, Papua New Guinea and Australia, the Dutch paints maker said, adding that it expects net cash proceeds of about US$1 billion after tax and payments to minority partners. The Dulux paint maker earlier divested its decorative paints operations in India and Pakistan for US$1.6 billion and €50 million (S$71.8 million), respectively. “The successful completion of our Asia portfolio review is part of an ongoing strategy to focus our portfolio on areas where we can achieve differentiating scale and strengthen our position,” AkzoNobel chief executive Greg Poux-Guillaume said in a statement. The Indonesia deal is expected to close separately in late 2026, while the remaining transactions are expected to close around mid-2027. AkzoNobel said it will now focus on the successful closing of its merger with US coatings maker Axalta, which was announced in November 2025 . Nippon Paint submitted multiple proposals to acquire AkzoNobel’s decorative paints business, the Dutch company said in July, valuing it at about €7.5 billion. That approach followed the withdrawal of a €12.5 billion bid for the entire company that Nippon Paint had pursued jointly with US-based paint maker Sherwin-Williams in June. The Financial Times, which earlier reported the South-east Asia deal, said Nippon remains interested in a larger deal for the decorative paint business, but that integration of the South-east Asia business could occupy the company for some time and AkzoNobel does not have plans to sell further assets from the business. events.title: Brazil heads to a runoff election after Bolsonaro and Lula fail to garner a majority of votes
events.summary: Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, and Brazil’s veteran President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will face off in a runoff for the top job of Latin America’s powerhouse economy BRASILIA, Brazil -- Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, and Brazil’s incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will face off in a runoff Oct. 25 for the top job of Latin America’s powerhouse economy after neither won a majority in Sunday's vote. The country’s electoral court in Brasilia said neither the 80-year-old incumbent, seeking his fourth non-consecutive term, nor the 45-year-old son of former President Jair Bolsonaro would garner the majority vote needed for an outright win. The court had Bolsonaro with just over 56 million votes to Lula’s 53.7 million, with 99.8 percent of the vote reported. The next presidential term is set to begin Jan. 5. The winner will be in charge of Latin America’s biggest economy and a population of 214 million. A win for Bolsonaro would increase U.S. influence in Latin America. If Lula wins, Brazil will keep its distance from Washington and continue to deepen its relationship with China. Flávio Bolsonaro addressed the press and a small group of supporters, including some wearing green and yellow Brazil jerseys and one woman wrapped in the Israeli flag, outside his Brasilia house. “Brazil wants change, that’s the reading of what happened today,” Bolsonaro said. “It’s the end of the Workers’ Party era,” he added, in a reference to Lula's party. Lula, seeking to be encouraging ahead of an uphill battle to beat Bolsonaro in the runoff, said the result was “unexpected” as he had thought he could win in the first round. “Tomorrow we start a new campaign,” Lula said. “I am very good in the knockout stage. We will see who has the best plan.” Both Lula and Bolsonaro will have three weeks to reach moderate voters who did not support them in the first round. Augusto Cury, a writer who finished in third place with 3.4 million votes, said he would not endorse either in the runoff. Ronaldo Caiado and Renan Santos, two candidates who garnered about 5.3 million votes combined Sunday, have previously said the same. In the campaign ahead, Lula is expected to try to capitalize on the popularity of his social policies and his rival’s many legal woes. While the once widely popular Lula saw his approval ratings plummet during his third term, standing up to the U.S. gave him a boost. And he still enjoys a strong base of supporters who credit his social policies for improving millions of Brazilians’ lives. But the incumbent faces a tough battle because of an affordability crisis and a corruption scandal that ensnared the same justice who led the investigation into Bolsonaro . Bolsonaro will likely lean into his messaging on affordability and link the president to corruption scandals. He has promised to crack down on Brazilian criminal groups and insisted that Brazil needs to strike better deals with the Trump administration, including in the rare minerals economy , second only to China. Bolsonaro also has campaigned on releasing his father and bringing him back to politics. Both candidates face image problems: Roughly half of Brazil’s population disapproves of the Bolsonaro family, and roughly half disapprove of Lula’s Workers' Party, according to multiple polls. Four years ago, Lula beat then incumbent Jair Bolsonaro by about 2.1 million votes. While it was a successful night for Bolsonaro, nothing is won yet, said Mayra Goulart, a political scientist from the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro. Lula should “look at the votes for Augusto Cury and Ronaldo Caiado and try to reduce abstention,” she said. Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials Father, son federally charged in connection to death of Ole Miss student District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' Reacting to the result, Alvaro Senra, 65, a history professor and Lula supporter in Rio de Janeiro said he felt “calm but very sad.” He watched the count with friends at a bar. “I think this is the result of conservatives working under the radar, including by neo-Pentecostal churches. But I think Lula can still win,” he said. Earlier in the day, Maria Ribeiro, a 50-year-old cellphone vendor from Brasilia, said she voted for Bolsonaro’s eldest son because she wants freedom to express her evangelical religion. She hopes he follows in his father’s footsteps. “I voted for his father, and I don’t regret it,” she said. The proximity to his father was what worried Lorena Zschaber, a 40-year-old photographer, who watched the results roll in at an LGBTQ+-friendly bar in downtown Rio de Janeiro. During his father’s presidency, “people felt more at ease to discriminate,” she said. “I’m an LGBTQ+ woman, I can’t think of anything worse happening than Flávio Bolsonaro being elected,” she added.

events.title: Can the KKK find a new foothold in the US?
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections The infamous hate group is trying to rebrand itself as the ‘Knights Party’ in an attempt to grow its base. Deleted: Experts have warned over the past decade of a resurgence in white supremacy in the United States, fuelled in part by the mainstream influence of political figures like President Donald Trump. Just this year, the Public Religion Research Institute released the results of a 2025 survey that asked more than 20,000 US adults to evaluate the statement, “Immigrants are invading our country and replacing our cultural and ethnic background.” list 1 of 3 White nationalists march on Washington DC ahead of Freedom 250 celebrations list 2 of 3 Why the US may stop collecting workplace race and gender data list 3 of 3 HRW says US civil rights enforcement reduced under Trump: What to know That belief is the cornerstone of the great replacement theory , a conspiracy that falsely claims that immigrants, Jews and nonwhite groups seek to supplant white people in Western countries. The research institute found that 32 percent of respondents – nearly one in three – nevertheless agreed with the idea. Critics have accused right-wing leaders like Trump of normalising such views, through rhetoric that paints immigration as an “invasion” and “an assault on Western countries”. Trump has also been accused of cosying up to white nationalists, even dining in 2022 with Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes, a key figure in the movement. When white nationalists engaged in a deadly clash with protesters in Charlottesville, Virginia, in 2017, Trump said there were “fine people on both sides”. Al Jazeera correspondent Phil Lavelle travelled to Boone County, Arkansas, to see whether one of the most infamous white supremacist organisations in US history had seen a bump in its influence midway through Trump’s second term. He spoke to Thomas Robb, the head of what was formerly known as the Knights of the Ku Klux Klan, a white supremacist group founded in the 1970s by David Duke. What Lavelle found was a group seemingly eager to rebrand. The group had shortened its title to The Knights Party, and members told Lavelle they were trying to re-centre their message around family and faith. But when Lavelle asked if a Black person would be welcome at the group’s church, Robb’s answer was simple. “No,” Robb responded. “Because this is a white nationalist church.” The Ku Klux Klan (KKK) has a long history of racism and violence in the US. The movement began at the end of the civil war in 1865, as a response to government efforts to expand civil rights to Black people and other minority groups. Through lynchings and other targeted acts of violence, the KKK attempted to block non-white participation in government and maintain racial divides. Robb, a Christian pastor, took over as the head of the Knights of the Ku Klux Klan – a faction of the KKK – in 1989. He has since attempted to broaden the group’s appeal. He changed his title from “grand wizard” to “national director”, allowed new members to participate confidentially by mail, and distanced himself from KKK violence in public outreach campaigns. Still, he has adhered to the racist philosophy his organisation is known for. “What do you make of politicians like Zohran Mamdani or Abdul El-Sayed?” Lavelle asked Robb in his interview, referencing two high-profile US politicians who identify as Muslim. “Well, first off, they’re not Americans,” Robb said. When Lavelle pointed out that El-Sayed was born in Michigan, Robb brushed off the contradiction. “I don’t care where he’s born. He’s not American.” He proceeded to draw a distinction between the children of white and non-white immigrants. Only the children of white foreigners can be American, Robb said, “because they’re white”. The Knights of the Ku Klux Klan is one of dozens of white supremacy organisations operating in the US. The Southern Poverty Law Center, an advocacy group, estimates that there are at least 152 such groups active in the US today, part of what it calls a rising trend over the last decade. Just this year, another white supremacist organisation, the Patriot Front, marched through Washington, DC , during the Independence Day holiday. Critics say Trump, at times, has echoed their rhetoric. Trump told The New York Times earlier this year that “white people were very badly treated” in fields like academics. He also instructed his second administration to dismantle diversity initiatives, and under his leadership, the government has launched probes into whether universities and companies like Nike discriminate against white people. In addition, Trump has given priority to white South Africans in refugee admissions, falsely claiming they are the subject of a “genocide”. Robb claimed the current rise in white nationalist sentiment began well before Trump, in 2008, during the election of Barack Obama, the country’s first Black president.

events.title: How India became dangerously addicted to Chinese imports
events.summary: Xi and Modi have vowed to address growing trade imbalances Take a walk into an Indian toy shop and as well as picking up a new favourite plaything for a child, you might just get an insight into how the nation is battling for a batter economic relationship with its all-powerful neighbour China. Six years ago, in an attempt to push local manufacturing and keep substandard toys out of its market, India raised tariffs on imported toys from 20% to 60% and eventually to 70%. Retailers were up in arms and said that domestic firms could never match the foreign-made stuff. But the combination of higher customs duties and quality control standards worked. Indian imports of toys fell by a third from nearly $300mn in 2020 to $100mn this year, while exports rose from around $129mn to $200mn in the same period. Moreover, the country was able to drastically reduce its dependence on China, which held a 70% share of the local toy market. The sector stands out as a rare exception in India's otherwise unsuccessful attempts to rebalance an increasingly lopsided trading relationship with its larger neighbour, which some experts say, is now among the most asymmetric in the world. Even as diplomatic ties between the two countries completely broke down following the Galwan Valley clashes in 2020 and Delhi announced a slew of anti-dumping duties and a ban on Chinese apps such as Tik Tok, its trade deficit with Beijing has only ballooned - from $44bn in 2020 to an eye-popping $112bn this year. "India's economic dependence on China continued to deepen while political, security, and investment ties were at their lowest point," Kevin Zongzhe Li, a Washington-based Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute's Centre for China Analysis, told the BBC. More worryingly, exports to China remained below pre-pandemic level even as imports doubled in this period. "China now supplies over 30% of India's industrial imports, and India depends on it for more than 100 critical products. And the imbalance is worsening," says Ajay Srivastava of the Delhi-based Global Trade and Research Initiative (GTRI). If the rapid pace of imports continues, bilateral deficit could jump to $134bn, giving Beijing even more leverage over Indian industry, according to Srivastava. Anti-China sentiment hit a fever pitch post border skirmishes in 2020, but relations have now thawed On the sidelines of the Brics summit in Delhi in September, amid a deepening thaw between the Asian giants, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping vowed to address , external these "structural trade imbalances and supply chain issues". But given how deeply entrenched Chinese imports have become to India's industrial economy, this will be a formidable task for Delhi, experts told the BBC. That's primarily because India depends on China to not merely consume end-products, but increasingly to produce industrial goods. To be true, India has reduced its reliance on imports of finished goods such as smartphones and solar equipment, and now produces more than a quarter of the world's iPhones. "Yet, production remains largely assembly-based and depends heavily on imported components, particularly from China," says Srivastava. It's the same story with industrial machinery, battery inputs, chemicals, solar cells, and manufacturing equipment. Electrical machinery and electronics alone account for 36% of imports, followed by machinery and mechanical appliances at 21.7%, while organic chemicals and plastics also have a significant share, according to the Observer Research Foundation (ORF) think tank. "Their interruption would not merely affect consumption; it would disrupt production itself," according to Soumya Bhowmik, a Fellow at ORF's Centre for New Economic Diplomacy, who argues that this reflects India's difficulty in substituting Chinese inputs with local production. Besides a growing reliance on inputs and raw material, Chinese imports to India are also being propelled by other macroeconomic trends. China has huge excess capacity in sectors from steel to solar panels and electric vehicles, while its slowing economy cannot absorb the output. Manufacturers are therefore increasingly turning to overseas markets, selling goods cheaply. China's trade surplus is expected to top $1tn for a second straight year. A lot of these goods are coming to Indian shores because it is rapidly expanding manufacturing across segments of the economy, but also as "Western markets impose tariffs and other restrictions", says Srivastava. India has reduced smartphone imports but depends heavily on China for components On the other hand, lack of access to the Chinese market remains a major challenge for Indian companies. "Indian products face a variety of tariff and non-tariff hurdles in China that make it difficult to scale exports," says Li.

events.title: Nearly 1,500 migrants arrive in Myanmar from Malaysia despite UN warnings
events.summary: Malaysia continues mass refugee deportations despite warnings from the UN about unsafe conditions in an active war zone. Nearly 1,500 Myanmar refugees and migrants deported from Malaysia have arrived in their war-ravaged country under an opaque repatriation scheme heavily criticised by human rights groups and the United Nations refugee agency. The 1,479 returnees, transported from Malaysia on board two navy warships and a hospital ship on Tuesday, arrived in southern Yangon early Sunday, Nay Lin Tun, a regional government minister, said. list 1 of 3 Malaysia gave refuge to Rohingya; now it wants them to go list 2 of 3 Malaysia sends Rohingya back to Myanmar despite safety warnings list 3 of 3 ‘They are crying’: Refugees in Malaysia in fear amid Myanmar deportation They are among 5,000 Myanmar nationals who will be repatriated in stages from Malaysia, where more than 10,300 others are being held in immigration detention centres, according to the country’s Home Ministry. Malaysia insists all returnees agreed to voluntary repatriation, but rights monitors have raised concerns that Myanmar refugees had little choice and warned that conditions for return remain unsafe. The UN refugee agency said this past week that its staff were not allowed to meet the Myanmar nationals to confirm whether their decisions to return “were genuinely free and informed”. Rohingya make up the majority of Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, but it remains unclear how many members of the persecuted Rohingya are among the returned group. The deportation was carried out during escalating raids on refugee communities in Malaysia by immigration officials, which led to the detention of more than 50,000 refugees in 2026. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced the repatriations in July against a backdrop of rising xenophobia towards refugees, particularly the Rohingya. Kuala Lumpur is moving ahead with plans to return a second group of more than 3,500 refugees and migrants, saying they have caused financial, social and security burdens. While Malaysia is not a party to the UN Refugee Convention and treats refugees as undocumented migrants, it is home to about 215,600 refugees and asylum seekers registered with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR). This includes more than 126,000 mainly Muslim Rohingya refugees. Myanmar pledged last month that returns will be “safe and dignified”. But Yap Lay Sheng, a senior human rights specialist with Fortify Rights, told the AFP news agency: “There’s no telling how the regime would treat returnees.” Myanmar has been accused of committing genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority. Earlier this year, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) opened its first genocide case it has heard in full in more than a decade. The UNHCR and rights groups said returnees could face persecution and forced military conscription in an active war zone. Myanmar has been embroiled in a civil war since the military seized power from the elected government in 2021. The war has killed more than 100,000 people since the coup, according to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) project. Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing, the military coup leader who was installed as civilian president in April, is expected to visit Malaysia soon to discuss the repatriation scheme.

events.title: They survived World War II and lost decades, but not 2026. Japan's century-old businesses are disappearing at a record pace
events.summary: Bankruptcies among Japanese companies more than 100 years old are running at a record pace in 2026, according to Teikoku Databank. Rising costs, labor shortages, a shrinking domestic market and succession challenges are testing Japan’s long-established businesses, experts told CNBC. The challenges are pushing some long-established companies to reassess their businesses, growth strategies and ownership structures. Founded in 1858, Japanese sesame oil maker Kadoya Sesame Mills has witnessed the country transform over generations — surviving world wars and Japan's asset bubble. Now, more than two decades after listing on the Jasdaq Securities Exchange in 2004, Kadoya is set to go private through a tender offer backed by Japanese private equity firm Integral. The move comes as the company navigates rising raw-material costs and heightened geopolitical risks. Japan's long-established businesses are being tested by factors ranging from a shrinking domestic market and labor shortages to succession challenges, experts told CNBC. Bankruptcies among Japanese businesses with more than 100 years of history are occurring at a record pace, reaching 112 in the first eight months of 2026, according to Teikoku Databank. Japan's century-old companies have achieved enduring prosperity through a long-term perspective fostered by family ownership, strong roots in local communities and a business approach that stays within their means, said Shigeto Nagai, head of Japan economics at Oxford Economics. Their long histories and years of capital accumulation have also left them with sound balance sheets and stable profit margins. "However, they are increasingly concerned that they cannot foresee a future of sustained high profits over the long term and fear they will gradually fall into decline," Nagai said. Rising costs and labor shortages have become major challenges for Japanese companies in the post-pandemic business environment, said Harumi Taguchi, principal economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. "Although inflation has made it easier for companies to pass on costs than during the deflationary period, many still cannot fully reflect higher expenses in sales prices," Taguchi pointed out. Higher costs are particularly difficult for smaller and domestically focused Japanese businesses to absorb given their weaker sales bases, she said. Pricing power is therefore a key factor in determining which companies can adapt. Bankruptcies linked to higher prices jumped 23.8% to 556 in the first half of 2026, while labor-shortage bankruptcies climbed 12.4% to 227, according to Teikoku Databank. Sube Shoten, a tofu maker founded in 1877 during Japan's Meiji era, reportedly ceased operations in May and began preparing to file for bankruptcy as low profit margins and a recent surge in raw-material costs clouded its business outlook. Another major challenge is intensifying domestic competition and labor shortages as Japan's birth rate declines and its population ages, Nagai said. Expanding overseas is another challenge as the domestic market, historically a stable source of revenue, continues to shrink. But there is no "one-size-fits-all" prescription, Nagai added. Succession is another growing challenge. Bankruptcies linked to a lack of successors rose 16.9% to 312 from a year earlier in the first half of 2026, according to Teikoku Databank. A weaker yen, corporate governance reforms, activist pressure and succession challenges among founder-owned businesses are pushing owners and boards to reassess their options, alongside broader pressures including inflation, tariffs, labor costs and interest rates, said Paul Aversano, managing director and global practice leader of Alvarez & Marsal's Global Transaction Advisory Group. "It is that combination, rather than any single issue, that is shaping decisions," he said.

events.title: Ethiopia’s forces retake Mekelle amid renewed Tigray fighting
events.summary: The capture of Tigray’s regional capital revives fears of another prolonged conflict, displacement and crisis. Addis Ababa, Ethiopia – The capture of Tigray’s regional capital Mekelle by Ethiopian federal forces and allied Tigray Peace Force fighters has revived painful memories of the 2020–22 Tigray war, with residents fearing a return to prolonged violence, displacement and economic hardship. The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) confirmed on Saturday that it had withdrawn from Mekelle, saying its regional administration would temporarily operate from another location. Government forces and allied fighters entered the city on Saturday, with a pro-government militia source, a humanitarian worker and a Mekelle resident confirming to the Reuters news agency on Sunday that they were in control of the city. The development comes less than four years after the Ethiopian government and the TPLF signed the Pretoria agreement that ended two years of devastating fighting. Berihu, a 32-year-old bajaj driver in Shire, northwestern Tigray, said the latest fighting had been particularly difficult to watch. “I feel very heartbroken knowing that Tigray has gone back to full-scale war,” he said in a phone interview with Al Jazeera. “We have already seen what the last war did to our people, and now it feels like we are going through it all over again.” The 2020–22 war killed hundreds of thousands of people, according to estimates, displaced millions and caused extensive damage to infrastructure and livelihoods. The African Union-facilitated agreement, signed in Pretoria in November 2022, ended the large-scale fighting, but key issues, including the status of disputed territories, the return of displaced people and the disarmament of Tigrayan forces, remained unresolved. In July, the TPLF said the Pretoria agreement had effectively collapsed, accusing the federal government of failing to implement key provisions. The federal government rejected that characterisation, saying it remained committed to the peace process while accusing the TPLF of undermining the agreement. The political dispute was accompanied by growing military tensions, including reports of sporadic clashes and drone strikes in parts of Tigray. The two sides also traded accusations over troop movements and preparations for renewed fighting. The capture of Mekelle marks a major development in the renewed conflict, putting the city once again at the centre of the fighting. In Addis Ababa, the developments have also alarmed residents who remember the consequences of the previous war. Abel, a 30-year-old shopkeeper, said the fighting had felt distant until explosions were heard in the capital . “I woke up and heard that my city had been hit,” he said. “You hear about fighting in Tigray, and it feels far away. But when you hear about explosions in Addis Ababa, you start asking yourself what will happen next.” Diplomatic sources said explosions were heard in several parts of the capital, including near the headquarters of Ethiopia’s military. Reuters separately reported that a source linked to an opposition alliance claimed the group had carried out drone strikes in Addis Ababa, including against military facilities. The claim could not be independently verified. For Abel, the economic consequences are as concerning as the fighting itself. “If the war becomes bigger, ordinary people will suffer,” he said. Bisrat, a college student in Addis Ababa, said the overnight explosions had reinforced his fear that Ethiopia could be entering a much wider conflict. “If Ethiopia goes into a full-scale war, ordinary people will suffer,” he said. “I fear seeing another Sudan.” Sudan has been engulfed in war since April 2023, when fighting broke out between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, displacing millions and creating a major humanitarian crisis. The current fighting also involves a wider set of actors than the Tigray war that ended in 2022. The TPLF is part of a broader opposition alliance that includes armed groups from several parts of the country. Fighting has also spread into Afar, while relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea have sharply deteriorated. Ethiopian officials have accused Eritrea of interfering in Ethiopia’s internal affairs and supporting forces opposed to the federal government. Eritrea has rejected the accusations. On Thursday, Ethiopia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced the closure of its embassy in Asmara and declared 10 Eritrean diplomats persona non grata, saying they had been involved in activities that posed a threat to Ethiopia’s national security. Eritrea subsequently announced that it was severing diplomatic relations with Ethiopia. The diplomatic rupture has added to concerns that the renewed fighting could acquire a wider regional dimension. In Mekelle, residents were left trying to understand what comes next after the TPLF withdrawal.

events.title: Auction clearance rate sinks to three-month low as property market slows
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Auction clearance rate sinks to three-month low of 48pc as property market slows The traditional spring selling boom is off to a poor start. ( ABC News: Kate Ainsworth ) Property sales for the spring season are off to a weak start. It comes off the back of two long weekends in major capital cities and the RBA lifting the cash rate again last week. Some economists predict capital city property prices could fall 10-15 per cent from peak to trough. Australia's auction clearance rate has slumped to a three-month low, while new data shows the number of unsold homes has surged by more than 20 per cent in the past year. Less than half the auctions that occurred across the country last week resulted in a successful sale. The preliminary clearance rate in the past week fell to 48.2 per cent, its lowest since late June (47.4 per cent) and the second-lowest preliminary reading for the year so far. It has also been hovering at or below the 50 per cent mark for several months, coinciding with a steep decline in property prices and weak sentiment in the housing market. In the past week, 1,223 auctions were held in the nation's capital cities. So there were 12.8 per cent fewer auctions than the previous week. It was also a significant 47.5 per cent drop from a year ago, according to new data from property research firm Cotality. Less than half the homes that hit the market and went to auction sold in the last week, Cotality data shows. ( Supplied: Cotality ) Sharp fall in number of auctions held Tim Lawless, Cotality's research director, said the weak result came off the back of long weekends in some states and the Reserve Bank's decision to lift interest rates for a fourth time this year. It also comes after changes in this year's federal budget that sent shock waves through the property sector , including heavily restricted negative gearing, and in many cases higher capital gains tax for sellers. Preliminary clearance rates across the major capitals last week compared with previous years. ( Supplied: Cotality ) Sydney and Melbourne "have been a drag on the national result", Mr Lawless said. In Sydney, 304 auctions were held in the past week, down 61 per cent to the week before. It was also a 38.5 per cent drop compared to a year ago. There were 670 auctions held in Melbourne. That was a 136 per cent jump compared to the previous week when the city was having the AFL grand final long weekend. But in the past 12 months, the number of auctions held in Melbourne has dropped 45.6 per cent, the largest decline of any capital city. Tim Lawless says clearance rates have hit a three-month low. ( ABC News: Jessica Ross ) Property taking up to six months to sell Another real estate analysis firm, SQM Research, also released new data, showing some homes were sitting unsold on the market for as long as six months. Homes that sat unsold for more than 180 days were clogging the market, with 10.5 per cent more older listings compared to a year ago. Old housing stock is clogging the market. ( Supplied: SQM Research ) Spring's traditional selling boom has ground to a halt so far this season, with the number of unsold homes across the country totalling 276,000 — a 21.6 per cent annual increase. "The bulk of the increase is property that has been on the market for one to six months and hasn't sold," SQM research director Louis Christopher said. "In Sydney, fewer vendors are listing than a year ago, yet total stock is up almost a fifth. That's a demand problem, not a supply surge." The housing market is slumping and experts warn more falls are to come. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) Brisbane and Adelaide have had the largest increase in the number of properties available for sale, up 43.5 and 39.5 per cent respectively, according to SQM's data. Melbourne, meanwhile, had 30.3 per cent more homes up for sale than it did a year ago. Perth's figure was up 21.3 per cent, while Canberra's was up 17.8 per cent. SQM's figures also showed there were 4,872 distressed sales across Australia in September, which was a 29 per cent jump compared to the same period last year. It follows the ABC reporting last week that Australian housing values had dropped for a sixth straight month, with many economists warning there will be further price falls ahead. Mr Lawless said Australian households were "deeply pessimistic" about the cost of living crisis, interest recent hikes and the budget's changes to property taxes creating "less favourable conditions". "Homes are taking longer to sell, auction clearance rates have held below average and advertised stock levels have risen across many markets," he said.

events.title: Marc Elias’ Democracy Docket sees Trump 2.0 success
events.summary: The News One of the Democratic Party’s most prolific lawyers also is becoming one of its most prolific posters. Marc Elias has argued dozens of cases around mail-in balloting and election access across the country and in front of the Supreme Court over the last decade. But he has also moonlighted as an election law content creator and advisor for Democracy Docket, a digital media company he founded in 2020 to focus on redistricting, gerrymandering, and voting access. What began as a hobby to help explain complex redistricting cases more effectively has grown into a serious media operation. Last month, Democracy Docket surpassed 500,000 free email subscribers, the company first told Semafor, including 70,000 subscribers paying $10 a month or $120 per year. The company also has a YouTube channel with more than 800,000 subscribers, a following that has grown significantly in recent months (the account has added half a million subscribers on the platform since January 2025). “In this era where so many political disputes, so many public controversies really wind up in court, and oftentimes the court arguments frame the public debate — I think lawyers have an obligation to speak directly and plainly in language that everyone, non-lawyers and lawyers alike, can understand,” he said. “That is something I’ve tried to do, particularly in the area of voting and elections, but really more broadly, in the area of democracy.” Elias told Semafor that he founded the outlet for a fairly prosaic reason: He’d maxed out the number of people he could send emails to on a private email listserv that he’d previously used to send election and redistricting law updates to a few hundred Democratic policymakers, executives, and officials across the country. The timing turned out to be convenient: COVID-19 lockdowns prompted a wave of court cases around mail-in balloting, an issue which Elias knew well and was, at times, directly involved in. Democracy Docket began posting public legal documents before many news outlets, gaining email subscribers and direct online traffic through Twitter and Facebook. Elias told Semafor that his readership is a mix of DC insiders, #Resistance liberals who watch Elias’ interviews on MS NOW, and legal and political professionals interested in keeping up with the ins and outs of election laws and voting access issues. While Elias told Semafor he dedicates just a few days a month to the management side, he acknowledged Democracy Docket has become a profitable enterprise. Asked how much money the company brought in each year, Elias declined to elaborate but said that the vast majority of the company’s revenue came from basic subscriptions, with a small but growing VIP tier of supporters paying $500 a year. Those projections would likely put the company in the ballpark of $9 million to $11 million in annual revenue. Max’s view Democracy Docket is part of a wave of new digital news outlets founded in the Trump era that have surged during the Republican president’s second term. While liberal and left-of-center audiences channeled their interest (and horror) with Trump during his first term by tuning into MSNBC, CNN, The New York Times, and The Washington Post, this go around, shares of those audiences have seemed to abandon traditional outlets for more ideological new media outlets positioned against traditional media. Outlets like Zeteo, The Bulwark, Crooked Media, and More Perfect Union have added millions of readers, listeners, and YouTube subscribers, even as cable news viewership continues to slide. Some of the movement appears to be ideological: Elias told me that some of the best days of membership for the site have come in the wake of blow-ups at major news outlets like CBS News, which he argues shows viewers were upset with what they saw as media owners’ capitulation to Donald Trump. But perhaps more interesting, Democracy Docket’s real innovation is in the continued erosion of the wall between real political players and the media that cover them. The proximity between Elias’ legal work and journalistic output is likely a bit too close for those who prefer a more traditional separation of church and state, though Elias insists that he’s fairly hands-off when it comes to the newsroom’s coverage. He said that he has occasionally disagreed with Democracy Docket’s stories and opinions. “Sometimes you’ll see they report it one way and then I write an opinion piece and I don’t correct them in my opinion piece, I just like say ‘this is what I think about the case, and if you want to know what I think the outcome of the case is, you know, become a premium member,’” he said. Notable Older outlets like the Guardian and The Atlantic have similarly benefited from increased left-of-center interest by explicitly positioning themselves as checks on the current administration — and even on some of their less-aggressive peers.

events.title: CEO’s podcast sparks tensions atop The Atlantic
events.summary: The Scoop Atlantic CEO Nicholas Thompson was talking about the media business on Vox’s podcast last month when host Peter Kafka asked him: How was the magazine’s editor-in-chief, Jeffrey Goldberg, feeling about the growing success of Thompson’s personal podcast? “We make a lot of money on the stuff I do,” he said. “Jeff likes when we make money.” Thompson’s response ricocheted around The Atlantic’s newsroom. Thompson’s podcast, , has emerged as a source of tension between the magazine’s business and editorial teams. Journalists have complained that the lucrative and high-profile show is not subject to The Atlantic’s editorial rules, input, or oversight — yet a casual listener could easily take it for an Atlantic editorial product. Thompson’s show is made by the magazine’s business side, and — like any number of contemporary podcasts — features interviews with technologists and business leaders, interspersed with sponsored content. When the podcast launched in 2024, the newsroom raised no objections; The Atlantic has featured a robust paid content arm for years through its creative marketing studio and custom events business. But as the show’s profile has risen in recent months, the podcast has caused increasing consternation internally. Thompson, despite his commercial role, is a well-known former tech reporter and former editor-in-chief of Wired. Last year, when he published a well-received memoir of his family and time as an elite long-distance runner, The Atlantic ran an excerpt . On , he has booked and interviewed top-tier guests, including OpenAI founder Sam Altman — leading staff to complain that the CEO’s bookings are, intentionally or not, undercutting the newsroom’s own efforts. According to four people familiar with the situation, the podcast has been a particular source of friction between Thompson and Goldberg. Goldberg, who also has a close relationship with Atlantic owner Laurene Powell Jobs, does not report to the CEO and instead reports directly to the Atlantic’s board of directors. (Goldberg had formally reported to Thompson’s predecessor, Bob Cohn.) Dissolving Lines The traditional separation between news outlets’ editorial and business halves has been facing pressure from both sides of that line. Axel Springer CEO Mathias Dopfner’s podcast has drawn world leaders, cultural figures, and executives. Axios CEO Jim VandeHei regularly writes columns and occasionally breaks news on the company’s site, in addition to steering its business. The growth of independent media in the Substack era has also created a generation of journalists who run both the business and editorial arms of their own small media outlets. In this media environment, Thompson’s sponsored podcast is hardly an outlier. But it’s the latest instance in which Thompson’s attempts to nudge the newsroom on the business side have run up against a more skeptical and traditionalist editorial staff. Deepening the tension are differing views about the substance of the AI story. Thompson inked a content-licensing deal between The Atlantic and OpenAI in 2024, angering newsroom staffers, some of whom view the frontier AI labs as having stolen journalists’ work for training. The publication’s editorial union publicly expressed skepticism of the deal and the publication’s policies around AI. The magazine’s tech editor published an op-ed saying publishers like The Atlantic were making a “ devil’s bargain .” In an August 2024 letter first reported by Semafor, editorial staff said OpenAI was hallucinating Atlantic stories and linking to aggregation of the publication’s reporting. And while The Atlantic has published largely skeptical coverage of major AI companies and their products’ impact on society, Thompson’s tone, in his podcasts and LinkedIn posts, has been more optimistic. The View From The Atlantic The Atlantic declined to comment. But one senior company source stressed that there are clear disclaimers demarcating content made by the business side of the company, even if the content itself can feel journalistic in tone — perhaps unsurprising in the case of , as Thompson is a former journalist. Max’s view The Atlantic is one of the clear media success stories of the second Trump term, fueled by Signalgate and other critical reporting and commentary on the Trump administration, a successful events business, and shrewd moves to capitalize on the public stumbles of its DC neighbor, The Washington Post. The 168-year-old magazine’s breakout journalism, its digital success, and a bit of good timing have given both Goldberg and Thompson plenty to brag about on the media podcast circuit. But strains at the top of the organization over its brand and direction reflect many premium news outlets’ dilemmas about survival and profit in a post-traffic, AI-ascendant media age. Marketers have infinite options for buying ads, meaning publishers no longer have the leverage they did when they controlled much of their own distribution. Meanwhile, independent journalists are developing direct relationships with advertisers and marketers, creating more fluidity between the editorial and business sides of their brands. Still, the old boundaries existed for a reason. Fragmentation has allowed many powerful figures to get their message across by circumventing traditional media outlets whose questions many CEOs and politicians don’t want to answer. It’s not surprising that Altman was willing to sit down with The Atlantic’s CEO on a sponsored business-side podcast, but not with the magazine’s tech journalists. Room for Disagreement Readers and audiences understand that when someone runs or owns a news outlet, they have the right to make it publish their opinions and thoughts, Kafka told Thompson. “It’s not against the law, but it’s also a little creepy.”

events.title: AI nonprofit will spend $10 million on journalism
events.summary: The Scoop A Silicon Valley nonprofit close to the AI safety movement is pledging $10 million by the end of 2027 to fund mainstream and independent coverage of artificial intelligence. The Tarbell Center for AI Journalism plans to announce that it is launching an institutional grantmaking fund, which executive director Cillian Crosson said will provide grants to newsrooms and other ambitious AI reporting projects. The first recipient of the grant is , NPR’s new video podcast from former hosts Kevin Roose and Casey Newton, which is receiving a $480,000 grant from the organization. Tarbell is also separately backing NPR’s “Power and Influence” desk, giving the public media outlet $250,000 to help expand its coverage of how AI intersects with politics, money, and power. “We think that having resources at newsrooms is an important part of ensuring strong coverage,” Crosson told Semafor. The new fund will “increase our support but it also allows us to more easily support a more diverse range of perspectives.” The organization, which is backed by groups including the deep-pocketed nonprofit Coefficient Giving , said it plans to fund investigative teams, AI verticals at national outlets, and other large-scale initiatives in new and legacy media. In particular, the organization is focused on expanding reporting and on frontier companies and the ways that AI companies and aligned political action groups are influencing American politics and tech regulations. It’s a significant expansion from the organization’s previous commitments, which have totaled $400,000 over four years. Tarbell’s previous grants focused on backing early-career journalists inside established newsrooms, offering media organizations reporting grants ranging from $1,000 to $20,000 to work on individual stories on AI. With increased monetary backing, the organization said it planned to issue grants between $50,000 and $500,000, but could make multimillion-dollar grants for the right projects. Funding and AI safety In recent years, Tarbell fellows have fanned out across several major news outlets, breaking stories that have often exposed reckless or aggressive actions by AI companies and frontier labs. Though Tarbell offers funding with no formal strings attached, it has drawn criticism from some in the AI industry and on the political right who see it as fueling what they view as exaggerated safety concerns. The subjects of some of Tarbell’s journalism, including OpenAI, have complained about the reporting and financial support from some organizations aligned with effective altruism, a loose philosophical movement whose concerns include an AI-driven apocalypse. As Semafor previously reported , cash-strapped news organizations have balanced concerns about optics of outside groups funding journalism with the much-needed financial support and aggressive journalists who have broken legitimate stories about AI and safety concerns. Semafor has not found instances where Tarbell interfered directly in any stories, and the organization is quick to point out that not all of the projects it backs are AI skeptics or strong AI safety proponents. In a telephone interview last week, Crosson reminded Semafor that the organization has two editorial firewalls: One between itself and its backers, and another between Tarbell and the media organizations it supports. It discloses its donors over $10,000, its fellows maintain complete autonomy over their reporting, and the organization asks news outlets it partners with to disclose when it has provided funding to support a journalist or project. In an interview with Semafor, Roose noted that Newton had worked with Tarbell at Platformer in recent years, and found the organization to be a strong supporter of independent journalism, and did not interfere or insert itself into any editorial content. “Their funding has been very useful in helping us get started,” Roose said. “It was a way for us to de-risk going out on our own. We’re feeling quite good about it and we’re grateful.”

events.title: Trump tells South Korea to sign on to Alaska LNG deal or 'I'll just charge them more'
events.summary: Trump said if South Korea does not sign on to the $50 billion Alaska LNG project he will charge them more or "double it up," without specifying what would be doubled. South Korea has said it is still assessing the Alaska project, with participation dependent on commercial viability and compliance with domestic legal procedures. Trump also announced an $8.4 billion oil recovery project that South Korean local media reported was not part of the countries’ agreement, citing Seoul’s industry ministry. U.S. President Donald Trump said he "didn't jump the gun" in announcing South Korea's participation in a $50 billion Alaska LNG project, warning Seoul could pay "double" if it does not sign on soon. His remarks come amid a discrepancy between Washington and Seoul over South Korea's planned energy and infrastructure investments in the U.S., with Trump announcing projects that Seoul has said are not yet finalized. "If they don't want to do it, that's OK with me. I'll just charge them more," Trump told reporters Friday, according to the White House. "Tell them if they don't sign shortly, I'm going to double it up." Trump did not specify what would be doubled. South Korean local media, though, raised the possibility that he was referring to higher tariffs on the country. When asked whether he had prematurely announced South Korea's involvement in the Alaska LNG project, Trump said he "didn't jump the gun." Trump's remarks come after South Korea said it was still assessing the Alaska LNG project, with any participation dependent on its commercial viability and compliance with domestic legal procedures. Separately, Trump said on Truth Social Friday that South Korea's investment deal "keeps getting BETTER," announcing an additional $8.4 billion enhanced oil recovery project. Enhanced oil recovery uses techniques such as carbon dioxide injection to increase the amount of crude oil produced from an oil field. South Korean local media further reported that the oil recovery project was not included in the agreements reached between Seoul and Washington, citing the country's industry ministry. The ministry was seeking to verify Trump's announcement and had contacted the U.S. through trade channels for clarification, according to the report.

events.title: Four African leaders issue joint declaration as Ethiopia war escalates
events.summary: Egyptian, Eritrean, Somali and Sudanese leaders also call for talks to end the civil war in Sudan. Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan have called for political and peaceful solutions amid escalating conflicts across the region, including Sudan’s civil war and major fighting in Ethiopia. The leaders of the four countries – Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki, Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Sudanese army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan – issued a joint declaration on Sunday following a meeting in New Alamein City in Egypt. list 1 of 2 Ethiopia’s government forces retake airport from Tigray rebels in Mekelle list 2 of 2 Ethiopian government forces seize Tigray capital Mekelle as rebels withdraw Ethiopia has accused Egypt, Eritrea and Sudan of backing the armed alliance fighting its government. Officials from all three countries have denied involvement. Earlier on Sunday, el-Sisi said that cross-border challenges required “a dialogue, not confrontation”. The joint declaration appeared to push back against several policies pursued by Ethiopia in recent years, highlighting widening rifts between Addis Ababa and its neighbours. The declaration backed Sudan’s military-led government and called for a political process led by Sudanese parties. Sudan has been at war since April 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). Sudan and Ethiopia have traded accusations of interference in Sudan’s civil war. The declaration also said control of the Red Sea should remain with the coastal states, seemingly in response to landlocked Ethiopia’s pursuit of sovereign access to the sea and a naval presence. Somalia’s Mohamud told Al Jazeera on Saturday that Mogadishu does not object to Ethiopia securing commercial access through Somali ports, provided it is agreed with Somalia. Egypt and Sudan, which have long disputed Ethiopia’s Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Nile, warned against what they called “unilateral measures” that harm downstream states. The joint declaration was issued as fighting escalated in Ethiopia between federal forces and a seven-group armed alliance, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which fought a brutal two-year war with the government that ended with a fragile peace deal in 2022. Government and allied forces retook the city of Mekelle on Sunday after the TPLF said it “temporarily moved out of” Tigray’s regional capital to “operate from somewhere else”. According to Ethiopian state media reports, former Tigray interim leader Abraham Belay said on Sunday that the federal government is preparing a new temporary administration for the region and hopes to hold regional elections within months. Ethiopian officials have accused neighbouring Eritrea of directly backing the rebel alliance in Ethiopia’s civil war. Eritrea’s Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel said in a post on X on Sunday that Addis Ababa was trying to create a pretext for attacking Eritrea.
