events.title: The job interview question you don't have to answer
events.summary: Prepare all you like, but there is often still one job interview question that leaves you feeling uncomfortable. While employers in the UK are within their rights to ask you how much you get paid in your current role, applicants are not obliged to tell them. Recruiters have been encouraged to stop posing questions about salary history and, in the EU, new rules will prevent them doing so. But in the UK, there is still a chance of it coming up, so how best should you answer? When interviewing or deciding on new staff, employers must not discriminate against an applicant based on so-called protected characteristics, including age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation. Sometimes it feels like interviewers, and interviewees, tip-toe around the subject of money. But Louise Rudd, a senior adviser at the workplace advice and conciliation service Acas, says there are no regulations that prevent employers from asking interviewees about their current salary, or their salary expectations. She says employers, if they do want to know, should ask each applicant the same questions to ensure they are treated fairly. A few years ago, a campaign was launched urging employers to stop asking new recruits how much they were paid in their previous jobs. It had its own hashtag - #EndSalaryHistory. The Fawcett Society, which campaigns for women and gender equality, said that asking the question risked maintaining historic unfair differences in pay due to gender, race and disability inequality. Rather than offering a salary based on skills, experience and performance, it meant employers rewarded an individual's perceived worth and negotiating skills instead, the society said. The Recruitment and Employment Confederation supported the move, urging recruiters not to ask. Employers in the EU will be banned from asking about salary history in new rules being rolled out across the bloc. But that's not featured in Cabinet Office plans in the UK, which instead concentrates on telling employers to publish salary information in job adverts . When you're going for a new job, you can reveal your current salary if you are happy to. Some people asked by BBC News out and about in London suggested they would reply with an inflated salary - so they get paid more in the next job. However, the risks of lying in an interview can far outweigh the possible reward. There are no requirements for you to disclose your salary if you don't want to. Rudd says some people might prefer to give their salary expectations, or outline their understanding of the salary range for the role. Recruitment firms often say applicants could instead focus on their skills and experience, so those are used as a measure of what they should be paid, not their salary history. Shazia Ejaz, director of campaigns at the Recruitment and Employment Confederation, says jobseekers should approach questions about pay with "realism but also confidence". "Candidates can focus on showcasing the value they bring, the benefits that matter most to them and to go to the interview knowing the market rate for the role," she says. "Jobseekers who have done their homework on salaries and can explain the contribution they will make are in the strongest position to secure the right package." What was your worst job interview? events.title: Manchester City must be relegated, says Canada’s ex-Leeds manager
events.summary: Jesse Marsch alleges Man City’s financial wrongdoing was widely known in the Premier League, and relegation must follow. Canada coach Jesse Marsch has ‌called for Manchester City to be punished severely over breaches of Premier League ⁠financial rules, saying his ⁠experience managing against the club left him convinced there were inconsistencies in the way it operated. City were found guilty of serious breaches of the Premier League’s ⁠financial rules over nine seasons from 2009-10 to 2017-18, with the league alleging the club used “sham” commercial contracts to inflate revenue and understate costs by more than 900 million pounds ($1.19bn). list 1 of 3 FC Barcelona accused of corruption in Negreira case: All you need to know list 2 of 3 Amid teen triumph and organisational chaos, Asian Games close in Japan list 3 of 3 Ireland refuse handshake with Israel and don armbands in Nations League tie The club has denied wrongdoing, saying the verdict contained material errors of law, principle and fact, and filed an appeal on Thursday against the independent commission’s ruling. Marsch, who managed Leeds United from 2022 to 2023, said the disparity between the clubs had been apparent to him during his time ‌in England. “I think Man City should be punished severely. I think they should have to go down, and by the way, everyone knew about it. Everyone knew,” Marsch told The Guardian in an interview published on Sunday. Marsch also pointed to the 2022 summer transfer window, when Leeds sold Raphinha to Barcelona and Kalvin Phillips to City, while both clubs reported making money. “That summer [2022], us and Man City were the only teams that said ⁠we made money,” he said. “For us, we did make money, because we ⁠sold Raphinha, we sold Kalvin Phillips. We had a lot left over from what we bought. “At the time, we weren’t in a position financially to not save. Our ownership didn’t have deep pockets. Whereas when ⁠Man City says this, I was literally like, ‘Are you kidding me? Is this some kind of joke?'” The American coach was also sceptical about ⁠City’s signing of Erling Haaland from Borussia Dortmund that summer. “When ⁠they said they got Erling Haaland for 52 million pounds ($69m), it’s like, ‘Yeah, OK, sure!’ So, I knew there were inconsistencies in it, but what can you do? You just put your arms in the air and go, ‘This is football’,” Marsch said. City’s appeal will be heard privately by an independent three-member board, with the club fully denying all charges. Potential sanctions include fines, points deductions and other sporting penalties, with relegation or ‌the ‌removal of titles also discussed as possible outcomes. It remains unclear whether any sanctions would be imposed before the appeal is decided.

events.title: Air Force removes all bombers from British base and redeploys them to the U.S. after a planned terror attack linked to Iran was foiled
events.summary: The U.S. Air Force has brought home its bombers stationed at a U.S.-run military air base in England used to strike Iran following an investigation into a planned terror attack at the RAF Fairford base. The bombers were redeployed to their home bases in the United States, according to a Pentagon official who was not authorized to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke Sunday on condition of anonymity. Aviation watchers such as the Military Air Tracking Alliance have observed dozens of B-52 and B-1 bombers operating out of RAF Fairford since the opening days of the Iran war. Observers noticed a host of B-1 bombers fly out of the base on Sunday. The move comes as President Donald Trump weighs options for his war on Iran — including new strikes — despite his initial promises to Americans that the campaign would  last a matter of weeks . “We have decisions that I’ll make about Iran. Iran’s been decimated. So the only question is — it’ll either be the easy way, or the hard way,” Trump told reporters on Saturday as he left the White House for a rally in Ohio. A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack, following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September. In total, six people have been taken into custody and then  released on bail  during the investigation. British authorities have  linked the incident to Tehran . Iran has denied involvement, but it has previously said it considers any base used to attack its territory  a legitimate target . U.K. officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arson and other attacks in Britain and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the U.K. if conflicts in the Middle East continue. RAF Fairford, located 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East. The U.S. military still  maintains a sizable presence  in the Middle East. On Thursday, a U.S. official said the recently deployed USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier, as well as the USS Malkin Island amphibious readiness group — a group of ships that together carry over 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines — are heading for the region. The official said the move could result in three carriers in the region as early as the end of October. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Cristiano Ronaldo can return to Portugal team if he wants, says Jesus
events.summary: Ex-Manchester United and Real Madrid star Cristiano Ronaldo left the Portugal squad on Wednesday, but the door is open for his return. Portugal superstar Cristiano Ronaldo can return to the squad if he wishes, despite walking out on his teammates, national team coach Jorge Jesus said on Sunday. The Portuguese showed they did not need the former Manchester United and Real Madrid forward as they became the first side to qualify for the quarterfinals of the 2026-27 UEFA Nations League with a 2-1 comeback win against Norway. list 1 of 4 Ronaldo-less Portugal beat Norway 2-1 to reach Nations League quarterfinals list 2 of 4 Fernandes calls Ronaldo and denies Portugal rift ahead of Norway game list 3 of 4 Portugal coach responds after Ronaldo leaves camp list 4 of 4 Why did Ronaldo leave Portugal’s training camp, and will he play again? Goncalo Ramos secured the victory for his side in the 86th minute after Joao Cancelo’s powerful finish had levelled Kristoffer Ajer’s stunning opener from outside the penalty area for World Cup quarterfinalists Norway. After the game, Jesus said he was prepared to allow 41-year-old Ronaldo to return to the national team but that it would have to be the player’s decision. “For me, Cris, in the next call-up, if he’s playing at Al-Nassr, he’ll be a player who can be called up,” Jesus told reporters, referring to Ronaldo’s Saudi club side. “If he wants to, he’ll return to the national team.” The coach said he would speak with Ronaldo if he wished before Portugal’s next matches in November. “If he wants to, as we did before this call-up, we talked before the call-up; we can talk before the next call-up,” continued Jesus. “But Cris is the one who’s going to decide.” Ronaldo walked out of the national-team camp on Wednesday after a dispute over his selection by Jesus, leaving his international future in doubt. Portugal’s leading goalscorer and most-capped player, Ronaldo was substituted in the Nations League opener against Wales on September 24. He was then an unused substitute in the 2-1 victory in Norway on September 27. When he was informed he would again be named on the bench for the match in Denmark, Ronaldo took a private flight back to Saudi Arabia. Portugal went on to win 4-2 in Denmark on Thursday, while rumours swirled about Ronaldo’s departure and whether he would play for the national team again. Ronaldo’s international teammate, Bruno Fernandes, spoke to the media on Saturday in the buildup to the return match against Norway in an attempt to settle a growing furore in Portugal about the matter. “He has a reserved place not only among the best of all time, but also in the hearts of all Portuguese people, and the most important thing is that we stop dividing things,” Fernandes said. “There are no divisions in the national team. It is one and will remain so, despite any noise that may come from outside… “We are outside of this controversy, but what I ask is that the country does not divide itself, does not make choices, that it respects all sides, but at the same time, Cris is and will be the biggest icon of our national team; he deserves everyone’s respect, regardless of who likes him more or [who likes him] less.” Jesus had said he would speak about Ronaldo after Sunday’s match with Norway, but added in the buildup to the game that the forward is a “symbol of Portugal”. The 72-year-old coach went on to say on Sunday that he had told Ronaldo he needed him in the squad for his first games at the helm after replacing Roberto Martinez following the 2026 World Cup. “Cristiano should end his time in the national team the way he wants; he’s the one who will decide how he wants it,” Jesus said. “That’s how we talked, the two of us – I said, ‘I need you’. In my first call-up, I said, ‘I need you, I need you to be close to me, playing or not playing, I need you’. And now I’m saying the same thing.” Ronaldo, who made his Portugal debut in 2003 at the age of 18, has said this will “probably” be his final year in football. The forward has been a fixture of the national team for more than two decades and has played at six World Cups. Portugal host Denmark in their next international on November 14, before completing their Nations League group in Wales on November 17. Ronaldo’s longtime rival for the title of the world’s best player, Lionel Messi, will play his final match for Argentina in a friendly against Benin in Buenos Aires on Tuesday.

events.title: Japan’s population is shrinking at an accelerating rate, but the nationalist prime minister is making it harder for foreigners to live there
events.summary: New census data over the past week showed Japan’s population shrank more quickly than in the prior tally. Also last week, the government rolled out tougher rules for foreign nationals who want to live in Japan. While foreigners make up just 3.4% of Japan’s population, the share has increased to a record high and a political backlash has been building—even as the country also grapples with rapidly aging demographics and the need to find new workers to sustain economic growth. On Tuesday, the latest five-year population survey detailed how stark Japan’s situation is. As of October 2025, the total population, including foreign residents, was 22.9 million, down 2.5% from five years earlier. The prior census in 2020 showed a dip of 0.7%. The number of Japanese nationals revealed an even steeper decline of 3.5% to 119.1 million, following a 1.4% drop in the 2020 count. Meanwhile, foreign residents jumped 40% to a record high of 3.84 million, and permanent residents climbed 17% to 947,125. Like other wealthy economies in Asia, Japan’s birth rate has been below the replacement level of 2.1 children per woman for decades, and the population has been in steady decline since around 2008. At the same time, Japan is aging, and the percentage of people age 65 and older rose to 29.4% in 2025 from 28.5% in 2020. In fact, adult diapers have been outselling baby diapers since 2011. The country is scrambling to find ways to encourage people to have more kids. For example, Tokyo’s metropolitan government launched a dating app to bring more couples together. Tokyo also started a four-day workweek and partial leave policy for city workers to help those who are parents balance childcare and work. By contrast, policies have turned more hostile when it comes to foreigners. On Thursday, the Japanese government increased fees for permanent residency to $1,271 from $64 — a 2,000% jump that marks the largest increase in the country’s history. The cost for a five-year residence permit shot up to $475 from $38. Japan also imposed more detailed requirements on income for permanent residents, who must now earn a minimum of $36,428 per year. And for the first time, applicants for permanent residency will be evaluated based on their Japanese language skills as well as their grasp of rules and customs. On top of that, the government can revoke permanent residency for not meeting pension contribution obligations, failing to pay health insurance and taxes, and violating immigration law or the penal code. The changes come as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has ushered in a more nationalist, right-wing stance. On the global stage, that has meant taking a harder line against rivals like China and North Korea, while also bulking up Japan’s military. Domestically, the pivot has translated to a crackdown on immigration and even tourism, drawing criticism that Takaichi is encouraging xenophobia. In July, the government hiked some tourist visa prices by more than 400%.  In a post on X ahead of the government’s new residency rules, Takaichi said many permanent residents could not maintain independent livelihoods. “The government recognizes that, with the increasing number of foreign residents, there are citizens who feel anxiety and a sense of unfairness, and is addressing this by making ‘foreign policy’ more ‘orderly’ so that both citizens and foreigners can live safely and securely,” she wrote. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Strikes by North Sea oil workers could ‘severely disrupt’ UK fuel supplies
events.summary: Union says staff left with no choice but industrial action after breakdown in pay talks with Texas oil firm Apache A looming strike by oil workers in the North Sea could “severely disrupt” UK fuel supplies, the Unite union has said, adding that staff were left with no choice after a breakdown in pay talks with the Texas oil company Apache. The union said Apache workers had “emphatically” backed strike action after being given what it said was an unacceptable pay offer that amounted to a real-terms pay cut for many employees, at a time when the company was “raking in eye-watering profits”. Unite said the operator had also set deadlines for reaching an agreement over back pay and indicated payments could be withheld, “leaving workers potentially thousands of pounds out of pocket”. Apache said it had “engaged constructively throughout the pay discussions” and added that it had offered a 4% pay increase for staff, “whose earnings already place them among the highest earners in the UK and whose offshore rota averages 153 working days a year”. Strike action could begin later this month, according to the union, and could involve more than 160 Apache offshore workers, including electrical experts, production technicians and radio operators. Any action would affect the Forties and Beryl oilfields, and could lead to one of the critical North Sea platforms, known as Charlie, “being brought to a standstill”, Unite said. That could ultimately result in the entire Forties pipeline system in the North Sea – which is said to handle almost a third of the UK’s oil and gas – “going down”, the union said, adding that the disruption could also ripple out and affect other large North Sea operators. Unite blamed the potential disruption on Apache’s failure to reach a pay deal, saying the company’s behaviour could have “far-reaching consequences for workers, operators and consumers”. Consumers have already been grappling with rising fuel and gas prices because of the US-Israel war on Iran, which has been disrupting supplies of crude and refined oil products from the Gulf. On Friday, British motorists were dealt a fresh blow when it emerged that the average price of diesel had climbed to a record £2 a litre . At the same time it was announced that leaders of G7 nations would release up to 100m barrels of their emergency diesel and crude oil stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off supplies of US diesel. Commenting on the potential strike action, the Unite general secretary, Sharon Graham, said: “We will not tolerate unacceptable pay offers.” Stevie Davies, a Unite industrial officer, said any disruption to Apache’s platforms “would have a direct hit on the Forties pipeline and potentially severely affect the UK’s fuel supplies”. The Texas-based APA Corporation, which is the parent company behind Apache North Sea Production, reported $1.4bn (£1.1bn) in after-tax profits and $9.2bn in revenues for last year. “We believe our final offer to the union is fair and recognises the contribution of our offshore workforce, alongside the wider benefits in our total rewards package,” Apache said. “The proposed pay increase is also in line with that awarded to our non-unionised employees earlier this year.” Apache also said it had contingency plans in place, and that it did not expect any strike action to affect other producers and their ability to operate through the Forties pipeline system. The plans included keeping “experienced personnel” on key sites, and it said any reduction in pipeline pressure as a result of industrial action would be similar to what occurred during routine maintenance outages. “As a responsible operator, we are planning to maintain safe operations throughout any industrial action,” Apache added. Planned strikes by Neo Next offshore workers, organised by Unite, were called off this summer after they secured a deal that the union said lifted the pay package by more than £4,000. The deal was reached days before workers were due to start a series of strikes from 22 July. Ineos, which operates the Forties pipeline system, was contacted for comment.

events.title: Money stolen by scammers hijacking UK social media accounts rises 400%
events.summary: Many cases involve criminals using other people’s identities to sell fake event tickets to friends and family The total amount stolen by criminals who hack into people’s emails and social media accounts and then pretend to be them has risen by more than 400% in a year, official UK data shows. In many cases, the scammers are hijacking people’s accounts in order to use their identity to sell fake event tickets – such as to sold-out gigs – to unsuspecting friends and family. The total reported amount stolen via email and social media account hacking reached £6.3m in the 2025-26 financial year, compared with £1.2m in 2024-25, according to the Report Fraud service run by the City of London police, which holds national responsibility for economic crime. However, the true total may be much higher as many scam victims do not report the crime, often because they feel embarrassed, and sometimes because the individual amount of money involved was relatively small. The Guardian previously featured the case of a music fan whose Instagram account was targeted by hackers, who used her identity to advertise tickets to an Oasis gig and stole £1,400 from her friends. She said the hackers impersonated her so well that her friends and family genuinely thought they were speaking to her. Others have been scammed by fraudulent WhatsApp and text messages in which a criminal pretends to be their child or a relative who is in an emergency situation and urgently needs cash. This has been dubbed the “Hi mum” scam . Data from Santander has shown that among customers of the bank, fraudsters pretending to be someone’s son were the most successful at extracting cash, followed by daughters. Ch Supt Amanda Wolf, head of Report Fraud operations, said: “For most people, being hacked isn’t just a cyber issue – it’s personal. It can leave victims locked out of important accounts, worried about what information has been accessed, and concerned that criminals may use their identity to target others.” She added that what starts with one compromised account “can quickly impact family, friends and colleagues as fraudsters exploit trusted relationships to commit further fraud”. Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Report Fraud is launching an awareness campaign urging the public to protect their online accounts from hackers by switching to passkeys where they are available. events.title: Nicaragua says it will withdraw from Central American Parliament
events.summary: The country’s crackdown on human rights has left it increasingly isolated in Latin America. Nicaragua’s government has announced it will withdraw from the Central American Parliament, a key regional body, as President Daniel Ortega and his co-president and wife, Rosario Murillo, consolidate power. The Foreign Ministry announced on Saturday that it would exit the six-country parliament, established to help promote human rights and democracy in Central America. list 1 of 3 International body votes to convene emergency meeting over Nicaragua list 2 of 3 US says it will use regional body to isolate Nicaragua list 3 of 3 Why has Nicaragua taken Germany to the ICJ over Gaza genocide? The announcement comes shortly after Friday’s passage of a resolution at the Organization of American States (OAS), calling on Nicaragua to restore civil rights and release political prisoners. The Nicaraguan government, however, said Saturday’s action was “in the full exercise of its sovereignty”. The government said the decision would take effect immediately, the latest in a series of withdrawals from regional and international organisations the country has undertaken. The Ortega-Murillo government has accused such international groups of being vehicles for outside intervention . Nicaragua pulled out of the OAS in 2023 and the United Nations Human Rights Council (UNHCR) in 2025 over criticisms of the country’s human rights record, which has deteriorated during Ortega’s tenure. Ortega has been accused of using the state to target critics and dissidents , including through imprisonment, torture and exile. A UN report released in September found the government was responsible for at least eight deaths in custody since 2018, when Ortega began a sharp crackdown on protests and dissent. The report also detailed inconsistencies in the government’s account of in-custody deaths, including that of Indigenous Miskito leader Brooklyn Rivera. A critic of the Ortega government, Rivera was detained for 32 months with minimal contact with his family before dying in May. The government blamed his death on the effects of a previous case of COVID-19, an assessment the Physicians for Human Rights group called “not medically coherent”. “A State that resorts to enforced disappearance and allows persons to die in its custody falls short of the minimum human rights standards required for credible democratic governance,” said Jan-Michael Simon, the group’s chair. The administration of US President Donald Trump has also been vocal in denouncing the Nicaraguan government’s abuses, including Rivera’s death. In July, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio published a statement calling Nicaragua’s government a “dictatorship” after it announced it would abolish the country’s upcoming elections. He also framed the Ortega-Murillo government as a threat to US national security. “Ortega’s pledge to abolish elections in Nicaragua proves his cowardice and fear of the Nicaraguan people’s will,” Rubio wrote. But the Trump administration has come under criticism for seeking to deport Nicaraguan citizens who were expelled under Ortega’s leadership. Human Rights Watch recently warned that the Trump administration had detained eight Nicaraguan nationals for deportation, seven of whom were among 222 political prisoners flown into exile in the US in February 2023, during former President Joe Biden’s administration. Nicaragua subsequently stripped them of their citizenship and branded them as “traitors” to the country. The Ortega government also seized any property they had in the country. Human Rights Watch urged the Trump administration not to deport the eight detainees, warning that they could face abuse if they were returned to Nicaragua. Four of the detainees reportedly have pending asylum cases. “After offering refuge to these critics of the Nicaraguan government just three years ago, the United States is now detaining and threatening to deport them,” Juanita Goebertus, Americas director at Human Rights Watch, said in a statement. “International law prohibits the United States from returning anyone to face the threat of persecution or torture. US authorities should not be trying to send these men back into danger.”

events.summary: The abrupt redeployment to the US comes after several ‘terrorism-related’ arrests were made outside RAF Fairford. The United States has made the abrupt decision to withdraw its bombers from the Royal Air Force (RAF) base Fairford in the western part of the United Kingdom, citing concerns about a potential attack. Media reports emerged on Sunday that an urgent redeployment was under way, with B-1 bombers leaving RAF Fairford for the US. list 1 of 3 New aircraft carrier, 10,000 US troops: Is the Iran war about to escalate? list 2 of 3 Iran says Hormuz to remain closed until US meets conditions list 3 of 3 War on Iran: Is escalation more likely than a deal? Roughly a dozen such aircraft had been based at RAF Fairford prior to the sudden departure. “While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” a Pentagon spokesperson told Al Jazeera. “The Airmen that operate America’s bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities – including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States – anywhere, anytime,” the official added. It is unclear precisely what prompted the withdrawal, which comes as the US and Israel remain embroiled in a war against Iran. RAF Fairford has served as a stopping point for US bombers participating in the war, which began more than seven months ago, on February 28. But the base, located roughly 160km (100 miles) west of London, has been rumoured to be the target of a “terror” plot involving Iran. On September 27, UK authorities arrested five men on suspicion of plotting to plant explosives near the base. Iran has denied any such scheme, and the men were released without charge a day later. Investigators discovered petrol, but no explosive devices, in their vans. Still, officials in the UK say they remain under investigation. On Thursday, British police also announced they had arrested a 25-year-old UK-Iranian dual national in London on suspicion of plotting an attack against the airbase. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggested last week that “Iran played a part” in the alleged plot, though he declined to provide details. “The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry,” Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans said in a statement. “As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement.” US President Donald Trump responded to the initial arrests by accusing the men of seeking to do “big damage” to US facilities. He also praised UK authorities for their efforts. “The arrest in the UK was fantastic. Working with Britain – it was an amazing job. We had them under investigation,” Trump said of the suspects. “We had them under view for a long time, and we got them.” Iran, meanwhile, summoned the UK ambassador to Tehran over the last week in protest of the arrests. The US has a long history of stationing forces at RAF Fairford during its wars in the Middle East, stretching back to the Gulf War in the 1990s. RAF Fairford has been the site of antiwar protests in the past. During one instance, in 2003, five protesters broke into the airbase in an attempt to destroy military equipment slated to be used in the US invasion of Iraq. The UK has largely declined to participate in the ongoing war on Iran, despite pressure from the Trump administration. events.summary: Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito told CBS News he has "thought about" retiring after the high court's last term but decided against it. Alito, 76, is the second-oldest justice on the bench, and speculation had swirled that he would retire while Republicans control the Senate and the White House. The possibility that Democrats might flip the Senate after November's election could jeopardize a potential Supreme Court nomination by President Donald Trump. Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito has "thought about" retiring after the high court's last term but decided against it, believing he could still make "a valuable contribution," he said in an interview with CBS News . Alito, 76, is the second-oldest justice on the bench, and speculation had swirled that he would retire while Republicans control the Senate and the White House — when the chances of swiftly confirming a GOP-backed candidate to the bench would be high. The possibility that the Senate could flip to Democrats after November's midterm election may make confirmation of any potential nominee of President Donald Trump more difficult or impossible if Democrats control the Senate. "I've been bemused by the retirement speculation; it's not too pleasant to look up and see the vultures circling," Alito said in a separate interview with "Fox News Sunday." "I don't have a calculation for it ... I think it would be foolhardy to make a calculation [that] I'm going to serve for a certain number of additional years." Alito's status as one of the court's most conservative justices has sparked the speculation that he would retire ahead of the midterms — a decision the justice ultimately has not made. Should Democrats take control of the Senate, they would effectively have veto power over a Supreme Court nomination. Justice Clarence Thomas, 78 — the court's oldest justice and a member of its conservative bloc — has also been on retirement watch. The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the United States, AP reported, citing a Pentagon official who was not authorized to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke on condition of anonymity. Aviation watchers such as the Military Air Tracking Alliance and others have observed dozens of B-52 and B-1 bombers operating out of RAF Fairford since the opening days of the Iran war, AP said. These observers saw many B-1 bombers take off from the base on Sunday. A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack, following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September. In total, authorities took six individuals into custody and later released them on bail during the investigation. British authorities have linked the terror plot to Tehran, although Iran has denied involvement. RAF Fairford is located 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London and has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East. More tankers struck in the Middle East At least two vessels were struck over the weekend in waters near Oman and Iran , the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre reported, as Tehran reiterated its position on Sunday that the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen unless its conditions for ending the war with the U.S. are met. On Saturday, the UKMTO, a British maritime security alert service, said it received a report of a crude oil tanker being hit by an unknown projectile four nautical miles east of Oman. It said another tanker was reported as being similarly struck Sunday in the Strait of Hormuz, causing damage to its engine room. Attacks on shipping in the strait, through which about a fifth of the world's oil supplies moved before the start of the U.S. and Israel-led war on Feb. 28, have been happening on a regular basis for weeks. "The Strait of Hormuz will not open until Iran's seven conditions based on the Islamabad Memorandum are met, and Iran will not regulate its national security with tweets from American officials," Iranian state media agency Nour News quoted Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf as saying Sunday. President Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian signed an interim deal in June, known as the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, that resulted in a brief hiatus in fighting. Tehran's conditions for allowing ships to proceed freely through the Strait of Hormuz include a halt to U.S. "acts of aggression," an end to the U.S. naval blockade of its ports and economic warfare, and the release of Iranian assets. A key demand of the U.S. has been that Iran dismantle its nuclear weapons program. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure reportedly came under renewed attacks. Reuters reported Saturday that Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said they had targeted a facility owned by Saudi Arabian oil giant Aramco in the capital Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones. The group said the attack was in retaliation for Saudi attacks on Yemen's Sanaa and other provinces. A large plume of smoke and fire rose above the facility, Reuters quoted a witness as saying. Saudi authorities have not commented on the reported attack. Aramco did not immediately respond to CNBC's emailed request for comment. If confirmed, it would be the latest escalation in what has effectively become a second front in the Iran war. Some investors say they expect full-scale fighting to resume in the Middle East. "The situation is fluid and volatile. To me, as we are developing and looking at the situation, it's not a question of if, but when the conflict resumes full force," Bader Al-Saif, founding president of Al-Saif Consulting, told CNBC's Access Middle East show on Friday. The ongoing attacks and prospect of a further escalation have driven energy prices higher in recent weeks, raising inflation expectations globally and putting upward pressure on government borrowing costs . Reports that the U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier strike group to the Middle East, along with an amphibious force carrying 2,000 Marines, pushed crude oil prices higher on Thursday.

events.title: Cornell case puts New York’s progressive image at odds with its rape laws
events.summary: New York lawmakers will review sexual-assault laws, including the ‘voluntary intoxication’ rule at the heart of the Cornell case. Last month, a woman identified as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit against Cornell University, the fraternity Chi Phi and the seven fraternity members she accused of gang-raping her on the night of October 19, 2024. Her allegations have triggered a nationwide reckoning in the United States over the prevalence of sexual assault on college campuses. list 1 of 3 Cornell rape allegations renew push to change New York sexual assault law list 2 of 3 ‘I want the truth’: NY governor appoints prosecutor in Cornell rape case list 3 of 3 Cornell president vows transparency amid outrage over fraternity rape case But the case has also reignited efforts to reform laws in the state of New York. While the left-leaning state has long presented itself as a leader in women’s rights, advocates say sexual assault survivors still face pervasive legal barriers when they seek justice. Erica Vladimer, a lawyer and founding director of Harassment-Free New York, a survivor-led nonprofit, told Al Jazeera that much of the legislation currently in the spotlight is the culmination of years, if not decades, of work. “These are bills that we have been fighting for for years when sexual violence is not in the news,” Vladimer said. She drew a line between the #MeToo movement, which began in 2017 as an online campaign to denounce sexual misconduct, and the current wave of outrage following Doe’s allegations. “It speaks to the fact that the #MeToo movement is not dead. It is a movement, not a moment,” Vladimer said. Already, leaders in Albany, the state capital, have signalled they would take action following the Cornell case. On Wednesday, the New York Assembly announced it had formed a working group to examine the state’s sexual-assault laws and develop recommendations for the 2027 legislative session. Still, advocates say more concrete measures are needed to address the crisis. “I appreciate that this work is happening,” said Lindsey Boylan, a New York City Council candidate. “It doesn’t undo the fact that rape culture is pervasive in the United States and very much so alive and well in New York.” Boylan was the first woman to publicly accuse former New York Governor Andrew Cuomo of sexual harassment in another high-profile misconduct case, back in 2020. She is among those calling for greater reform. Here are some of the measures advocates are pushing state lawmakers to adopt or amend: The Cornell University case has brought renewed attention to New York’s “ voluntary intoxication ” statute, a legal loophole that can make it harder to prosecute sexual assault when a person has willingly consumed alcohol or drugs. New York Governor Kathy Hochul pledged on Friday to work with lawmakers to close the gap. “It should not matter whether they chose to use drugs or alcohol. Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang rape. Period,” Hochul said. Under the current state law, a person who voluntarily drinks or takes drugs is not considered “mentally incapacitated” during an assault, even if they become too intoxicated to consent. That can make it harder for prosecutors to bring a sex-crime charge. The law primarily recognises incapacitation in the context of sexual assault when a person was involuntarily intoxicated, unconscious or otherwise “physically helpless”. That distinction has become central to the Cornell case. Doe has acknowledged that she consumed substances before the alleged rape, saying that she was pressured into drinking alcohol and taking the dissociative drug ketamine. The Tompkins County district attorney initially declined to bring charges, pointing to the law’s stance on “voluntary intoxication”. But the investigation has since been reopened, amid public pressure. New York is one of 19 states in the US that distinguish between “voluntary” and “involuntary” intoxication when it comes to determining consent in sexual violence cases. But the Cornell case has spurred a push to remove the distinction from the law books. Critics have argued that sexual assault is no less grievous if a victim is drunk or has chosen to take drugs. “I mean, to have New York, a supposedly progressive state, penalise people who are sexually abused for drinking is disgusting,” Boylan told Al Jazeera. Vladimer, for her part, explained that distinguishing between “voluntary” and “involuntary” intoxication as a means for pursuing sexual assault cases shifts the focus onto the actions of victims, rather than perpetrators. “We essentially have codified victim-blaming by saying if you become voluntarily intoxicated and then are sexually assaulted, you essentially cannot seek justice in our court system,” Vladimer told Al Jazeera. In June, the New York state Senate unanimously passed a bill to allow sexual assault charges regardless of whether a victim is intoxicated voluntarily or involuntarily.

events.title: Ireland refuse handshake with Israel and don armbands in Nations League tie
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Republic of Ireland football players again wear black armbands and refuse handshakes with Israel in UEFA Nations League. Ireland players again wore black armbands in recognition of Palestinians killed in Gaza and bowed their heads during the Israeli national anthem before the teams’ second UEFA Nations League football match on Sunday. The League 3 Group B match ended in a 1-1 draw and, despite being played behind closed doors and on neutral ground, was once again played out in a confrontational manner. list 1 of 4 ‘Everyone knew’: Canada boss Marsch wants Man City relegated for breaches list 2 of 4 Cristiano Ronaldo can return to Portugal team if he wants, says Jesus list 3 of 4 Man City whistleblower Pinto says he ‘received death threats’ over leaks list 4 of 4 No handshakes and a delayed ceremony as India beat Pakistan at Asian Games Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher stepped in as captain for Dara O’Shea, who was excused to be with his wife for the birth of their child, and pointedly avoided shaking hands with Israel captain Dor Peretz, despite completing the usual pre-match formality with the referee and one of his assistants. Kelleher’s action was a repeat of O’Shea’s, who refused to shake Israel captain Manor Solomon’s hand before the first match in Debrecen, Hungary, last week. Ireland went on to win that game 3-0 through three first-half goals. Solomon was dropped to the bench for Sunday’s match in Backa Topola, Serbia. Israel forward Sayed Abu Farchi was back in the squad after serving a suspension for getting sent off following his gun-simulation goal celebration during Israel’s 3-1 defeat to Austria on September 25. Finn Azaz, whose mother has Israeli heritage, was among the Irish substitutes after playing from the start against Austria on Thursday. Troy Parrott’s penalty in the 39th minute, after a foul by Peretz on Jimmy Dunne, gave Ireland a 1-0 halftime lead. A disagreement also broke out on the sidelines as the players made their way off the field for the interval, although the referee quickly intervened. Peretz secured a point for Israel with a poked effort from close range in the 47th minute. Sunday’s game was initially supposed to be played in Dublin, but the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) moved it to a neutral venue for “operational reasons” in June following widespread calls for a boycott in protest of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. The FAI said the game would be played with no fans present. It followed the FAI’s motion the previous November calling on UEFA to ban Israel from club and international competitions. All the Irish players had been under pressure from home – where affinity with Palestinians is strong – to boycott the second match against Israel, though the pressure was greater during the first game. “I felt that pressure growing day by day, and it’s getting almost to a breaking limit now,” Ireland coach Heimir Hallgrimsson said at the time. Ultimately, only reserve goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu decided to skip both of the contentious games, saying in a statement that it was his “personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong”. More than 160 Irish sportspeople had signed an open letter urging the FAI to reconsider its decision to go ahead with the two games. Before the departure for Hungary, people protested outside the team hotel in Dublin for the players to boycott the matches. The SIPTU trade union displayed a huge poster in central Dublin beside the River Liffey asking the players to “Go with your conscience!” and “Don’t play with genocide” beside an image of a blood-splattered ball. Former Ireland coach Brian Kerr said the FAI had “lost the respect of the Irish people” for going ahead with the games. But the FAI argued UEFA could sanction the team. Ireland is cohosting the 2028 European Championship with England, Wales and Scotland. Protesters threw tennis balls with Palestinian flags onto the field during Ireland’s 2-2 draw with Austria on Thursday. A man with a Palestinian flag also tried running onto the field. On Saturday, an Israeli journalist stated during the pre-match news conference that the Irish players had called the Israeli players “monkeys” during last week’s game, leading to an immediate rebuke from Irish communications officer Kieran Crowley, who said it was “a lie” and ended the news conference. The players had only decided to go ahead with the fixtures after a dramatic day in Debrecen before the first match, when both the news conference and training were delayed for hours while they deliberated. They reportedly voted 14-8 in favour of continuing after Bazunu’s withdrawal that morning. Ireland’s national broadcaster RTÉ was only providing stripped-back coverage of both games against Israel to meet contractual obligations. There was no studio presentation, commentary on the international feed, or analysis.

events.title: Tom Cruise suffers one of the worst movie debuts of his career. Reviews were so bad Warner Bros. ran ‘decide for yourself’ ads
events.summary: On the cusp of the studio’s merger with Paramount , Warner Bros.’  “Digger”  flopped in its opening weekend, handing Tom Cruise one of the worst debuts of his career and serving as a bitter final note for Warner Bros. as a standalone studio. No. 1 in North American theaters instead went to Amazon MGM’s  “Verity,” extending the streak for Colleen Hoover adaptations at the box office. It debuted with $32.6 million. The film, directed by Michael Showalter, stars Dakota Johnson as a writer hired to ghostwrite a book series by an incapacitated author (Anne Hathaway). But all eyes were on how “Digger,” one of the year’s biggest gambles, would perform. Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s critically panned satire grossed a paltry $8 million domestically. Cruise is typically a big draw overseas, but international sales, $12 million from 74 markets, were also weak. After reviews so bad that Warner Bros. opted to run “decide for yourself” ads, estimates for “Digger” had been revised down over the past week. It’s a painfully rough start for a movie that cost at least $125 million to make. Reports have pegged the production budget closer to $150 million. The marketing spend is estimated at another $100 million. “Digger” had been positioned as a potential awards-season heavyweight, dated almost exactly the same as Warner Bros.’  “One Battle After Another”  was last year. “Digger” is a similarly politically charged release that handed a large budget to a top filmmaker working from an original story. But this big swing by Warner Bros. Motion Picture Group co-chairs Michael De Luca and Pam Abdy won’t pay off as well as “One Battle After Another.” It grossed $213.2 million worldwide and, more importantly,  won best picture at the Academy Awards. ‘Digger’ flops at a moment of Hollywood transformation The disappointing opening comes just as Paramount Skydance is closing its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery . After U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín on Wednesday  approved the $110 billion deal , Paramount said it would close the merger on Tuesday. In a flush year for Hollywood, Warner Bros. has failed to get one film to $100 million domestically, though its December release, “Dune: Part III,” will easily cross that. De Luca and Abdy are expected to depart Warner Bros. this week. Mass layoffs are anticipated to follow. “‘Digger’ collapsed this weekend and the new management of the combined Paramount and Warner Bros., David Ellison and Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg, will soon decide what kind of movies they want from WB,” wrote David A. Gross, a film consultant who publishes a newsletter on box office figures. “Paramount does not have a recent history of making big, auteur-driven films like this — that strategy appears to be over and out.” Critics (51% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes) slammed “Digger” as a strained climate change farce, though Cruise’s over-the-top performance was received more warmly. Audiences agreed, giving it a “C+” CinemaScore. Cruise has spent most of the last decade starring in “Mission: Impossible” movies and “Top Gun: Maverick,” both franchises that have allowed him to remain a top action hero into his 60s. The 64-year-old’s last major box-office disappointment was 2017’s “The Mummy,” which grossed $409.2 million worldwide on a $195 million budget. To help sell “Digger,” Cruise pulled out all the stops. He even granted his first lengthy magazine interview in years. ‘Avengers: Endgame’ retakes all-time crown Last weekend’s top film,  “Avengers Endgame: Encore,” slid to seventh place with $4.4 million domestically and $14.4 million overseas. But the Marvel re-release’s second week allowed “Endgame” to just nudge ahead of “Avatar” to reclaim the title of highest grossing film ever, not accounting for inflation. The two films have traded spots in recent years with re-releases. “Endgame” now tallies $2.9255 billion, while “Avatar” has $2.9237 billion. The rest of the top-sellers in cinemas over the weekend were holdovers: Zach Cregger’s video game adaptation  “Resident Evil”  for Sony Pictures; Lance Oppenheim’s A24 drama  “Primetime,”  with Robert Pattinson as “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen; and Paramount’s  “Heart of the Beast,”  starring Brad Pitt as a retired veteran who treks through the Alaskan wilderness with his combat dog after a plane crash. In its third week, “Resident Evil” came in second with $12.5 million. “Heart of the Beast” followed with $11 million. And “Primetime” collected $8 million in its second weekend. Top 10 movies by domestic box office With final domestic figures being released Monday, this list factors in the estimated ticket sales for Friday through Sunday at U.S. and Canadian theaters, according to Rentrak: 1. “Verity,” $32.6 million. 2. “Resident Evil,” $12.5 million. 3. “Heart of the Beast,” $11 million. 4. “Primetime,” $8 million. 5. “Digger,” $8 million. 6. “Forgotten Island,” $7.2 million. 7. “Avengers: Endgame: Encore,” $4.4 million. 8. “Drishyam: The Conclusion,” $2.7 million. 9. “Practical Magic 2,” $2.7 million. 10. “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” $2.5 million. events.title: Sam Altman said 'the world should accept some bad things happening' for the benefits of AI
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Decoded by POLITICO that he does not accept "the really catastrophic risks" of AI. Heather Diehl/Getty Images OpenAI's Sam Altman diverged from Anthropic's views, saying that we should embrace AI despite risks. Altman agrees with tougher AI regulations, but advocates for a "lighter touch." He believes people will do "orders of magnitude more good stuff than bad stuff" with AI. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said there was a fundamental difference in worldview between his company and rival Anthropic on artificial intelligence regulation, arguing in an exclusive interview with Decoded by POLITICO that the technology's benefits justify accepting some risks — and that AI should remain broadly accessible to the public. "I think there's a lot of daylight," Altman told Decoded co-author and POLITICO senior tech reporter Brendan Bordelon. Asked specifically where he diverges from Anthropic and its CEO Dario Amodei, Altman said, "we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency." Anthropic has long been viewed as the strongest proponent of AI regulations within the industry, a stance that until recently was at odds with the lighter touch approach favored by OpenAI. But the policy differences between the two leading AI firms have narrowed in recent months, with OpenAI coming out in favor of tougher rules as it grapples with high-profile hacking incidents and rogue behavior by its models. Altman agreed with Amodei's call last month to slow the development of the most advanced AI models. His company has followed Anthropic in endorsing new state laws that impose stricter safety requirements than what the ChatGPT maker had previously supported — a shift from its prior state strategy . And OpenAI lobbyists recently endorsed a bipartisan House proposal that would require top AI companies to embed outside safety evaluators. Despite the convergence, Altman tried to distinguish his firm's regulatory stance from Anthropic's. "I disagree, but I understand the perspective of people who are like, 'This technology is going to get so powerful, and it's so dangerous, that a single lab in San Francisco should have it and make sure nothing bad happens, and kind of figure out how to dole out the benefits,'" said Altman. But he called it "a completely unacceptable tradeoff" that runs counter to the "lighter touch regulatory stance" backed by OpenAI. "I wouldn't take a trade of saying like, 'We'll make sure there's no major hacks, there's no kind of like misuse of this technology, there's zero scams, there's zero all the other bad things that will happen," said Altman. "Because I think people will do tremendously — orders of magnitude more — good stuff than bad stuff." The OpenAI CEO later added that he does not accept "the really catastrophic risks," including the potential for "a serious loss of control to AI." The interview, appearing in Monday's debut edition of Decoded and its accompanying daily podcast, also delved into President Donald Trump's new AI accord with top tech firms and his attempted rebrand of AI to "super intelligence;" the rash of autonomous hacking incidents carried out by OpenAI models and whether the company should face legal liability; Altman's thoughts on AI industry money flowing into U.S. politics; the influence of effective altruists inside OpenAI; and his views on key political power players including French President Emmanuel Macron to California Gov. events.title: Tories to pledge to scrap Environment Agency and Natural England
events.summary: Shadow chancellor will also promise to scrap affordable homes regulations as part of strategy to refocus on growth The Conservatives will announce a bonfire of regulations including abolishing affordable homes and community funding rules as well as scrapping Natural England and the Environment Agency . The shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, will say the party intends to “streamline regulations” that protect nature and oblige developers to include affordable homes and community services such as GP surgeries, to speed up infrastructure and housebuilding. The announcements on Monday are a signal that the party intends to refocus on the economy, an area where it has made relatively little progress in the polls. Tory strategists believe there is a major opening to make gains against Reform and Labour, given the limited focus on growth from Andy Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey, at the Labour conference last week. The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch , published a new tract on Sunday called The Right Way, which she said would be the bedrock that underpinned the party’s policy development before the next election. Polls have the party still trailing third behind Labour and Reform UK. Introducing the document – inspired by Margaret Thatcher’s The Right Approach from 1976 – Badenoch said the Conservatives still expected to win the next election and needed to “hit the ground running … We will need to be ready from day one, having already shown people what kind of government we are going to be.” “Keir Starmer didn’t have a plan. That’s why he’s gone,” she said. “Andy Burnham doesn’t have one either and that is why I know the announcements he is making will all come to naught. We have to be different, different from Labour, and different from the party we were two years ago.” In a slew of announcements at the Conservative party conference on Monday, the Tories will pledge measures that they claim would cut the price of a new home by £50,0000, including scrapping net zero regulations on housebuilding, such as the Future Homes Standard, which requires all new homes in England to be zero-carbon ready. The party will promise to replace section 106 agreements and the community infrastructure levy that oblige developers to build a proportion of affordable housing and support school and health service demands locally. Instead, there will be a “one stop” levy on developers, Griffith will say. The party has also pledged to abolish Natural England and the Environment Agency, “moving to a more streamlined regulatory landscape to protect our environment”. Griffith will say in his first speech as shadow chancellor that the Tories would continue to back the expansion of Heathrow airport and leave the Aarhus convention, which makes it easier for community groups to oppose developments. Conservative shadow Treasury ministers will be tasked with finding new ways of simplifying tax for individuals and businesses, Griffith will say, calling the tax code “a cat’s cradle of complexity”. Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning In his speech, he will say: “No one else is coming to save our economy. Only we can inject reality, tell the hard truths and make this a country we are proud to hand on to the next generation. “Our task just got bigger. We face a prime minister that wants to return Britain to an imagined past. A socialist fever dream of the 1970s. Cheaper homes, lower taxes and less red tape. This will be the most ambitious deregulation project in a generation. We will be more prepared than ever before. We will set out our plans line by line. Every bill, every regulation, every chapter.” Griffith will say that the government must speed up the building of a Heathrow third runway in whatever way it can. “I refuse to accept for a single moment that the country of Brunel and Bazalgette, of the vaccine taskforce and the Mulberry harbours , has to sit around waiting until the 2040s to get a third runway built,” he will say. Burnham has recently expressed personal scepticism about the Heathrow third runway, saying he would take differing views seriously. The new shadow housing secretary, Katie Lam, will say the scrapping of housing regulations and of enforcement bodies would mean “anti-growth ideologues can never again hold our country hostage”. The party said Natural England and the Environment Agency were preventing too many homes being built and adding unnecessary costs to building. Both bodies would be scrapped, with their necessary functions brought directly into Defra.

events.title: 140 Years of Everyday Moments
events.summary: As DFI Retail Group marks its 140th anniversary, Group Chief Executive Scott Price says the company’s future will depend on fulfilling the needs of our customers, investing in innovation and continuing to earn trust in the everyday moments that define modern retail. A morning stop for breakfast before work. A coffee picked up between meetings. A grocery stop on the way home. A stop for health and beauty products. A weekend trip to choose furniture for a growing family. A rewards offer that helps make the weekly shop go further. These are ordinary moments in Hong Kong life. Yet for DFI Retail Group, they represent the foundation of a business that has grown with the city for 140 years. Founded in Hong Kong in 1886, DFI has evolved from a local enterprise into one of Asia’s leading retail groups, serving millions of customers every week through brands spanning food, convenience, health and beauty, home furnishings and loyalty rewards. For Scott Price, Group Chief Executive of DFI Retail Group, the anniversary is not only a milestone in the company’s history. It is also a reminder of the role retailers play in daily life, often in ways that consumers rarely stop to consider. “Retail is woven into people’s lives in ways that often go unnoticed,” Price says. “It is there in the everyday decisions people make for themselves and their families. When retailers do their job well, they make life a little easier, a little healthier and a little more convenient.” DFI is marking its 140th anniversary under the theme “140 Years of Everyday Moments”, a phrase Price says reflects both the Group’s history and its continuing purpose. While anniversaries are often viewed as opportunities to look back, DFI is using the milestone to recognise the customers, team members and communities that have shaped the business, and to focus on how retail must continue adapting to changing expectations. Price explains that few industries are as closely connected to the routines of everyday life as retail. Across DFI’s portfolio, customers encounter its brands at different moments and for different needs. From supermarkets such as Market Place to Mannings and Guardian for health, wellness and self-care products, to 7-11 for a snack or collectible, and to IKEA for homewares, Price says its brands are connected by a common purpose: Serving Asia sustainably for generations with everyday moments. That role has become more important as lifestyles have changed. Consumers today are busier, more digitally connected and more discerning. They expect retailers to provide not only the right products, but also convenience, value, reliability and a seamless experience across physical and digital channels. In a city such as Hong Kong, where time, space and household budgets are constant considerations, retail is expected to work harder for customers. “Customers consistently value businesses that understand their needs and earn their trust,” Price says. “That has remained true even as the way people shop has changed dramatically.” Adapting Through Generations of Change Reflecting on DFI’s 140-year history, it has unfolded alongside Hong Kong’s transformation from a trading port into a global financial and commercial centre. During that period, the retail industry has been reshaped by urbanisation, rising living standards, changing family structures, technological innovation and the emergence of digital commerce. Shopping habits have shifted from traditional high-street transactions to omnichannel experiences, loyalty ecosystems and data-driven personalisation. For retailers, the challenge is no longer simply to operate stores. It is to understand customers across multiple touchpoints and respond quickly to changing needs. “Over more than four decades in Asia, I’ve seen enormous change in how people shop and interact with brands,” Price says. “But customers consistently value businesses that understand their needs and earn their trust.” Price explains that maintaining that trust requires continuous investment. As such, the Group is strengthening its capabilities in technology, talent, supply chain and customer engagement, while remaining focused on the fundamentals of quality, service and value. The company is also operating in a market where expectations of retailers are broadening. Customers increasingly want businesses to act responsibly, support healthier lifestyles and contribute positively to the communities in which they operate. For Price, these demands are not separate from the future of retail. They are central to it. Retailers that succeed over the long term, he believes, will be those able to combine operational excellence with a deeper understanding of people’s lives – how they shop, what they value, how they make choices and what kind of support they expect from trusted brands. In such a competitive and fast-changing sector, trust has become one of retail’s most important assets, Price says.

events.title: Court tosses 10-year manslaughter sentence due to an AI-generated video of the victim ‘created from the imaginings’ of his sister
events.summary: An Arizona man’s  10-year manslaughter sentence  has been tossed in a case where a video generated by artificial intelligence portrayed the deceased victim addressing a judge before the punishment was imposed. In a decision released Wednesday, the Arizona Court of Appeals concluded Gabriel Paul Horcasitas must be resentenced in the 2021 shooting death of Christopher Pelkey because the AI video wasn’t reliable. The court found the video crossed the line, saying it didn’t reflect actual events and presented statements made in the footage as coming directly from the victim. “Indeed, rather than document an event or recording a particular moment, the AI video presents a depiction of the victim and his thoughts created from the imaginings of the victim’s sister,” the three-judge panel wrote. Jessica Gattuso, an attorney who represented victims in the case, and Kristen Reller, Horcasitas’ lawyer, declined to comment Thursday on the decision. Reller had argued Superior Court Judge Todd Lang violated due process protections by relying on AI evidence. Gattuso and prosecutors told the appeals court that the lower-court judge didn’t err, saying the footage was an accurate representation of Pelkey’s character. In what’s believed to be a first in U.S. courts, Pelkey’s family used AI to create a video of his likeness to give him a voice. Pelkey’s sister, Stacey Wales, raised the idea of her brother speaking for himself after struggling to figure out what he would say. Wales expected an appeal on the sentence and was disappointed the AI video was cited as the reason, saying her only goal was to humanize her brother for the judge. “It feels unfair because there is a convicted murderer sitting in prison that has blankets and walls of protection around their rights. Where are the rights for the victim?” Wales said. A victim appeals lawyer has told the family that using AI again could result in another appeal. “We will continue to let his voice be heard in whatever allowable medium we can convey that through the court system,” Wales said. The AI-generated victim impact statement was played during a May 2025 sentencing hearing after nine of Pelkey’s family members and friends stood before the judge describing how emotionally devastated they were by his killing. Authorities say Horcasitas, 55, fatally shot Pelkey, 37, during a November 2021 road rage encounter at a stoplight in Chandler, a suburb of Phoenix. Pelkey, who was unarmed, was shot after getting out of his truck and walking toward Horcasitas’ vehicle. Horcasitas was convicted of manslaughter in Pelkey’s death and endangerment for a gunshot that struck another vehicle at the intersection during the encounter. The AI rendering of Pelkey said he wished he could still be with his friends and family, voiced a belief in forgiveness and said it was a shame Horcasitas had encountered him because “in another life, we probably could have been friends.” The video didn’t request a specific prison sentence. Horcasitas’ appellate lawyer argued her client had no meaningful opportunity to rebut material in the AI-generated video. It’s not clear if attorneys or the court were aware in advance that an AI-generated video would be used. But attorneys representing Pelkey’s family said in court records that Arizona law does not require victims to disclose statements they plan to make in court to prosecutors, defense attorneys or the judge — and that victims can exercise their rights by speaking before the court or submitting statements that are written or recorded on audio or video. In a statement Thursday, the Maricopa County Attorney’s Office said its prosecutors knew the victim’s family would address the court during sentencing but weren’t aware of the nature of it. While the use of AI within the court system is expanding, it’s typically been reserved for administrative tasks, legal research and case preparation. In Arizona, it’s helped  inform the public of rulings in significant cases . But using AI to generate victim impact statements marks a new tool for sharing information with the court outside the evidentiary phases. Reller told the appeals court that the video doesn’t disclose who wrote the words used by the AI version of Pelkey and wasn’t backed up with evidence establishing that its contents accurately reflected Pelkey’s views. It also had an “undue emotional weight” and conveyed an authenticity that wouldn’t have been there had a family member read the same words aloud, Reller said. Horcasitas’ lawyer contended the judge weighed the statements made in the AI-generated video when deciding on a sentence, but prosecutors argued Lang didn’t consider the footage when issuing the punishment. Shortly before delivering the sentence, the judge commented that he “loved that AI” but didn’t say from the bench whether the video factored into his decision. Lang said he felt Pelkey’s “obvious forgiveness of Mr. Horcasitas reflects the character I heard about today.” The family’s lawyers say the judge was already inundated with relevant information from Pelkey’s family and friends before the AI video was played — and that nothing in the video was inflammatory. Horcasitas’ attorney didn’t object to the AI video. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

The Green Party, which received 6 percent of the vote in the UK’s national elections in 2024, said ⁠it regarded Zionism as “an ethnonationalist political project” and repeated its call for Britain’s Labour government to end all arms trade with Israel. In a swift response, Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the policy went “far beyond the boundaries of legitimate political debate” and called on other British political parties to condemn the resolution. “The Greens have adopted not only the green of Hamas, but also its ideology: the elimination of the State of Israel through armed struggle,” the ministry wrote on social media. Israeli President Isaac Herzog labelled the move “a disgrace and a shame”. Writing on social media, he said: “Those who claim the antisemitic lie that ‘Zionism is racism’ deliberately endanger Jews and Israelis everywhere.” Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid said it is “not Zionism that’s racism, it is the Green Party”. The Movement for Progressive Judaism, a British group, said: “The Green Party has made ⁠antisemitism party policy and become a racist party”. It added that the support of some Jews for the motion did not mean it would not be used to discriminate against others. During the vote, the Green Party also reaffirmed its “commitment to Palestinian liberation, the right of return, Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS), and a full arms embargo against Israel”. It also reiterated support for “the establishment of a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine”, the party said in a statement. The motion was backed by a majority of 1,022 to 813. Party leader Zack Polanski , who is running for Parliament in former Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s London constituency, did not vote. In an interview with UK media outlet Sky News, the Greens’ co-deputy leader Mothin Ali said that the heavy casualty toll during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and its ongoing attacks were the context for the vote. The Green Party has five sitting members in the UK’s 650-seat parliament. Following the passage of the resolution, Polanski and other Green Party members said in a joint statement they would “continue to stand in opposition to genocide, ethnic cleansing, apartheid and the illegal occupation” and “call out the heinous crimes of the Netanyahu government”.

events.title: Residents fear there is no stopping $32b hyperscale data centre
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Western Downs residents fear being steamrolled as council assesses $32b data centre Ross Thornton says he is "mildly opposed" to the hyperscale data centre outside Dalby. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) A proposal to build a massive data centre near the Western Downs town of Dalby has locals wondering about the details of the plan. Anthropic has already signed a deal to use a portion of the site despite no approvals being issued. Some residents are petitioning against the plan, while others would like to meet and learn more. Dalby antiques dealer Ross Thornton is surrounded by history but worried about the future now that a $32 billion data centre is proposed just out of town. "People don't know enough about it," he said. Dalby is a country Queensland town 200 kilometres from Brisbane. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) The 70-year-old is calling for a public meeting amid fears residents will be steamrolled in the push to embrace the artificial intelligence boom. Anthropic has signed a deal in Australia to use the first of four buildings at the proposed hyperscale facility, well before it has received any approvals. The Queensland government confirmed it will be taking over from local governments as the "responsible assessor and coordinator" of data centre applications in a yet to be released planning framework. About 50 per cent of the Western Downs is cropping land. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) Mr Thornton has lived through the rapid industrialisation of the country town before, when the coal seam gas industry swept through more than a decade ago. "It caused a boom-bust cycle and no-one wants that," he said. "[We want to know] what's the impact going to be … and any of the pros and cons relating to it." Dalby antiques dealer Ross Thornton wants a public town hall for more information on the proposed data centre. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) A petition to parliament opposing the Western Downs Digital Park has gained more than 21,000 signatures — more than any petition currently open in Queensland. "We know that when big business comes in, the locals don't have a say," Angela Prenzler, who has been promoting the petition, said. Angela Prenzler has lived in Dalby all her life and is concerned about the proposed data centre. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) The Dalby resident said she was sceptical of the developer's plans to predominantly use rain and recycled water for its operations. "We are always in drought," Ms Penzler said. She said the online petition was gaining traction, including in other country areas. "They know it could happen in their regional town too," Ms Prenzler said. Dalby businessman Doug Machin, who owns a machinery business, a café and a grocery shop in town, feels conflicted about the project. Doug Machin and his daughter at the Dalby Machinery Centre. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) "You never knock back development," he said, then added it would be challenging to source the suggested 1,500 jobs required to build the data centre. "If you went to most businesses and farmers, we just don't seem to be able to get the [workers]." Unlike New South Wales and Victoria, Queensland has no dedicated data centre planning pathway. The Crisafulli government said it was in the process of developing a framework that would "mirror its reforms to renewable energy development". "This will ensure a consistent and transparent framework across the state, as many councils don't include data centres in their planning schemes, which creates confusion and inconsistency," the government said in a statement. "Any deals done must be with the backing of councils and communities." The Western Downs region is known as the "energy capital" of Queensland but has historically been an agricultural area. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) Western Downs Mayor Andrew Smith said he had been assured the project in his region would remain under his council's purview — but it may be out of the council's hands. Singapore-based developer Zerra DC has applied for "prescribed project" status, which means Queensland's coordinator-general could step in and fast-track approvals to prevent "unnecessary delays". "We've had good conversations with the state. We're confident in our ability to assess large scale development," he said. Chinchilla resident Shay Dougall earned her doctorate researching the impacts of the coal seam gas industrialisation of the Western Downs and says history should guide decision-making. Shay Dougall says residents deserve to have a say about what happens in their area.
