events.title: Iraq transports its oil through Strait of Hormuz as US-Iran war chokes exports
events.summary: Iraq 's state oil company has moved its own crude beyond the Strait of Hormuz for the first time in decades as the US-Iran war threatens the country's primary export route. The Iraqi Oil Tankers Company shipped two million barrels of crude through the waterway on a very large crude carrier, director general Ali Qais was quoted as saying by state media. The move was aimed to shift part of Iraq's oil exports from the existing free-on-board Basra port model to transit the strait and take advantage of better sale and pricing opportunities, he added. The company is now in talks to buy specialised crude tankers “as soon as possible and to compete with regional peers”, Mr Qais said. Since the Iran war broke out in February, Iraq has been facing one of its most serious economic and security situations. Opec's second-largest producer depends on oil for at least 90 per cent of its revenue. Most of its exports – about 3.3 million barrels a day before the war – crossed the Strait of Hormuz after leaving its southern Basra terminals. The strait has been effectively closed by Iran since the conflict broke out, with shipping disrupted by missile and drone attacks, insurance surges and naval confrontations. Total Hormuz flows in September stood at 6.02 million bod, less than a third of February's 20.64 million bpd, according to Kpler, highlighting the continued disruption to the region's main oil export artery. Iraq has been caught in the middle of the war, with pro-Tehran armed groups having launched drones towards Gulf states from Iraqi territory, prompting countries in the region to hold Baghdad responsible. Meanwhile, ships crossing Iraqi waters near the strait have been at increased risk, forcing Baghdad to offer discounted rates on services at Basra Port and causing buyers to demand delivery outside the waterway. The government has been struggling to revive alternative routes – including a proposal to reopen the Iraq-Turkey pipeline through Ceyhan and another to move crude to Syria by land – but these solutions would only cover a fraction of Iraqi exports. Iraq has been able to move three million barrels of oil a day since the beginning of September, Oil Minister Bassim Khudair said last month. Opec’s second-largest producer is now looking to further boost its production as it expects alternative pipelines and the country’s improved export infrastructure comes on stream, he told the Iraqi News Agency. “The government plans to increase export capacity to five million barrels a day after the completion of the strategic pipelines extending to Fishkhabour and Baniyas, in addition to the export terminals in the Strait of Hormuz,” he said. The latest shipment indicates that Iraq has adopted the strategy of moving oil past the Strait of Hormuz to guarantee delivery and secure better prices, rather than leaving buyers to shoulder the war risk premium. The tanker company, once a major fleet operator in the 1980s, has been trying to rebuild itself after successive wars and rounds of sanctions. Buying its own VLCCs would provide Baghdad with more control over its main source of income.

events.title: ‘They call every week’: the phishing attacks targeting past victims
events.summary: Scammers reuse personal details harvested from fake Esta websites – and texts and calls can keep arriving for months W hen the British actor Lisa Riley was preparing to travel to the US last year, she applied online for an Esta so she would not need a visa. After finding the site through a Google search she filled in her passport, bank and personal details and waited for the confirmation, which normally takes just under an hour. When it failed to arrive, she emailed an address from the site where she had paid and got back a message unlike any she had seen before, with a link to a website that displayed a jumble of words and letters. It was then she realised she had been scammed. But that was just the start of her problems, which persist to this day. She has been repeatedly targeted by criminals, receiving text messages and calls many times every week. Riley was the victim of a fraud where criminals create websites similar to the legitimate one run by US Customs and Border Protection (CBP). After fooling unsuspecting applicants they pocket a fee and use the personal details of victims for later scams. Riley lost £16 – the cost of an Esta back then – but says there has been a huge increase in the number of scam calls and texts she has received in the 17 months since the fraud happened. Often the person claims to be from her bank with queries about a money transfer. “Calls are once a week, easy – sometimes twice a week,” she says. “And the texts even more often.” Research from Nationwide building society suggests that 15% of people have given personal information to something who later turned out not to be genuine, leaving them open to future frauds. “Criminals do sadly retarget people after an initial scam,” says Annya Burskys, head of fraud operations at Nationwide. “They take the personal information they have gained and either sell it on to other scammers or use them to make follow-up bank impersonation calls , texts and emails appear more convincing.” The fake Esta site that stole Riley’s personal details looked very similar to the official one and showed up high in search results, she says. “The webpage was absolutely identical so there was nothing that would remotely make me fearful up until [I realised],” she says. Criminals can use AI to recreate legitimate government sites and will frequently use key words such as “Esta”, in the domain name to try to portray legitimacy. A spokesperson for the US CBP says some sites may demand action by the applicant quickly, a common tactic by criminals to try to get people to act without thinking something through. Only use the official Esta website, which has a .gov address, or the mobile app. “Applicants should protect their Esta confirmation number and payment details, retain application records, and review financial statements for unauthorised charges,” says the CBP spokesperson. “Suspected fraud should be documented and reported promptly to the applicant’s financial institution and appropriate local government reporting channels.” In the UK that means telling your bank and Report Fraud . If you have inadvertently handed over your personal details you are at risk of future scams, so be alert to unexpected calls, texts or emails, says Burskys. “Don’t feel pressured to act. A genuine call or message from your bank will never ask you to move money, never ask you to share codes, and will never tell you what to say to your bank or friends, family,” she says. “Take a moment to verify who you’re speaking to and contact your bank directly using trusted contact information from your bank card or search for the official website if you’re unsure.”

events.title: Ministers explore how to stop regional leaders misusing planned new spending powers
events.summary: Labour wants to make sure mayors and council chiefs in England can be held to account for extra revenues devolved to them Ministers are mulling over how to ensure that England’s regional leaders do not misuse their newfound spending muscle, as Whitehall prepares to devolve more revenue to local levels. Ideas under consideration include a new select committee in Westminster, enhanced reporting rules and a new audit body focused on local and regional government. The Guardian understands the idea has even been mooted of allowing spendthrift mayors to be recalled by the electorate, as can happen to rule-breaking MPs. The government will publish a white paper on “rewiring the state” later this month, setting out detailed plans to hand over more income tax revenue to regional mayors. Rachel Reeves suggested the idea in her Mais lecture earlier this year , and it has been adopted by Andy Burnham’s government, which sees devolution as a big part of its growth policy. However, officials are concerned about how to ensure local leaders are fully accountable for what they do with the additional cash – including in between elections. Meg Hillier, the chair of the Treasury select committee, said she believed hers would be the right body to scrutinise the use of the additional spending powers. “It’s clear that one of the prime minister’s key ambitions is to take spending power out of Westminster and hand it to local leaders,” the Labour MP said. “It is absolutely critical, though, that strong, clear scrutiny structures are established which match this move to localism. It would be reckless to hand out new powers without ensuring there are transparent mechanisms to hold mayors to account for their decisions.” Hillier added: “One way to do this is to establish clear lines of authority running through departments and up to ministers, which will allow existing select committees to judge this work. “A core role of a select committee, particularly the Treasury committee which I chair, is to ensure politicians are publicly held to account for how they decide to spend taxpayers’ money. That is just important at a local level as it is on a national scale.” The Audit Commission, which had the specific task of overseeing local government spending, was abolished in 2015, with its role split across several other bodies. As well as shoring up accountability, it is understood there have been lengthy discussions in government about how to balance the need to incentivise local leaders to encourage economic growth, with the imperative to ensure funding is stable over time. The Institute for Fiscal Studies said last week that the government should use “equalisation payments” to prevent the funding of areas with the highest share of income tax, such as London, pulling ahead of other regions. David Phillips, the IFS’s devolution expert, said: “With more skin in the game of economic growth, mayors will be more incentivised and empowered to support growth through local policies and investments. But careful design will be needed to prevent richer areas’ funding unfairly pulling ahead. “The government must also decide how big a gap in funding it is willing to see between ‘winners’ and ‘losers’ in the years ahead.” Burnham has made clear his intention of accelerating devolution, with his new No 10 North office focusing on the regional aspects of growth policy.

events.title: Singapore debuts a state-backed dating app for young government workers as it works to slow a demographic crisis
events.summary: Singapore’s FirstDate joins government-backed matchmaking programs in Tokyo and Seoul, emerging against the backdrop of Asia’s persistently low fertility rates. Government-backed services may hold advantages in official verification, limited-choice design and lack of monetization. The latest pilot comes after Singapore expands financial and childcare support for families earlier in August. Singapore is asking its young government workers to trust the state to find them love matches. FirstDate , a government-built dating platform being piloted in Singapore, is the latest in a slew of state-backed matchmaking initiatives against the backdrop of Asia's persistently low fertility rates. It follows Japan's AI-powered dating app Tokyo Enmusubi and South Korea's Seoulting , programs launched by the Tokyo and Seoul governments in 2024. The experiments emerge amid a rising demographic crisis — official government data put the total fertility rate at 0.80 children per woman in South Korea , 0.87 in Singapore and 1.14 in Japan — among the lowest in the world and far below the replacement level of 2.1. Government intervention in a field as personal as romance has prompted skepticism and jokes among social-media users, some of whom describe the initiative as "dystopian." "Finally, state-assigned spouses," one Reddit user wrote in a discussion of the platform. But the Asian city-state's matchmaking service may have conventional dating apps beat on certain fronts, experts said. One potential advantage of state-backed matchmaking is the government's ability to make verification against official records a condition for entry into the program. The trade-off: participants must entrust sensitive personal and dating information to the state. FirstDate requires participants to register using Singpass, Singapore's national digital identity system, to verify participants' identities, ages and legal marital status. Seoulting applicants must provide proof of Seoul residency, marital status and economic activity. Accepted documents include employment certificates, business-registration records or income statements. Tokyo's screening goes further. Tokyo Enmusubi applicants must complete an online interview, on top of photo identification, proof of income and single status. Commercial dating platforms such as Bumble generate revenue through subscriptions and paid features, giving them a financial interest in attracting, converting and retaining paying users. FirstDate advertises neither subscriptions nor paid features, and GovTech says users' data will not be monetized. It also presents one match per cycle, giving both participants 72 hours to decide whether to connect. "Dating apps are incentivized to provide people with tons and tons more choices," said Dr. Norman Li, a professor of psychology at Singapore Management University. Restricting those choices could encourage users to consider each introduction more seriously and reduce "choice paralysis," he added. "It's hard to settle on anybody when you feel like you have unlimited choices." FirstDate uses the Gale-Shapley Stable Marriage algorithm to pair participants using their stated preferences. But the algorithm's output is only as useful as the preferences fed into it, said Dr. Teo Chung Piaw, Dean of the National University of Singapore Business School. FirstDate primarily derives those preferences from questionnaires. Conventional dating platforms, by comparison, can also learn from users' behavior — such as which profiles they view, select or reject — to estimate what economists call "revealed preferences" where users may describe an ideal partner type, but actually be drawn to different characteristics. "FirstDate could plausibly produce more compatible matches," Teo said, but the key question is "whether stated preferences estimated from the questionnaire predict real interpersonal compatibility better than the revealed-preference signals generated by conventional dating apps." The algorithm is not unique to government matchmaking: Hinge introduced a modified version for its "Most Compatible" recommendations in 2018. In terms of relationships to private-sector dating apps, Shn Juay, CEO of Coffee Meets Bagel Worldwide, said that she doesn't see it "as competition so much as part of a shared effort." Hinge and Bumble did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment. FirstDate is not Singapore's first foray into state-supported matchmaking. The government established the Social Development Unit in 1984 to encourage marriage among university-educated singles through social events and mixers. Singapore is also looking at other ways to tackle its demographic challenges, expanding financial and childcare support for families in August in a bid to reduce the economic costs of having children, which are seen as one of the major deterrents to expanding families in the city-state.

events.title: Ukraine’s surprise robot offensive exposes a vulnerability in Putin’s war machine
events.summary: Ukraine’s surprise robot-led offensive in the Donbas appears to have reversed more than a year of Russian territorial gains around Lyman. Dubbed "Operation Vivaldi," the offensive has retaken 176 square kilometers, with Ukrainian forces using drones and unmanned ground vehicles to strike behind Russian lines while limiting risks to personnel. Security experts say the offensive is not a decisive breakthrough, but demonstrates how Ukraine’s expanding use of robotic systems is reshaping frontline warfare. A surprise Ukrainian robot offensive in the eastern Donbas region appears to have reversed over a year of Russian territorial gains, according to security experts, dealing a strategic blow to Russian President Vladimir Putin 's territorial ambitions. Details of the Ukrainian counteroffensive, dubbed "Operation Vivaldi," have started to come to light in recent weeks, offering rare insight into the fast-changing nature of frontline combat operations amid Russia's full-scale invasion . As part of the ongoing operation, which started in May, security experts said Ukraine's Third Army Corps had been able to deploy large bomber drones and remote-controlled robots behind enemy lines around Lyman in the northern Donetsk Oblast, apparently catching Russian forces off guard. Russian forces have been seeking to encircle Ukraine's so-called fortress belt cities that make up the remaining Ukrainian-held territory in the region for the past 12 months. The third phase of Operation Vivaldi, however, liberated an additional 51 square kilometers, taking the total area of territory retaken to 176 square kilometers, Ukrainian Brigadier-General Andrii Biletskyi said on Sept. 28. The latest phase of fighting inflicted over 2,000 Russian losses, with over 250 Russian soldiers taken prisoner, he added. Patrick Bolder, a defense expert and strategic advisor at the Hague Center for Strategic Studies (HCSS), described the offensive as a "big bloody nose" to Putin's minimal war aim of seizing Ukraine's Donbas region. Alongside demonstrating an ability to keep details of the operation secret, running disinformation campaigns against Russia and orchestrating a months-long air operation to disrupt logistical supplies to the frontline, Bolder said Ukrainian forces had managed to secure control of the air in the Lyman area, denying Russia the use of its drones. Ukrainian forces were then able to deploy their own drones to drop unmanned ground vehicles behind enemy lines to attack the Russian troops from behind, Bolder said, without endangering their own personnel. "They put this together masterly," Bolder said. For the Kremlin, "gaining the Donbas is very far away at the moment because the Ukrainians have come into better defendable positions now — which will make it harder for the Russians to try to do this again," he added. A spokesperson for Russia's Embassy in London was not available to comment when contacted by CNBC on Friday. 'A powerful message to Moscow and Kyiv's partners' Security experts made it clear that Ukraine's robot offensive should not be seen as a decisive breakthrough. It does, however, send "a powerful message to Moscow and to Kyiv's partners that the highly innovative Ukrainian military remains capable of defeating Russia on the battlefield," according to David Kirichenko, an associate research fellow at the Henry Jackson Society, a U.K.-based national security think tank. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy lauded the success of Ukraine's Third Army Corps when he met with soldiers carrying out the counteroffensive, describing the operation as "important in many ways" for Ukraine's defense overall, and the Donbas region especially. "One particularly promising area now is replacing our warriors with ground robotic systems wherever possible," Zelenskyy said in a social media post on Sept. 30. "During Vivaldi, this capability allowed us to accomplish many things. We will scale it up so that, more and more often, a drone rather than a warrior carries out the most dangerous tasks at the front," he added. ( US Coast Guard via AP ) The US Coast Guard has found a "debris field' in its search for an air ambulance that went missing over the Atlantic. The Canadian-registered aircraft was carrying six people from Bermuda to Boston in the United States. The Coast Guard said the search would continue. Searchers have found debris from an air ambulance that was carrying six people when it went missing over the Atlantic during a flight from Bermuda to Boston. The "debris field" was found off the coast of Nantucket, in the US state of Massachusetts, following the disappearance on Saturday, the US Coast Guard said. Four Canadians and two Bermudian nationals were aboard, the Coast Guard said in a statement. It added that the next of kin of those missing had been notified and one of its cutters would keep searching the water overnight and into Sunday. According to the Coast Guard, the Federal Aviation Administration reported that the Gulfstream G100 aircraft lost contact very early on Saturday morning. Air traffic audio indicates that it may have been "coming in blind" when a storm loomed ahead shortly before it disappeared. The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast, according to air traffic control audio posted by LiveATC.net. "Roger, you said you're coming in blind. Is that what you said?" a controller can be heard asking the pilot. The plane may have lost its navigational instruments as a storm seen on radar moved across its path, former US Department of Transportation inspector-general Mary Schiavo said. The plane also descended sharply from its cruising altitude of around 7.3 kilometres to around three kilometres, according to preliminary data from flight tracking site FlightRadar24. "Something bad happened with this big drop, and they flew into this big storm," Ms Schiavo, an aviation attorney, said. "It's a terrible place to have a loss of your instruments and be flying blind. "It's very easy to get disoriented and not know if you're turning, climbing, descending, etc." The Canadian-registered air ambulance jet had four crew and two passengers aboard when it departed Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport for the night flight to Massachusetts, according to a statement from the Bermuda airport's operator, Skyport. Transport Canada was closely monitoring and working with authorities on search and rescue efforts, the country's Minister of Transport Steven MacKinnon said on X. The Bermuda government is in contact with US authorities and the families of the passengers, Bermuda Premier David Burt wrote in a statement posted on Instagram. "We are praying that all six people will be found safe," the statement said. The US National Transportation Safety Board said it was gathering information about the situation, but it did not say immediately if it would investigate. events.title: Not SGX’s fault if stocks have no liquidity, says chairman: Markets this week
events.summary: In this column, ST’s business correspondents unpack the latest developments in Singapore and global markets during the week – and explain what they mean for investors. In taking full control of the Starbucks business in the region, DFI Retail Group will transfer its 50% stake in Maxim’s Caterers to Hongkong Caterers for US$340 million (S$434.7 million) in cash. SINGAPORE – Listed companies should proactively disclose their three- to five-year strategies so that investors can better understand their businesses and growth prospects, with board chairs leading the effort, Singapore Exchange (SGX) chairman Koh Boon Hwee said on Oct 1. He was speaking at an event organised by the Singapore Institute of Directors . Koh said Singapore has strongly signalled its desire to reform its stock market, and more capital is already starting to flow in. However, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) cannot solely depend on the SGX to boost their valuations, as the bourse does not create liquidity nor demand and supply. He said: “If you say that the market misunderstands you, it is your job to make sure that it understands you. If you say that there is no liquidity, it is because you have not been talking to the people who might have an interest in buying or demanding the stock.” Therefore, it is incumbent upon companies and their leaders to communicate their growth strategies to the public. “The exchange can’t do that for you, neither can it guarantee that your counter will be liquid.” Koh said privatisation could be an option for companies whose shares are thinly traded and which are reluctant to disclose their long-term plans publicly. His comments echoed a point made in his annual letter to shareholders on Sept 29, in which he said that “privatisation is not a tragedy but a rational and often healthy outcome”. “For a listed company with limited growth prospects, low trading liquidity and persistently low valuations, going private is a sensible path,” he wrote. “It serves little purpose for a company to remain listed simply so that an exchange can preserve its company count.” CDL tumbles after revealing 3-year plan The counter fell 5.7% by midday after its plans were unveiled before the market opened, and later closed 8.1% down at $7.59. It continued to slide and closed the week at $7.04, the lowest since November 2025. Explaining why CDL’s share price fell, analysts said weak market conditions and the interest rate outlook could make it difficult for CDL to divest $6 billion worth of assets as planned. Details on where CDL intends to invest an additional $5 billion are also lacking. In addition, doubts remain over whether the feud between chief executive Sherman Kwek and his father, executive chairman Kwek Leng Beng, has truly subsided. In early 2025, the father accused his son of orchestrating a boardroom takeover. The elder Kwek was also absent from the Sept 28 unveiling of the road map, which left questions on succession from the media unanswered. Others noted that some institutional investors have been dumping CDL shares in a typical “buy the rumour, sell the news” fashion, while some have also been short selling the shares. CDL had said on Sept 28 that it plans to sell $6 billion worth of non-core assets, including $1.8 billion worth of hotels, over the next three years. The company will also deploy $5 billion of growth capital, with Singapore remaining the principal market for new investments. A third of the funds has been earmarked for investments in China, where the property market has been weak, and Japan. In addition, CDL plans to achieve a dividend payout of more than 35% annually, increase its assets under management from $5 billion to $10 billion, and lock in more than $1 billion in profit after tax and minority interests to be realised from divestment gains, over the three years. DFI takes full control of Starbucks in Asia DFI Retail Group’s shares jumped 6.6% when the market opened on Oct 1 and closed at US$3.41, the week’s peak, before falling the following day to close the week 6.1% lower at US$3.10. The company said on Sept 30 that it will take full control of Starbucks’ licensed operations in the region , including Singapore, from Maxim’s Caterers, following a reorganisation. Currently, DFI and Hongkong Caterers each own a 50% stake in Maxim’s Caterers. The new arrangement will see Hongkong Caterers retain Maxim’s other food and beverage businesses, which include five brands in Singapore: Genki Sushi, sen-ryo, Yakiniku Like, Butahage and Uoharu. The reorganisation is slated to be completed by end-March 2027 and expected to immediately boost DFI’s revenue and profitability. DFI will transfer its 50% stake in Maxim’s to Hongkong Caterers for US$340 million (S$434.7 million) in cash, which it intends to deploy for growth or return to its shareholders as special dividends.

events.title: Syria 'pressing on accelerator' to attract US investors
events.summary: US investors see an opportunity to invest early in Syria as the transitional government races to establish a pro-business environment and attract foreign capital. “We see that the door is open, and we're coming early,” Steve Lutes, vice president of Middle East Affairs at the US Chamber of Commerce, said in an interview. “I think US companies made it very clear across a different range of sectors that they're looking to be strategically engaged, to be a long-term partner in helping Syria get back up on its feet and excel economically.” Mr Lutes spoke to The National after the Chamber of Commerce hosted a round-table with Syrian President Ahmad Al Shara and Foreign Minister Asaad Al Shibani on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly last month. He also recently led a delegation of more than 50 American businesses and 80 delegates to Damascus. The delegation – which included Baker Hughes , Caterpillar, Visa and dozens of other US firms – marked a significant step in re-establishing Washington's economic relationship with Syria after the 13-year civil war. It also came shortly after the US lifted its state sponsor of terrorism designation on Syria, which had been a prominent roadblock to the country’s reintegration into the international financial system. Syria’s government has moved quickly to attract investment since the fall of Bashar Al Assad's regime in 2024. The World Bank estimates it will cost $216 billion to rebuild the country. Some investment pledges from the Gulf have already moved towards implementation, including DP World's $800 million investment commitment to Tartus Port. At the same time, Syria has also courted foreign investors from Silicon Valley to Riyadh. “They're really pressing on the accelerator to try to move things forward,” Mr Lutes said. He added that the Chamber of Commerce was turning significant attention towards Syria's banking sector , which has undergone a rapid transformation under the current government. Mr Al Shara carried out the country’s first international Visa transaction in August. “It's so foundational to everything else,” Mr Lutes said. QNB and Mastercard issued the first internationally accepted payment card in Syria. The World Bank has also approved a $100 million grant to help establish a digitally enabled financial sector. Last Sunday, Central Bank of Syria Governor Mohammed Raslan told official news agency Sana that the government expected foreign investment in establishing new banks to surpass $1 billion in the coming period. The US Treasury Department on Thursday held a round-table in New York to support the country's financial sector and reconnection to the global financial system. Finance Minister Yisr Barnieh said in a LinkedIn post that discussions had focused on advancing anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing standards, among other reforms. Treasury Assistant Secretary for Terrorist Financing and Financial Crimes Jonathan Burke also stressed financial connectivity remains a vital component to combatting illicit finance and supporting Syria's reintegration into the global financial system, according to a readout. Public spending in Syria for first six months of the year totalled roughly $3.7 billion, compared to a public revenue of $2.7 billion, according to the finance ministry's first-half 2026 budget report. That leaves a fiscal deficit of about $1 billion. “The biggest challenge at the end of the day are the budgetary constraints and how are they going to finance and pay for it all,” Mr Lutes said. Damascus said it was implementing new measures to control public spending, including reviewing investment projects. Mr Barnieh wrote in a social media post on Monday that the measures would not affect salaries, wages or spending on essential needs such as health, education, water, energy, security, public safety and necessary operational maintenance. Gulf partnerships While the state sponsor of terrorism delisting removed the final pillar in the US sanctions architecture, investing in Syria continues to carry reputational risks. It remains on the Financial Action Task Force's grey list, and parties may have previous links to sanctioned actors. Mr Lutes described the Chamber of Commerce’s delegation to Damascus as an “exploratory” one to give US companies the chance to identify sectors for investment and re-establish trust with Syrian officials. Several US companies have already signed memorandums of understanding and other agreements with Syria including ConocoPhillips, Chevron, Baker Hughes, Hunt Energy and Ardent LNG. Gulf partners have joined some of these projects including Qatar's UCC Holding, which signed an agreement with Chevron and Syria's state-run petroleum company to develop the country's first offshore oil and gasfield. Mr Lutes anticipates more US companies could go down similar routes with Emirati, Saudi or Qatari partners who already have relationships with the country. Doing so could mitigate some risks and increase US investor confidence. He added that he hopes the delegation will become an annual occurrence. He also said the chamber is engaging with the Syrian government on addressing policy regulatory issues. “We're not going out of business any time soon. There's a lot of work for the chamber to support US companies that are interested in doing business in Syria, so we're going to be at this … for many years to come,” Mr Lutes said.

events.title: Regional audiences to lose Network 10, as licensee warns of TV's future
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Network 10 to disappear in parts of SA, NSW's Riverina, after no deal made Network 10 channels will disappear from Mount Gambier, Riverland and Griffith TV screens. ( ABC News: Jak Rowland ) Audiences in Mount Gambier and the Riverland in SA, and Griffith in NSW, will lose terrestrial Network 10 channels on Friday. Network 10 and license holders WIN failed to come to a new agreement after months of negotiating. WIN says it will be "challenging to maintain services", due to the economics of regional broadcasting. Viewers in parts of regional South Australia, and parts of the Riverina in New South Wales, will lose access to Network 10's terrestrial channels, after the network and license holder, WIN Network, failed to reach an agreement. WIN has announced it will stop broadcasting 10, 10 Drama and 10 Comedy in the Mount Gambier, Riverland, Griffith and Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area, with the final broadcasts to be on Friday, October 9. The network had flagged its agreement with Network 10 would expire in July, and that the channels would be pulled. However, local audiences were given a three-month reprieve , with Network 10 saying it would provide its feed "free of charge" to WIN while the parties worked on a deal that has not eventuated. WIN Network says the decision reflects the economics of regional broadcasting. ( ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters ) In a statement, a WIN Network spokesperson said providing Network 10 services to the impacted markets was "no longer viable". "This is a business decision that reflects the realities of regional broadcasting," they said. "Regional markets carry high transmission and infrastructure costs, while digital disruption continues to erode audiences and advertising revenue. "These economics will continue to make it challenging to maintain services across regional Australia. "WIN recognises this will be disappointing for viewers and thanks them for their understanding." The move follows a similar loss of Seven Network channels to the same markets, after Seven and WIN failed to reach an agreement before Seven's deal expired last year. The channels were eventually restored after a multi-day shutdown that saw the channels replaced with red screens advising they were "no longer available". Audiences in Mount Gambier, the Riverland and Griffith temporarily lost Seven Network channels last year. ( ABC South East SA: Eugene Boisvert ) Job cut fears at one of Australia's largest toilet roll manufacturers How a 'piece of rural propaganda' became 'compulsory listening' for Aussies Soccer player with broken leg endures 70km car trip between hospitals Regional women share postpartum journeys to create change A Network 10 spokesperson said audiences could continue to access the network's channels online and via its app. "WIN holds the broadcast licences in the Riverland, Mount Gambier and Griffith regions and although Network 10 has worked closely with WIN to explore options to maintain local access to its content, WIN has advised that continuing to operate them is no longer commercially viable," they said. The WIN Network holds the broadcast licenses in Mount Gambier, the Riverland and Griffith. ( ABC South East SA: Eugene Boisvert ) It is not the first time a regional market has lost Network 10 channels due to the financial challenges of regional broadcasting. In 2024, audiences in Mildura, Victoria, lost their Network 10 channels when Mildura Digital Television (MDT), which carried 10's signal to the market, was closed by co-owners Seven and WIN. The networks said "it did not make commercial sense" to keep MDT going, as it had been unprofitable throughout its existence. A government spokesperson said the decision was a "commercial matter" and that it was up to the networks to explain it to the community. "The government continues to support Australian broadcasters through a range of measures including the deferral of the Commercial Broadcasting Tax, which will deliver an estimated $111.3 million in savings for the sector," they said. "We know how important free-to-air TV is and are examining ways to ensure it continues to be delivered in a sustainable way in the future, with public consultation now underway.

events.title: Houthis target Saudi oil facility as hostilities escalate in Yemen
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Iran-backed Houthis target Saudi oil facility as hostilities escalate in Yemen Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis say they targeted a Saudi Arabian oil company in retaliation for Saudi attacks on Yemen. The fighting has worsened the already appalling humanitarian conditions in Yemen. Iraq's state-owned Oil Tanker Company says it has transported 2 million barrels of Iraqi crude aboard a large crude carrier through the Strait of Hormuz. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis say a targeted attack on a Saudi Arabian oil company facility near the capital Riyadh is retaliation for Saudi attacks on Yemen. The foes have traded strikes since the Houthis seized all of Yemen's Red Sea coast and took control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait in a lightning offensive last month. Houthi-affiliated channel Al-Masirah TV reported that Saudi aircraft hit Sanaa with 26 strikes, after earlier reporting "Saudi aggression" against the Yemeni capital. Houthis say they targeted a Saudi oil facility, south of Riyadh. ( AP ) Two correspondents in Sanaa reported hearing loud explosions and seeing warplanes firing missiles at the city. In Saudi Arabia, flames and smoke were seen rising on Saturday afternoon from an Aramco facility south of Riyadh. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had targeted an oil facility in Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones. They said the attack sparked fires at the targeted sites. Al-Masirah also reported missile strikes on the telecommunications network in Yemen's north-western governorate of Saada, one of the group's strongholds. After several years of calm, Yemen was plunged back into civil war in July, pitting the Iran-backed Houthis, who control most of north-west Yemen, including Sanaa, against Yemen's internationally recognised government. The government, based in the city of Aden, controls much of the country's south and east, a region that is larger but much less populated. A big, expensive, global excursion into hell What so many of the current major global conflicts have in common with the debacle in Iraq is their undefined, or sometimes not truthfully defined, missions. Hostilities were reignited after four years of a fragile truce when Iran sent a plane to Sanaa carrying a Houthi delegation. The flight did not seek authorisation from Saudi Arabia, contravening a decade-old practice. Riyadh retaliated with strikes on Sanaa airport, and in response the Houthis attacked Saudi territory for the first time since 2022. Since then, fighting has intensified, with the Houthis launching a lightning offensive in which they seized control of coastal regions along the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Houthi fighters took over the Red Sea port of Sanaa in Yemen. ( AP ) They have also struck multiple Saudi targets, including oil infrastructure and Riyadh, while also announcing a naval blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea. The renewed fighting has worsened the already appalling humanitarian conditions in Yemen, one of the world's poorest countries, with the World Food Programme warning on Friday that three-quarters of the population was unable to meet its basic food needs. Fighting in recent days has centred on Taiz, where dozens of combatants were reported killed on Friday by sources on both sides. The Houthis reported 55 of their fighters had been killed, while government sources said 26 troops had died. The Houthis have moved on strategic islands in the Red Sea and are now putting one of the richest and most powerful nations in the Middle East in a tricky spot. The Houthis said on Friday Saudi Arabia had launched 94 strikes against areas under their control in the previous 24 hours. Saudi authorities reported a Houthi projectile had damaged a school in the city of Najran near the Yemeni border. Riyadh has reportedly requested help from the United States, a call so far rebuffed by US President Donald Trump . Meanwhile, Iraq's state-owned Oil Tanker Company transported 2 million barrels of Iraqi crude aboard a large crude carrier through the Strait of Hormuz, in what its director general described on Saturday as the company's first such operation in decades. A week of Houthi attacks threatens oil and markets The Iran-backed Houthi rebels have made their biggest land grab in years, reigniting Yemen's 12-year long civil war and pushing up global fuel prices. The announcement means the company is transporting the crude through the strait rather than delivering it at the port of Basra, giving state oil marketer SOMO greater flexibility in how and where it sells the crude.

events.title: Ethiopian federal forces retake Mekelle airport from Tigrayan fighters, residents say
events.summary: Ethiopian federal forces have retaken Mekelle’s airport from Tigrayan fighters KAMPALA, Uganda -- Ethiopian federal forces have taken the airport in Mekelle, the capital of the northern Tigray region, according to people in the city who spoke to The Associated Press on Saturday, reversing a takeover by Tigrayan fighters that prompted the suspension of commercial flights last month. It wasn't immediately clear when federal forces recaptured Alula Aba Nega Airport. Those who provided the information declined to be identified for fear of retribution amid uncertainty over who controlled the city. Severe disruptions to internet and cellphone networks have made gathering and verifying information from Tigray difficult. Details of how the airport changed hands, including whether fighting took place there, remained unclear. “The military is in full control of the airport. That much I can confirm,” an Ethiopian general said on condition of anonymity. Neither the Ethiopian government nor the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, or TPLF, had issued an official statement on the airport’s reported capture. It wasn’t clear who controlled Mekelle itself. An AP contributor in the city said residents feared looting amid the uncertainty. “Many reports indicate that the government and allied forces have begun to control Tigray’s capital,” said Jalale Getachew Birru, an Ethiopia analyst for ACLED, an independent global monitor that collects, analyzes and maps data on conflict. The AP could not independently verify those reports. TPLF fighters seized the airport on Sept. 23, prompting Ethiopian Airlines to suspend flights to Mekelle and the Tigrayan cities of Axum and Shire. The African Union urged restraint, warning that renewed tensions threatened the peace agreement signed in 2022. Federal troops are fighting alongside allied Tigrayan forces against the TPLF. The AP previously reported that the Tigray Peace Force, a breakaway faction of the Tigrayan rebels, was operating alongside federal forces in the neighboring Afar region. The reported change in control follows a sharp deterioration in relations between Ethiopia and neighboring Eritrea. Ethiopia on Thursday ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave and announced the closure of its embassy in Eritrea. Eritrea said that it would sever diplomatic ties. Ethiopian authorities have accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF , an allegation Eritrea has denied. The U.S. State Department in a statement Saturday urged Ethiopia and Eritrea to show restraint and return to talks. Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' “Increasing cross-border tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea have the potential to affect the entire region,” State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said. “The Horn of Africa cannot sustain another military conflict and humanitarian crisis. A conflict jeopardizes ongoing U.S. collaboration on shared interests with both countries.” The government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed , if it takes control of Mekelle, is very likely to leave regional security in the hands of the Tigray Peace Force, which comprises former members of the Tigray Defense Forces, Birru said. Abiy has tried and failed to subdue Tigray’s rebellious leaders in recent months, with TPLF Chairman Debretsion Gebremichael openly challenging him. Renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 peace deal that ended a devastating two-year war between federal troops, backed by Eritrea and allied militias, and the TPLF. “This is an extraordinary and largely unexpected turn in a war whose direction looked very different only days ago,” Getachew Temare, an independent attorney and human rights defender who is from Ethiopia, said of the possible fall of Mekelle in an analysis posted on X. “But the most consequential question is not whether Mekelle falls. It is what this fall means politically.” He said the emergence of the Tigray Peace Force makes the current conflict different from the previous one. When Mekelle fell to federal forces in November 2020, the TPLF “retained something far more important. A substantial political and social constituency for armed resistance remained intact. Within months, Tigrayan forces returned to Mekelle and the military balance was dramatically reversed.” The fighting has brought renewed hardship to civilians still recovering from the previous 2020-2022 war. Residents of Mekelle told the AP earlier this week that communications, banking and other essential services had been disrupted. In September, residents described fears of renewed isolation following the suspension of flights. They also reported that roads connecting Tigray and Afar had been closed to civilian traffic, although the AP couldn't independently verify the closures. Kiyaro reported from Hamburg, Germany.

events.title: Thousands pack arena in Belgrade as Serbia's leader Vucic launches prime minister bid
events.summary: Thousands of supporters of Serbia's populist leader Aleksandar Vucic have packed Belgrade's largest arena for the launch of his campaign for prime minister BELGRADE, Serbia -- Thousands of supporters of Serbia's populist leader, Aleksandar Vucic, packed the largest indoor arena in Belgrade on Saturday for the de facto launch of his campaign for prime minister that will culminate in a pivotal election set for Oct. 25. The early election, which polls suggest could be tight between Vucic's party and a group of candidates fielded by a student-led protest movement, was called before Vucic resigned as president on Sept. 27, cutting short his second term by more than seven months. Vucic, who is constitutionally prohibited from running for a third term as president, declared upon resigning that he would lead his populist Serbian Progressive Party in the parliamentary election. If his party wins a majority of seats, the parliament is expected to elect Vucic as prime minister. Dozens of buses from across Serbia clogged streets around Belgrade Arena on Saturday as supporters arrived at the rally in the capital carrying Serbian flags and banners bearing Vucic’s picture. The event, televised by dozens of channels across Serbia, capped a week of Vucic touring towns and villages in an apparent bid to shore up his popularity that's been shaken after almost two years of sustained anti-government protests. The youth-backed movement that led the protests has demanded accountability for the Nov. 1, 2024 train station canopy collapse that killed 16 people in the northern city of Novi Sad. The movement's struggle for justice over the tragedy and against corruption has grown into a nationwide political force whose electoral arm, the Student List, will attempt to oust Vucic’s government after 14 years in power. Vucic himself has been either prime minister or president for the past 12 years. The Student List includes university professors, teachers, experts and others from across the political spectrum. Yet Vucic has accused those behind the movement of seeking to “bring Serbia to a halt,” and claimed, without providing evidence, that it's backed by unspecified foreign agents. And they know that.” The election is taking place amid heightened political tensions in Serbia, with reports of incidents and physical altercations at campaign events. International observers have described previous elections in Serbia as marred by multiple irregularities and violence. While formally a candidate for European Union membership, Serbia’s accession process has stalled under Vucic, who maintains close ties with Russia and China. European institutions have warned of democratic backsliding in Serbia in successive reports tracking the progress of candidate countries. Rights and media freedom groups have separately warned of police violence , arbitrary detentions, unauthorized surveillance and threats against journalists. events.title: SA's first musical theatre company brings talent home in debut stage
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Joey Haenen (front left) will play the lead role in Catch Me If You Can, the debut production of SA musical theatre company Full Circle. ( Supplied ) When Joey Haenen graduated with a music theatre degree in Adelaide, he knew he had to move states. "There is no work here and so you've got to move over east, that's where most of the agents are," he said. "You do all your auditioning over there and hopefully you'll land a gig." Haenen moved to Melbourne, like Jazz Garcia who spent a year getting her name known while paying for her passion through a day job in speech pathology. "There's just a lot more musical theatre opportunities in Melbourne, we don't really have anything in Adelaide," she said. The exodus from South Australia to the east coast has been happening for decades, a talent drain Jo Casson was determined to stop. Jo Casson says South Australia has been crying out for a professional musical theatre company. ( Supplied ) The arts veteran joined forces with others to form Full Circle, the state's first-ever professional music theatre company. "I discovered in the middle of last year that every other major city has a professional local theatre company and Adelaide didn't." Ironically, it's a full circle moment for the company's choreographer Zoe Komazec-Kermond, who returned from the east coast after a career performing in shows including Cats, Matilda and Mary Poppins. "There is so much talent in South Australia, so much talent and we do sometimes feel like we have to go away in order to achieve what we want to achieve," she said. Zoe Komazec-Kermond says a new SA musical theatre company will convince performers to come home. ( Supplied ) With such a rich vein of talent, Casson said forming the new company made sense. It has the backing of well-known arts lover and philanthropist Pamela Wall AO, but the company is seeking more support, as well as applying for grant funding. Full Circle will stage the musical Catch Me If You Can as its opening number, a stage version of the story that Leonardo DiCaprio took to the big screen and earned rave reviews. When the company held auditions, it attracted more than 100 performers for the 25 roles. Haenen was working and had to push his case with an audition video he sent to producers. The 21-year-old rising star's absence from the auditions did not stop him from landing the lead role of Frank Abagnale Jr. "What I love is just being able to get little bits of Joey in each of the characters every time and that's such a great joy," Haenen said. Garcia, who earned a contract among the show's ensemble, said the three-day auditions were exhausting. "The dance call was extremely strenuous, I'd say that was one of the longest kind of dance audition processes I've ever been in," she said. Jazz Garcia (middle) would love to travel back to South Australia to perform with Full Circle. ( Supplied ) More than 30 creatives and technical crew have been hired with the final cast a mix of South Australians and others returning to the state. "Everyone could sing, everyone could dance and everyone could act, so it made our job really hard to pick our final cast," Komazec-Kermond said. Beetlejuice, Waitress, Back to the Future and Dear Evan Hansen were major musicals which cancelled shows recently, with one producer citing increased cost pressures from "touring across vast distances between Australian cities". Full Circle said it was different because it would not have the high costs of touring a show nationally, like many others. However, Casson said getting productions into the country was a goal in future years. Full Circle wants to stage two musicals a year for the next two years, before increasing to three after that. Jazz Garcia believes more performers will build careers in South Australia after a new musical theatre company was formed. ( Supplied ) Those both on and off the stage realised the importance of pulling off the show and demonstrating the company should be here to stay. "It's a huge responsibility and I think we're going to do a really good job," Garcia confidently predicted. "There's so much buzz in Adelaide at the moment around Full Circle, so it's really up to us to produce the very best version of this show that we can," she said. Catch Me If You Can is at Futures Theatre in Paradise from November 5-7.

events.title: Tesla’s Cybercab had a rocky first month in Austin. Now comes the hard part: expanding
events.summary: A month after the Cybercab launched in Austin, Texas, Tesla has 169 of the driverless cars authorized for commercial use in the state. Investors are counting on Tesla growing its Robotaxi and Cybercab business as the core automotive unit faces heightened competition from Chinese EV makers. Reviews of the Cybercab in Austin have been mixed, with some paying passengers complaining of long wait times and drop-offs in the wrong place. In the month since Tesla's Cybercab rollout in Austin, the company has almost quadrupled the number of its driverless, bronze two-seaters authorized for commercial service in Texas. For Elon Musk to achieve his ambitions, growth has to pick up. The unusual driverless vehicles, with no steering wheel, pedals, rear or sideview mirrors, or outside door handles, have received mixed reviews from paying passengers, who shared videos and posts online after the launch on Sept. 3. Criticisms have included lengthy wait times , pickups and drop-offs in the wrong place, and technical difficulties with the vehicles' butterfly doors o r trunk closing improperly. Improving its driverless technology and rapidly growing the Robotaxi service are key to Tesla's effort to reignite investor enthusiasm. Auto sales have been sluggish for an extended period, and the shares have been a loser on Wall Street this year, down 18%, the only megacap tech stock that's failed to generate positive returns for investors. On Friday, Tesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter vehicle deliveries, lifting the stock almost 5%, but the company still posted a 2% year-over-year drop. Tesla's core automotive business has seen consecutive annual revenue declines as it faces pressure from Chinese EV makers like BYD and Xiaomi, which are selling more affordable, innovative models while Tesla ramps up exports to key markets, especially in Europe and Asia. Meanwhile, Alphabet's Waymo continues to open in new cities. It's now in 15 U.S. markets, with 15 more on the horizon, according to the company's website . It's also announced planned international launches in London, Tokyo and Munich. In Texas, Waymo had 1,154 autonomous vehicles authorized for commercial use as of Friday, including 359 of its new Ojai models, which feature a low step and doors that slide open and shut. Waymo is conducting more than 500,000 paid rides every week and has completed 270 million fully autonomous miles of commercial driving domestically. It currently has over 4,000 driverless vehicles in commercial operations in the U.S. Tesla had 45 Cybercabs authorized for commercial use in Texas at the time of its Austin unveiling, a number that rose to 169 as of Friday, according to Texas Department of Motor Vehicles' public records. Tesla's hometown of Austin is the only city where it currently operates Cybercab as part of its driverless ride-hail service. The company's Robotaxi fleet in Texas also includes 420 Model Y vehicles equipped with Tesla automated driving systems, which are not yet available to individual car buyers. Austin has emerged as a popular early market for robotaxis because of relatively lax state regulations and the capital city's vibrant tech community. Amazon's Zoox is also testing in Austin. Growing beyond Austin is the next challenge for Tesla's Cybercab. Beyond technical issues, the company faces potential regulatory hurdles to expansion. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) initiated a so-called audit query after the Cybercab launch to make sure the vehicles comply with federal safety standards. NHTSA originally ordered Tesla to respond by Sept. 30 to a long list of safety questions, but the company obtained an extension, an agency spokesperson told CNBC via email. Ethan McKanna, an Austin resident and former Tesla intern, told CNBC that he's taken rides in every type of autonomous vehicle available to public riders in the city. The 20-year-old McKanna, now a sophomore studying computer science at Texas A&M University, has also created a site called RobotaxiTracker.com , which uses machine learning to analyze data streaming in from traffic cameras and other public records, to show how autonomous services are working in U.S. cities. McKanna said he's caught about 30 Cybercab rides and has been taking Waymo rides since they debuted in Austin in 2024. With the Cybercab, McKanna said he likes having his "own space with access to a massive screen, media controls and apps," and he found the drive quality "very smooth." The "pick up, drop-off experience," he said, was not yet refined and the butterfly doors that extend out are "less convenient" than more traditional doors, or doors that slide open. It also takes patience, he said. "There was so much demand that wait times were often like 45 minutes plus," he said, referring to the period when the Cybercab first rolled out. That's come down with more "equalized demand," in recent weeks, he said.

events.title: 'Flying boat' history behind Sydney's first international airport
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts History behind Sydney's first international airport at Rose Bay, where flying boats were the norm Some may assume the new terminal in Western Sydney is the city's second international airport, but it is historically the third. Almost a century ago, Sydney experienced its golden age of aviation via flying boats. By the end of 1934, the first regular air mail service between Australia and England began. Flying boats were the chosen mode of transport as they could carry much larger freight loads than the land-based aircraft of the time, and had cheaper operating costs. Two Qantas Empire Airways flying boats at Rose Bay in 1939. ( Supplied: Mitchell Library, State Library of New South Wales ) That same year, Qantas Empire Airways was established as an international airline joint venture by Australia's Qantas and Britain's Imperial Airways. In 1938 the airline moved its operations from Brisbane to Sydney, settling on Rose Bay in the east thanks to its calm waters and central location. And so began the Rose Bay Water Airport. While Rose Bay's airport was mostly used for mail services, expensive travel also became a commodity for wealthy travellers. Flights travelled along the east coast to Singapore then via stops at Bangkok, Calcutta, Karachi, Alexandria, Basra, Marseilles and onto Southampton. Rose Bay became home to Sydney's first international airport in the 1930s. ( Supplied: Mitchell Library, State Library of New South Wales ) First class travel 'cream on the cake' While air mail was the financial basis for the Qantas Empire Airways flying boats system, "the cream on the cake" was its first class offerings for passengers. The Qantas Empire Airways route map. ( Supplied: Qantas Empire Airways ) David Crotty, former curator of the Qantas Heritage Collection, who still does consulting work with Qantas, said the return fair from Sydney to Southampton was about £342. "In those days it was a heck of a lot of money, considering you could buy a new Chevrolet car at that time in Sydney for about £330," he said. The air trip would take approximately nine and a half days, compared to a five week ship journey. "The flying boats typically took somewhere up to 15 passengers, and there were a series of cabins. In one cabin you could smoke … there was room to wander around and the seats could be reclined back." A Qantas promotional image of passengers. ( Supplied: Qantas Heritage Collection/Museums of History NSW ) It was the first time Australia had in-flight service, with Qantas employing stewards who had worked on ships. "They didn't cook on board but they had a little galley kitchen where warm meals could be served," Mr Crotty said. It was a brief but "romantic period" for aviation, because when World War II heightened, the service's travel offering ended so the flying boats could assist with military activities. How flying boats supported the war effort The flying boats played a number of roles during World War II. Civil Aviation Historical Society president Phil Vabre said this included shifting military equipment in Darwin to running services to Nouméa, which served as a base for the United States in the war. "Later on they were largely employed up and down the east coast ferrying personnel, cargo and mail up into New Guinea in support of the war," he said. "One by one they either were crashed, a couple were shot down … the air force had also taken some Empire flying boats early on in the piece." Flying boats played a vital role in World War II. ( Supplied: Mitchell Library, State Library of New South Wales ) It was not until after World War II that commercial land airports and their aircraft became more widely used. "Flying boats were commercially difficult to operate … there's a lot of difficulty operating off water for various reasons," Mr Vabre said. "During the war lots of big airports had been built all over the world and land planes had developed to a significant degree." A commemorative plaque remains at Rose Bay's waterfront promenade. ( ABC News: Liam Patrick ) Rose Bay Water Airport had quite an impact on Sydney. The first scheduled commercial passenger flight directly between Auckland and Sydney took place in 1940 on a Tasman Empire Airways Limited flying boat landing into Rose Bay. In its later years, the flying boats at Rose Bay were used for passengers travelling to and from Lord Howe Island until the island's land airport was built in 1974. Rose Bay Water Airport then closed that same year. Rose Bay today still has seaplanes for scenic trips around Sydney.

events.title: Federal judge calls Flock ‘indiscriminate mass surveillance’
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. A federal judge ruled this week that a Tulsa, Oklahoma sheriff’s deputy violated a woman’s Fourth Amendment rights when using Flock Safety to search for her license plate without a warrant. As reported by 404 Media , this ruling does not create a binding precedent, but it is one of the first times that a federal judge has ruled that a Flock search is unconstitutional. In this case, Judge Sara Hill said the deputy should have obtained a warrant before searching the Flock database for the woman’s license plate, as he had “no apparent reason” for the search “other than the fact that [the woman’s vehicle] had a California license plate.” The deputy then used the woman’s travel history in Flock as part of the justification for searching her car, where he allegedly discovered 91 pounds of meth. But Judge Hill wrote that all evidence obtained after the Flock search “must be suppressed as the fruit of a poisonous tree.” Judge Hill also took broader aim at warrantless searches of the Flock database, writing that tracking people’s location — even when they’re in public places — becomes “constitutionally problematic when law enforcement can indiscriminately and passively catalog your whereabouts over an extended period of time and then use that information for any purpose whenever convenient.” “This is a type of indiscriminate mass surveillance,” Hill wrote. “It is not targeted on a single individual, as in [ Carpenter v. United States , a Supreme Court case focused on how government agencies access location data from cell phones ]. It is a tool that collects information about all vehicles that pass by any network-connected camera at all times, and it serves up the information to law enforcement on demand.” Hill joins a growing chorus of Flock critics from across the political spectrum. Numerous local and state governments, including Florida and Texas , have said they will stop using the technology. And on Friday, Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the Block Flock Act , which would bar federal agencies from using automated license plate readers such as Flock. Flock CEO Garrett Langley — who we’ll be interviewing on-stage at TechCrunch Disrupt — has called for a “compromise” between privacy and safety and offered an apology to women who have been stalked by law enforcement officers using the Flock system. And with all those cancellations, Flock has also reportedly offered voluntary employee buyouts as a way to shrink its workforce. events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman said the company has stopped using nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) in its dealings with government agencies as it seeks approval to build new data centers. Garman’s statement is just one sentence in a longer blog post in which he tried to push back against widespread suspicion of data centers, and to make the case that they’re actually good for communities. NDAs are a significant piece of the broader data center backlash. For example, environmental activist Erin Brockovich recently said that the number one complaint she’s heard about data centers is transparency , with these projects following a common pattern: “projects announced after permits are already secured, developers who don’t return calls, local officials who signed NDAs before their neighbors knew a project was being considered.” As a result of that backlash, New York announced a one-year moratorium on permits for large data centers , and according to Garman, there are more than 100 data center moratoriums currently being considered across the United States. “If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations,” Garman claimed. “As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.” Garman also attempted to puncture what he said are four big myths around data centers: that they consume too much water, that they increase electricity costs, that they emit an enormous amount of pollution, and that they don’t provide any benefits to their communities. Pointing to an Amazon report about its own water usage , Garman said that “direct data center water consumption” only accounts for 0.5% of all industrial water usage in the United States, “orders of magnitude less than golf courses, almond farming, and many other industries.” Nvidia recently said its new cooling system eliminates “pretty much all water usage” inside the data center , but those claims — like Amazon’s — seem to ignore the broader water usage involved in electricity generation and chip manufacturing. Scientists have also said they need to study data centers’ water and energy usage independently , since there are no federal or state requirements around how tech companies report this data. As for electricity rates, Garman said they’ve only gone up in some states with large numbers of data centers, while they’ve gone down or at least grown more slowly in others. And he argued, “In instances where energy rates are going up, it’s primarily because the grid is old and hasn’t been invested in and expanded before the demand arrived.” On the other hand, an independent watchdog said recently data centers were the main culprit behind a 76% year-over-year price increase on America’s largest electrical grid. When it comes to pollution — an issue that the NAACP is currently suing Elon Musk’s SpaceX/xAI over — Garman complained that critics focus on the maximum amount of pollution allowed under data center permits. For example, a planned Amazon data center in Texas is permitted to release 33 million tons of carbon dioxide per year, which is more than any other power plant in the United States. “The truth is data center generators almost never run,” Garman said. “They’re idle 99.9% of the time (they run roughly 10 hours per year, mostly for required maintenance testing).” As for the community benefits, this is where Garman wrote, “We no longer use nondisclosure agreements with the government agencies we work with on our projects.” Plus, he said, “Over the past three years, Amazon has contributed more than $1 billion to communities across the U.S. in which we have a meaningful data center presence.” Will this be enough to quell community suspicion? Perhaps not — Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently argued that the AI backlash is “fundamentally a crisis of trust, ” where people assume governments and tech companies are always “cooking up some new way to screw them over.” Similarly, writer Jasmine Sun noted that when data center opponents are presented with the tech companies’ arguments, their response is usually, “I don’t believe them.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Can you really rely on your phone to save you in a bushfire?
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts When a bushfire comes, what happens if the phones go dead? Who warns you of disaster when your mobile fails? One community has a plan On January 8, 2026, Victorian authorities began warning a catastrophic fire rating had been declared for the following day. Conditions would be "the most dangerous experienced this summer", the Country Fire Authority (CFA) said. One brigade in central Victoria issued a clarion call on social media: "160 people died on Black Saturday in the district 12 response area" on a similarly risky day. Further west, in Castlemaine, Fiannuala Morgan was encouraging her parents to leave their property in the bone-dry, flinty hills outside of town. Fiannuala would be staying in Castlemaine, a town of about 7,000 people etched out of gold rush-era buildings and wide, sleepy streets. By 9 o'clock the following morning, it was 31 degrees. "I was aware of this catastrophic rating but did not have an integrated sense of what that actually meant," Fiannuala tells me. "Because when the fire started, it really went from zero to 100 in a matter of seconds." Everything seemed to happen at once. When a ferocious hot wind arrived, it was as if the door of a giant oven had burst open. The power went out. The emergency app on Fiannuala's phone lit up, showing multiple fires had started. "And then my phone stopped working, but not completely," she says. "The first thing that happened was my emergency app froze. And then I tried to call my mother, and I couldn't get through on the phone. I tried to send a text to either my mother or my father, and that didn't work either." A few kilometres away, a grass fire was racing through paddocks towards the nearby orchard town of Harcourt, known for its juicy apples. Fiannuala knew about the fire because she was able to call her brother in Melbourne, even though other calls were failing. "So then, he was updating me about what was happening on the VicEmergency app." At some point, Fiannuala left her house and walked up a nearby hill to try to get reception. From the hill she watched as a thick cloud of smoke turned the blue sky an ominous shade of orange. Her brother told her the wind was pushing the fire towards Castlemaine. "I had always thought that Castlemaine was a very safe place if there was a fire but suddenly you realise, oh gosh, there's actually nowhere in these conditions that is safe," she says. Back at home Fiannuala put her Persian cat in the bath because the air conditioning had dropped out along with the power. The blackout had also rendered the NBN useless . She didn't have a backup battery-powered radio, so she turned on her car radio to listen to the ABC's emergency broadcast. "But by that point," she says, "the broadcasting tower at Mount Alexander had burned". Alone, and with dwindling access to information, she decided to find her parents, who were now sheltering at a friend's house nearby. "It was not responsible of me to go," she says. "There were no traffic lights … people were driving erratically." Fiannuala found that her parents had patchy mobile phone signals and couldn't access the emergency apps either. "Sometimes you could use your phone and sometimes you couldn't," she says. As the afternoon progressed, emergency warnings "to shelter indoors now" were being issued for nearby Harcourt. The fast-moving grassfire would eventually destroy 66 dwellings. The only certainty was that there wasn't any. Some houses and business were mangled, blackened wrecks, others stood undamaged beside them. Lives were up-ended. But a wind change turned the flames away from the larger town of Castlemaine. For Fiannuala, a lecturer in publishing and communications at the University of Melbourne, the day brought a "completely new awareness of risk". She has channelled the experience into understanding why multiple forms of communication failed and what that means for regional communities in Australia facing increasingly severe natural disasters in an era of climate crisis. The communication networks that support essential services like bushfire warnings have "not been adequately strengthened", she has warned , and recent changes, like the rollout of the NBN, the retirement of copper-wire landlines (which were more reliable during power outages), and the shutdown of the 3G network, have left communities like Castlemaine dangerously unaware of the fragility of the communication systems they should be able to rely on in an emergency. There is every chance that the next time this happens, the outcome could be fatal.
