events.title: Verity is the latest Colleen Hoover novel to get a film adaptation
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Verity Crawford (Anne Hathaway) is a renowned author who seeks help in the film Verity. ( Supplied: Amazon MGM Studios ) Hollywood loves a Colleen Hoover adaptation. The latest is psychological thriller Verity. In the film, struggling writer Lowen Ashleigh (Dakota Johnson) is hired as a ghostwriter for renowned author Verity Crawford (Oscar winner Anne Hathaway). It starts out as an assignment taken under mysterious circumstances, with Lowen recruited by Verity's husband, Jeremy (Josh Hartnett). Lowen Ashleigh (Dakota Johnson) is a struggling author hired as a ghostwriter. ( Supplied: Amazon MGM Studios ) But when Lowen uncovers what appears to be chilling autobiographical confessions in Verity's notes, she wrestles with these disturbing and twisted revelations. Verity is a glossy thriller punctuated by its beautiful people and slick presentation. It's a fun watch that ends on a tantalising cliffhanger, which is almost as scandalous as it is unexpectedly satisfying. Verity is married to Jeremy Crawford (Josh Hartnett). ( Supplied: Amazon MGM Studios ) But critics have both emphatically praised the film and have had scathing reactions. The Sydney Morning Herald called Verity "perfect for these post-truth times". Mamamia referred to it as a "delicious" thriller. But The Nightly called it "diabolical", saying it was "embarrassing" for its A-list stars to be "dragged" into the film. Who, meanwhile, has categorised it as a "straight to DVD territory" type of movie. One of Hoover's biggest outings since It Ends with Us As far as Hoover adaptations go, Verity comes after Reminders of Him (2026) and Regretting You (2025), but the internet is still talking about 2024's It Ends with Us. Justin Baldoni and Blake Lively settle legal battle over It Ends With Us scandal The pair settle their civil case two weeks before a trial had been set to begin in New York. That movie was overshadowed by the off-screen drama between its two stars, Blake Lively and Justin Baldoni. They have settled their legal battles in a civil case. Lively had alleged Baldoni conspired with publicists to pre-emptively destroy her reputation after she privately accused him of sexually harassing her on the movie set. From Misery to Yellowface, books about writers are favourites among the authors who pen them, and audiences also love a behind-the-scenes look at the literary world. It's fertile ground for novelists writing about a world they're familiar with, setting the stakes high in an imagined narrative. The authentic details an author can bring to such a story are what make them so spicy and alluring as they blend reality and fiction. Verity is based on the worldwide best-selling novel of the same name by Hoover. Colleen Hoover is a trailblazer. ( Eric Charbonneau/Getty Images for Sony Pictures ) In 2012, Hoover was the first self-published author to top The New York Times bestseller list, which she did again with Verity in 2018, and is a pioneer of modern indie publishing. She has since had a great deal of mainstream success. Verity was Hoover's first thriller. She had already authored 16 romance books prior to that and amassed millions of fans. In adapting the novel, director Michael Showalter aimed to produce a film as closely aligned with the book as possible. "The book is a big hit, people love it, so let's make a movie out of the book," Showalter said. "My approach was to do it the way it was in the book wherever possible. "Let people see what a true adaptation would look and feel like and honour that." events.title: G7 to release millions of barrels of oil and diesel after Trump threat
events.summary: The G7 has announced 100 million barrels of oil and diesel will be released to ease supply concerns that have caused prices to skyrocket. It includes a "substantial release" of diesel within 20 days, with discussions around "additional diesel releases as necessary", G7 leaders said in a statement. The group of advanced economies, including the US, said the move would begin immediately and would last for four months. Under the measures, which come after US President Donald Trump had threatened to ban diesel exports , there will not be any "export restrictions on energy and energy products" between G7 members. The G7 includes the US, UK, Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France, with the EU also represented at its meetings. Donald Trump had warned he would ban diesel exports from the US if European countries did not agree to put more of their own stocks onto the market. That would have eased pressure on prices for US consumers ahead of November's midterm elections, but pushed up prices elsewhere. On Friday, he said on social media: "Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately." His Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had argued US farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar. Speaking later at the White House, Trump said an export ban on diesel was "never really on the table". Referring to the decision by the G7 to release fuel from reserves, he added that "what Europe did was a great thing." "Europe has a lot of diesel and they're going to be making a major world contribution - and so are we," he said. "And we're not going to be doing the export ban, we're going to be doing what we're supposed to do." Trump had first said he backed a diesel export ban early last week, and was still considering it on Thursday, as his administration put pressure on Europe to tap its supplies. Diesel is used heavily by the haulage industry and in agriculture, meaning rises in the cost of the fuel feed through into essentials such as food. Emmanuel Macron chaired a meeting of G7 leaders to agree the release of fuel reserves Following a meeting of G7 leaders, French President Emmanuel Macron said the bloc had agreed to release reserves of "up to 100 million barrels" within four months under the co-ordination of the International Energy Agency (IEA). The UK was represented at the meeting by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who said the measures would "stabilise energy supplies, build resilience in supply chains and shield households and businesses from price shocks". Macron said the co-ordinated action would "bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel". Highlighting the agreement not to pursue export bans, Macron said "President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point". In the joint statement, G7 leaders said: "We will implement our commitments with a co-ordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels to begin immediately over four months, including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners." It is not yet clear which partner countries will release stocks, nor how quickly. The 100 million barrels will comprise a mix of diesel and crude oil. The price of global benchmark Brent crude oil briefly dropped below $100 a barrel, but rose back to around $102 by Friday evening. Before the US and Israel invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73. Matt Smith, director of commodities research at Kpler, said oil had risen again due to renewed strikes between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen. "Oil prices were selling off strongly due to the announcement of strategic stock releases in Europe, but they reversed course on rumours of Saudi Arabia planning an offensive into Yemen as it looks to re-establish a safe path via Bab-Al Mandeb," he said. European countries had pushed back against US threats to turn off American diesel, against a backdrop of the US-led war in the Middle East and reduced supplies from Russia and China. The G7 leaders said they will also co-ordinate maintenance schedules to avoid multiple refineries being shut down at the same time, while encouraging countries with the capacity to do so to ramp up refining of diesel in particular. Watch: Why did Trump threaten to ban US diesel exports? Avoiding a ban on US diesel exports will offer significant relief to countries which are reliant on imports of the fuel, including the UK, where prices at the pump topped £2 a litre for the first time on Friday . Over half of the UK's diesel is imported, with 31% of those imports coming from the US. The US is one of the world's leading diesel suppliers, with domestic refineries churning out roughly four to five million barrels every day, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA). Americans consume about 3.6 million barrels of that.

events.title: UAE Property: 'Who pays to install an EV charger at a rented villa?'
events.summary: Question: I rent a villa in Dubai and recently bought an electric car. There is no charging point at the property, so I asked my landlord whether I could have one installed at my own expense. He initially agreed, but is now saying that because the charger will remain with the villa when I eventually leave, I should also pay for any approvals, electrical upgrades and reinstatement, if required. The community management told me I cannot simply appoint an electrician and install one myself. With more people buying electric cars in Dubai, I imagine this is going to become a common issue. Who is responsible for getting permission, and if I pay for something that ultimately improves the landlord's property , can I take the charger with me when I leave? James, Dubai Answer: This is an interesting issue and one I suspect we'll see much more frequently as electric vehicle ownership increases. I would not install anything without written approval. An EV charger isn't simply an appliance you plug into the wall; it can involve alterations to the property's electrical infrastructure and, potentially, the community's systems, so the landlord and relevant community or building management may need to approve the installation. The question of who pays is largely something for you and the landlord to agree on. If you're requesting the charger for your personal use, it's reasonable that the landlord may expect you to meet the installation cost. Equally, you're correct that a professionally installed charging point potentially becomes an improvement to his property and could make it more attractive to future tenants. I'd therefore negotiate before spending anything. Agree in writing who pays for the equipment, installation, approvals and electricity consumption, and importantly, what happens when your tenancy ends . If the charger can be removed without damaging the property, you may want the agreement to allow you to take it. Alternatively, if the landlord wants it left behind, perhaps he contributes towards the installation. This is ultimately less about who is “right” and more about documenting the arrangement properly. The mistake would be spending thousands of dirhams improving somebody else's property and only discussing ownership of the equipment when you're moving out. Q: My wife and I bought an off-plan apartment in Dubai largely because of the view shown to us when we purchased. The sales presentation, brochure and agent all made a big point of the open waterfront view and we paid considerably more for that particular unit. Construction is now well advanced, but we've discovered another building is planned on the plot directly in front of ours. The developer says master plans evolve and that our sales and purchase agreement (SPA) doesn't guarantee a permanent view. I appreciate Dubai is constantly developing , but if somebody pays a premium specifically because a property is marketed with a particular view, surely the developer cannot simply change it afterwards? Do buyers have any protection in this situation? Jonathan, London A: This is a very good example of why buyers need to distinguish between what is shown in the marketing material and what is actually contractually guaranteed. A beautiful rendering showing uninterrupted water, golf-course or skyline views doesn't necessarily amount to a contractual promise that those views will remain forever. The starting point should therefore be your SPA, together with the approved plans and any documents incorporated into the sale. Look particularly for provisions allowing the developer to modify the master plan, surrounding plots, building configuration or overall development programme. I would also retain the original brochure, emails, WhatsApp conversations and anything else demonstrating how the apartment was represented when you purchased it. If you were specifically charged a premium for a particular view and this can be evidenced, that information could become important. I would also ask the developer for details of the proposed building and establish whether it was already part of an approved master plan when you purchased or represents a subsequent change. Those are potentially quite different circumstances. The fact that the view influenced your decision doesn't automatically establish that you're entitled to compensation, but if something material was expressly represented and the eventual product differs substantially, it's certainly worth obtaining independent legal advice. There's also an important lesson here for anyone buying off-plan . Don't simply ask the agent what your apartment overlooks today. Ask who owns the land in front of it, what that plot is designated for and what could legally be built there in the future. In a rapidly developing city like Dubai, today's empty plot isn't necessarily tomorrow's view. The opinions expressed do not constitute legal advice and are provided for information only. events.summary: President Trump's top cabinet members huddled for hours at Camp David on Friday to discuss next steps in the Iran war and the Saudi-Houthi conflict in Yemen, three U.S. officials told Axios. The last time a similar meeting took place was in June 2025, just days before Israel went to war against Iran. Behind the scenes: Vice President Vance chaired the meeting, the officials said. Among the other participants were Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, White House envoy Steve Witkoff, CIA director John Ratcliffe, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. "Things were decided or at least deeply discussed," one of the officials said, referring to the crisis in the Middle East. The White House declined to comment. Driving the news: With negotiations stalled, President Trump is considering resuming major combat operations in Iran. "Now I have to make a decision: either Iran signs the deal, or it won't exist any longer," he said on Thursday. At the same time, Trump is being asked to join Saudi Arabia's planned offensive against the Houthis in Yemen. The Saudis are urging the president to conduct airstrikes against the Houthis. Trump has been leaning against it, but U.S. officials say he could change his mind. What he's saying: On Friday afternoon, while his advisers were at Camp David, Trump was asked by reporters what his next move on Iran will be. "If I told you, you would have a major story," he said. "But you will see. It is working out very well. Iran is not doing well."

Meta’s Muse, a personal AI agent that books travel, fills out forms, and shops on a user’s behalf, has already proven popular with the masses, but a new side project could be particularly alluring to tinkerers and hackers. On Friday, the company introduced Muse Gadgets , an open-source project that lets developers build their own hardware that connects to Muse. Meta is providing open-source firmware (the low-level software that runs a device), and a Linux software development kit (SDK), along with a few project ideas to get users started. These include giving Muse a color e-ink display or loading it onto a stick that plugs into a TV’s HDMI port. There don’t appear to be many limits, either. Users can set up a low-cost hobbyist computer like a Raspberry Pi or an off-the-shelf ESP32 board, and then connect Muse “to your displays, buttons, sensors, actuators, and whatever else you’ve got lying on your workbench,” Meta notes. The company has also set up a Discord channel to support users. Meta has already tried the code itself, naturally. Nat Friedman, head of product at Meta’s Superintelligence Labs, said in a post on X that the company built a gadget called Muse Home Link. The USB-C-powered device lets Muse connect to a home network and talk to the smart devices on it, including speakers and smart TVs. Meta made 5,000 of these Home Links, in fact, and is giving them away for free to Muse subscribers while supplies last, according to Friedman. Considering Friedman’s post about Home Link received nearly 30,000 views in a few hours, we’re guessing those freebies have been claimed. Friedman said Home Link would be ready to ship a few weeks. Muse Gadgets may not have wide appeal, but it fits nicely into Meta’s all-in strategy to make Muse more than a standalone chatbot. Meta isn’t content to push Muse on everyday consumers; it’s also trying to woo small businesses and enterprises. The company earlier this week introduced Muse for Small Business, which is free with usage limits and connects Muse to tools such as Shopify, Dropbox, and Slack. It has also launched a new business unit, Meta Enterprise Platform, to help it push its AI offerings to businesses and corporate customers. events.title: Sanders introduces bill to ban the federal government from using Flock
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Flock Safety, whose cameras scan license plates across the country, continues to draw public anger, and now Senator Bernie Sanders wants the federal government out of the business altogether. Sanders on Friday introduced the Ban Flock Act , which would bar federal agencies from using automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) or tapping into data collected by readers run by local police and private companies. Despite its title, the bill doesn’t call out nine-year-old Flock in the text but rather covers any and all ALPR systems. The bill allows exceptions only for toll collection and for uses that Congress approves in future legislation, which would have to limit data retention to 48 hours. State and local governments would be dinged financially for not complying if the bill became law. (Like most bills, this one faces long odds.) Starting the first fiscal year after enactment, they would lose grants from five federal departments, including the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security, unless they ban the tech. Americans could also sue the federal government over violations, and state attorneys general could enforce the law. Flock is the largest ALPR vendor in the U.S., according to Sanders, with more than 120,000 cameras. In a blog post back in February, the company — currently valued by its venture backers at north of $8 billion — said its network processes more than 20 billion vehicle reads each month. Under increasing pressure from communities that are protesting the product, suspending their use , and, at an escalating rate, canceling their contracts, Flock has tightened its rules. In August, CEO Garrett Langley, who’d previously said that how police use the cameras is up to local agencies, announced a new default data retention period of seven days, down from 30. Customers must also now use an audit tool that locks officers out pending review when it flags unusual searches. In one of the highest-profile cases of an officer abusing Flock’s platform, a former Milwaukee officer pleaded guilty to misconduct after searching for his then-partner and her ex 179 times, listing the reason as “investigation.” (During a recent podcast interview, investor Jason Calacanis suggested a “double-key” system in which two people must approve a search, and Langley said the idea is “on the whiteboard.”) Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Senator Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) are co-sponsors. events.title: Saudis plan major offensive against the Houthis, but U.S. won't join for now
events.summary: Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces are planning a major counteroffensive against Iran-backed Houthis in the coming days — an effort to push them away from areas on the Red Sea coast that control the Strait of Bab al-Mandeb, two U.S. officials say. Why it matters: For the second time in recent weeks, the U.S. rebuffed Saudi pleas to join the operation and conduct airstrikes. But U.S. officials say that could change if the operation runs into problems. The Bab al-Mandeb Strait is a vital artery for global trade and Saudi oil exports. Control over it gives the Houthis and their Iranian backer a powerful new point of leverage over the U.S., its Gulf allies and the world economy. Driving the news: In recent weeks, the Houthis took over key areas of the southern Red Sea coast that control the strait. They also increased missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia. The Saudis retaliated with airstrikes against Houthi targets. Behind the scenes: A U.S. official said the Saudis have been planning the operation for weeks and that plans were approved by Saudi leadership several days ago. The operation will include ground forces loyal to the internationally recognized government in Yemen with Saudi air cover. On Thursday, Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid Bin Salman called Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to brief him on the planned operation and ask again for U.S. airstrikes against Houthi targets, the U.S. official said. A U.S. official said that the U.S. "is not going to take kinetic action for now." Last week, President Trump was close to ordering a strike on the Houthis after a request from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS), but eventually decided to hold off . Between the lines: Trump is caught between wanting to help his friend and ally MBS, and avoiding getting entangled in a new front in the Middle East. The U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) also had serious reservations about launching strikes in Yemen and saw it as a distraction from its focus on Iran, a U.S. official said. Zoom in: U.S. officials say the U.S. military is helping the Saudis with everything short of direct combat, mainly intelligence and targeting data. One U.S. official said that in the last two weeks, the U.S. military provided the Saudis with more than 200 Houthi targets to strike. The official said the strikes significantly increased pressure on the Houthis.

events.title: Complaint over senior NT public servant who ran private NDIS provider
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Senior NT public servant was sole director of private NDIS company in Alice Springs for years Kudzai Mutsunge ran the NDIS business Life Aspects while holding senior roles in the NT Department of Children and Families. ( ABC News Graphics: Jess Henderson ) A senior public servant responsible for child and family support in Central Australia was simultaneously running a National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) provider company in Alice Springs. The Department of Children and Families has confirmed it forwarded a complaint about her involvement in the NDIS provider Life Aspects to an integrity process. The status of the process remains unclear. Documents obtained by the ABC show the department has recently strengthened its internal conflict of interest procedures, especially for staff with the power to influence NDIS referrals. A senior Northern Territory public servant responsible for child and family services in Central Australia spent nearly three years as the sole director of a private National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) provider in Alice Springs, and for 15 months also owned a 50 per cent stake in the business's parent company. The Department of Children and Families plays a significant role in the NDIS system in the NT, with the most recent figures from 2024 showing more than 300 children in its care had active NDIS plans. An ABC investigation has confirmed public servant Kudzai Mutsunge ran the NDIS business Life Aspects while holding senior roles in the Department of Children and Families, and held shares in the business's parent company, Japhin The Teacher Pty Ltd, from December 2024 to February 2026. Life Aspects is registered to provide a range of disability services, including assistance with independent living and support coordination, an area that involves arranging other providers for people with disability. Kudzai Mutsunge was the sole director of Life Aspects for almost three years. ( Supplied ) The ABC has seen no evidence that any child in the care of the department was a Life Aspects client. The department has referred a complaint about a potential conflict of interest to an internal integrity process. Ms Mutsunge wound up her directorship and shareholding in Life Aspects earlier this year, one week before an anonymous complaint was sent to the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission in March. A separate complaint went to the Department of Children and Families in August, from the Alice Springs-based Disability Advocacy Service (DAS). On August 21, the department told the service it had referred the information "through the appropriate internal integrity processes" and was coordinating with the National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) "where relevant". The outcome of that process, if any, is unknown. In response to questions from the ABC, the department declined to say whether Ms Mutsunge had declared a potential conflict of interest or sought approval for outside work, saying it could not comment on individual employment or conduct matters. Kudzai Mutsunge ran the NDIS business Life Aspects while holding senior roles in the Department of Children and Families. ( ABC News: James Elton ) The ABC understands Ms Mutsunge quit the department on September 11. Ms Mutsunge said she did not "endorse or agree to the allegations or characterisations" put to her by the ABC about whether her roles presented a potential conflict of interest, and said she could not respond to further questions within the timeframe provided. Under the NT public service code of conduct, employees must declare any perceived, potential or actual conflicts of interest in writing to their chief executive. The department's acting chief executive Karen Broadfoot said it had "zero tolerance" for a failure to declare a conflict. Ms Broadfoot said that where integrity matters involved the NDIS, the department would also coordinate with the Australian Federal Police when relevant. The NDIA said it could not comment on ongoing investigations. DAS chief executive Scott Richardson said government officials needed to be held to a higher standard on potential NDIS conflicts, to ensure they "don't have access to participant information that they could then benefit from, or family could benefit from". DAS chief executive Scott Richardson says government officials should be held to a higher standard on potential NDIS conflicts. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) In a meeting in March, Ms Mutsunge reportedly told DAS staff that she was "operationally removed" from placement decisions, and denied any role in referring children to NDIS providers.

events.title: Tracing Hardware Design From Physical Devices to RTL (Infineon, TU Munich)
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at Infineon Technologies and Technical University of Munich published a technical paper titled “From Physical Devices to RTL Models: Abstraction and Validation in Hardware Engineering.” “This paper introduces the foundational principles underlying hardware engineering models and argues that abstraction is their defining characteristic. Because abstraction necessarily omits detail and constrains what engineers can build, models are inherently incomplete in specific respects – or, as George Box famously observed, “All models are wrong, but some are useful”. At the same time, abstraction is essential for simplification, which is key to managing complexity. More abstract models also tend to simulate faster because fewer details must be considered. This paper subsequently examines a range of abstraction methods in digital design – sometimes referred to as design disciplines – including lumped models, value-discrete models, and time-discrete models. Together with constraints that define the validity of the abstraction and design guidelines, these abstraction methods establish design disciplines. This paper further relates these forms of abstraction to pre-clustered design elements such as transistors, gates, registers, and transfer functions. events.title: Golf club spends $30k on water changes, only for policy to change
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Mowbray Golf Club spends $30k on water changes, only for TasWater to change policy General manager Hayden Roberts says the club has taken a financial hit for no reason. ( ABC News: Morgan Timms ) Businesses and sporting clubs faced significant bill increases from July 1 after a TasWater policy change on sewerage charges. Some decided to change their water connections, on the advice of TasWater, only for the billing system to then be changed again. One golf club is calling for compensation after spending $30,000 on changes that have now been made void following the policy change. A golf club in Launceston is calling for compensation from TasWater after spending an estimated $30,000 on water infrastructure works in response to billing changes, which were then essentially reversed. Mowbray Golf Club saw its water bill double from $20,000 to about $40,000 due to a TasWater policy change to charge based on the size of a water pipe connection, rather than sewerage usage, from July 1. The charge was based on the club's 100-millimetre connection, which it says it only uses in drought conditions and instead relies on its own storage for irrigation. In response, the club decided to sever the 100mm connection and connect its clubhouse and other services to its 50mm connection at significant cost. The club says it decided to sever its 100mm connection on the advice of TasWater. ( ABC News: Morgan Timms ) It increased fees for its members by 10 per cent to help pay for the works. Club general manager Hayden Roberts said they chose to go ahead with the works after being told by TasWater that reducing connection size was the easiest method. "I know we're not the only ones that have done such," he said. On Friday, TasWater announced a change in response to concerns from businesses and sporting clubs. It would take fixed sewerage charges from $20,000 to under $1,000 and charge 100mm connections as 20mm connections, with refunds offered for bills paid since July 1. The change came too late for Mowbray Golf Club, however. "I think it's only reasonable at this point that TasWater remediates these situations, whether it be credit or an outright refund of works completed. "We've actually lost an asset in the process of this removal of connection." TasWater says changes had 'unintended consequences' TasWater contacted the club in response to the policy change but had not made assurances regarding compensation. Callan Paske from TasWater says the changes had unintended consequences. ( ABC News ) TasWater general manager of customers and community Callan Paske said the water authority was aware of other clubs and businesses that had made changes to their connections based on TasWater advice. "We're working with those impacted clubs to ensure that we can work through what the final solution is for them," he said. The change in sewerage charging followed an inquiry by the Tasmanian Economic Regulator, which required TasWater to move from an equivalent charging method to a fixed and variable method. This is similar to methods used in other states. Mr Paske said it had disproportionately impacted sporting clubs and businesses, which was addressed by the change announced on Friday. "What this shows is that in any tariff reform there is nuance and we need to fix those outlier impacts that are in unintended consequences of major change," he said. Water infrastructure challenges remain TasWater again faces a challenge in how to fund upgrades to its aging infrastructure. The changes have hit its bottom line by between $7 million and $14 million, according to Mr Paske. "We've got aging infrastructure, failing pipes, we've got growth that we need to cater for, and we've got environmental impacts that we're having that are not what Tasmanians want to see," he said. The change came following discussions between TasWater, the economic regulator, councils and the state government. Premier Jeremy Rockliff said it was a "significant and lasing outcome" for businesses and sporting clubs. Shadow treasurer Dean Winter said the government had the power to veto TasWater's corporate plan, and questioned why this had not occurred following successive significant price increases.

events.title: How employees forced OpenAI’s president to back down
events.summary: The Scoop On June 1, OpenAI chief strategy officer Jason Kwon gave employees a preview of a blog post denying the company had any connection to Leading the Future, a super PAC established to defend AI from regulation. OpenAI president Greg Brockman’s support for the super PAC “has been in a personal capacity, not on behalf of the company,” Kwon wrote in an internal Slack message. Not everyone on his staff bought it. One OpenAI employee took to Slack to warn of a dangerous trade-off: The company’s aggressive political activity threatened to drive researchers to Anthropic, and hamstring OpenAI in the all-out race to recursively self-improving AI. The post earned 24 “agree” reactions and a solitary eyes emoji. The next day, Kwon gave ground to a different internal critic: The company, he said on Slack, was “taking reputational hits.” They had drawn “some clear public lines,” but “I wish we’d done it even sooner.” Ten days after Kwon’s post, Brockman backed out of the second half of his public $50 million commitment, saying he felt “terrible about the fact that LTF keeps reflecting on the company” in a post first reported by The New York Times. Brockman’s message received 40 hearts, five checkmarks, and three thank-you emojis. The episode, part of a set of Slack messages shared with Semafor, offers a window into the complex internal politics of the handful of companies shaping the global future of artificial intelligence. Outsiders observing the tribal world of San Francisco frontier labs often see OpenAI as the “accelerationist” cousin to the safety-oriented Anthropic. The rare glimpse inside the company’s Slack illustrates a more complex reality: Many of OpenAI’s developers, engineers, and researchers — whom the company is fighting to keep in intense talent wars whose bidders also include Meta, Google, and an array of startups — aren’t sanguine about unregulated AI. And they dislike being associated with the political group’s aggressive tactics. A spokeswoman for OpenAI declined to comment. One employee initially placated by Kwon’s post followed up two days later flagging that Brockman’s money would be used to fund an X account the employee described as “an LTF sockpuppet ( confirmed here ) that posts stuff like “ [sam altman is] a caterpillar that murders insects and stitches their dismembered body parts onto its back as armor .” (Twenty-two other employees responded, “WTF.“) A source familiar with the situation told Semafor that employee pushback was definitely part of Brockman’s decision, but that he had his own qualms that began with LTF targeting New York Assemblymember Alex Bores, an AI safety advocate running for Congress in New York. The person said that Brockman had expected the PAC to focus more on supporting allied candidates. The people running LTF appeared not to understand the complex internal dynamics of frontier safety policy — and how the whole industry would react to attacking someone running on that platform. At different points, the person added, Brockman gave pointed feedback to LTF; the source noted they hadn’t heard of the PAC attacking candidates since Bores. Since then, the PAC has overwhelmingly donated to front-runners in congressional races. And candidates LTF has endorsed or implicitly supported have come out in favor of a bill from Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar that would pause frontier AI development and criminalize attempting to build superintelligence, OpenAI’s stated goal . Leading the Future LTF launched in August 2025, well before AI became a major public issue. The group boasted more than $100 million in commitments, with $50 million to come from Brockman and his wife Anna. OpenAI’s global affairs chief Chris Lehane had helped set up the PAC, which followed a model he pioneered for the crypto industry. OpenAI sought to characterize the PAC as a totally independent entity, but employees — encouraged by critics on X — were skeptical. Staff were complaining about the connection in February, Wired reported, and Transformer reported that employees confronted Lehane in a meeting in May, pushing the company to explain its relationship with LTF. Kwon’s June 1 Slack message sought to defuse the controversy. “Many have posted questions,” he wrote, about the nature of the relationship between OpenAI and LTF. At the end of the multi-paragraph message, he concluded, “Thank you to everyone who has given feedback on this topic and pushed for a stronger company statement, in particular” before tagging three employees. It worked — for about an hour. More than 80 employees reacted with approving emojis, and the first reply was excited and appreciative. But then others questioned the group’s independence, highlighted LTF’s controversial and backfiring track record, and worried about the super PAC’s toxic effect on OpenAI’s brand and retention of senior researchers. The messages were shared with Semafor on the condition that they not be quoted directly out of concern that employees would feel uncomfortable seeing their messages reproduced verbatim, potentially chilling future Slacktivism. The dispute flared up again on June 11. One worker posted a Transformer article in which the director of LTF’s sister lobbying group, Build American AI (BAAI), which does not disclose its donors, texted journalist Veronica Irwin, “For this project I’m funded by four separate entities … OpenAI is just one of them” (OpenAI told Irwin and other journalists that the company had not provided funding to the groups). Just over an hour later, Brockman weighed in for the first time, denying the story’s claim that OpenAI backed BAAI and assuring staff that he’d given nothing to the organization (though as employees noted later in the thread, LTF gives money to BAAI). He then apologized for how LTF reflected on the company and abandoned his additional $25 million donation. Initially, responses in the thread under Kwon’s post ping-ponged between appreciation and recrimination, with approving Slack reactions hovering in the 20s and 30s for each variety. But skepticism and pointed questions mounted. A day later, Kwon weighed in again, addressing a disappointed employee. “I generally agree with what you’re saying, including the part about taking reputational hits for their activities. This is one of the reasons it made sense for us to draw some clear public lines about what we don’t condone. I wish we’d done it even sooner,” he wrote. “I don’t think we are asking people to believe that separation of scope and control means no accountability. I can’t speak for Greg but it does seem like LTF is in the process of adjusting. I interpret that as accountability in action.” Kwon also noted that Brockman had only provided “a fraction” of LTF’s funding. “Critics stick it on him / us because we are visible, and what that means is that we have to be even more visible about our own things,” he wrote. “That includes what we’re for and the types of political tactics we do not condone. events.title: Fishers warn snapper, kingfish prices could soar under proposed catch limits
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Snapper, yellowtail kingfish price could soar under proposed catch limits Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry Fishers say stricter limits would see snapper and kingfish prices rise. ( ABC Coffs Coast: Claire Simmonds ) Stricter limits have been proposed for snapper and yellowtail kingfish to help rebuild stocks in NSW fisheries. Commercial and recreational fishers are opposed to the changes. The NSW government has extended the consultation period for the proposed changes until February 15. Seafood shops and fishers are warning snapper and yellowtail kingfish could become unaffordable if catch limits are tightened. Both species are popular menu items, but stocks of kingfish in particular were described as "dangerously low" in a recent statement from the NSW Agriculture Minister Tara Moriarty. The state government has proposed reducing the annual kingfish catch from 250 tonnes to 120 tonnes a year. The snapper take would remain at 300 tonnes a year, but the proposal would include commercial monthly catch limits and a bag limit of three, with only one over 70 centimetres for recreational fishers. Naeco Blue Seafood's Adam Hambley says he cannot see people willing to pay any more for snapper and kingfish. ( Supplied: Adam Hambley ) Adam Hambley, who owns a seafood shop in South Grafton in northern NSW, said stricter limits would lead to higher prices. "If we see a $5 increase on the whole fish, we're going to see a $20 increase in the fillet, so you're going to near $80-90 a kilo for snapper fillets… I don't believe that anyone here will pay that much," he said. On a regular day, Noel Gogerly would pull in up to 40 kilograms of snapper while commercially fishing at Tuncurry on the NSW mid north coast. Under the proposed reforms, he would be allowed 10 kilograms, which he estimated would cost him up to $300 a day. Fisherman Noel Gogerly says the changes could cost him hundreds of dollars a day. ( ABC News: Lauren Bohane ) Mr Gogerly said any fish thrown back were unlikely to survive due to internal damage caused by the pressure change when pulled from the deep ocean. "You're going to have snapper just laying on top of the water," he said. Charter operators and recreational fishers are also worried. Under the changes yellowtail kingfish limits would drop from five per person to one per boat. Charter fishing operator Craig McGill said the proposed changes would ruin his business. Craig McGill says if the proposed changes to catch limits for yellowtail kingfish are implemented it could destroy his business. ( ABC News: Supplied ) "That would probably be the end of me," he said. "I get four guys on board; for me to have to tell them that they've got to share one kingfish, or that one guy gets to take one kingfish and the others can't catch one … they all pay a premium to come charter fishing with me." Michael Mashado estimated the proposed changes would cost his tackle store in Eden, on the NSW far south coast, up to $200,000 in sales per year. "Nobody's going to come and buy the quantity of gear to go and catch one kingfish or three snapper," he said. Mr Mashado said fishing was one of the south coast's biggest tourism industries. Michael Mashado says the proposed changes could have a broader impact on local towns where fishing is a major tourist attraction. ( Supplied ) "If you look at a family that comes here with a big boat, they spend [money] in the tackle shop, they spend it at the pub, they spend it at the supermarket," he said. The DPIRD said the proposal aimed to allow historically depleted fish stocks to recover, while still allowing some commercial and recreational catch. "We know approximately recreational fishers take about 50 per cent of the catch, as do commercial fishers, for both of these species," DPIRD director of fisheries management Heath Folpp said. Public consultation on the proposed changes was extended until mid-February in response to industry concerns. Fishers have warned any snapper thrown back would likely not survive.

events.title: Big Bend border wall construction blocked by judge
events.summary: A federal judge blocked the Trump administration from pursuing border wall construction in the Big Bend region in Texas on Friday. The big picture: The construction inside the national park sparked local outrage and environmental concerns, with Friday's decision handing the Department of Homeland Security a loss in its quest to rapidly expand the Southwestern border wall. Driving the news: The administration is barred, for now, from building border barrier or infrastructure — or engaging in any " construction or ground disturbing activities" — in the Big Bend sector, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone said in a brief order . The administration paused border wall construction in the park back in August, with U.S. Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott saying he'd visit and discuss with local stakeholders. DHS did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Catch up quick: The local challengers urged the court to prevent the administration to restart construction, alleging the administration overstepped its authority on multiple fronts and warning of harm to the environment and recreation. "Once bulldozers clear vegetation, roads are cut into previously undeveloped terrain, lights mounted, and steel barrier infrastructure is effected, those qualities cannot be restored through monetary compensation or after-the-fact relief," they argued in an August motion. This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

events.title: One Nation makes election promise to revive Victoria's timber sector
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts One Nation promises to revive Victoria's native timber industry but cannot cite the cost Topic: Forestry, Logging and Timber Industry One Nation has pledged to let loggers back into native forests in Victoria if it wins the state election. ( Supplied: Victorian National Parks Association ) One Nation has promised to resume native timber logging in Victoria if it wins the state election, but has not said how the policy would be funded or achieved. The party says its policy also includes provisions to protect old-growth forest and native habitat. The Victorian Coalition is finalising its timber policy ahead of the election. Two years after sawmills fell silent in Victoria's native forests, the logging industry could be revived if there is a change in government at the November election. While the Coalition and One Nation have committed to restarting native forest logging, which was shut down by the Labor government in January 2024 , it is unclear what it would take to get the industry back on its feet. One Nation's Narracan candidate Ben Lucas said the policy supported country-of-origin labelling laws on timber and wood products, and a self-funding model in which harvest revenue supported forest improvement and fire prevention. He said the party would consult industry leaders and audit the millions of dollars Labor spent on the logging industry transition fund before settling on a new approach. He said the party would incentivise the use of Australian timber in construction through a "local wood first" policy in government procurement and would ensure timber was extracted using a selective harvesting model. "You can't take away the forestry industry from a town like Noojee and replace the economy with a truffle festival once a year," Mr Lucas said. Pauline Hanson with Ben Lucas during a visit to Gippsland in August. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) But when pressed for details, Mr Lucas would not clarify how much it could cost or what would be involved in reopening native forests to logging. "This is a broad policy and it's very open-ended, but with clear guidelines on how we want to do it and why we want to do it," Mr Lucas said. "We've got the words on paper and if we get in, we can have some influence on how that happens." The Liberal-National Coalition is still working through the details of its policy, but Nationals leader Danny O'Brien previously vowed to restore native forest logging. Nationals MP Melina Bath, whose portfolio includes timber, said the coalition was finalising its policy but also backed a return to logging. "We will be announcing a suite of packages and policies in relation to this," Ms Bath said. "They're still going through a parliamentary process and we make sure … that we've done our costings correctly." Victoria's Regional Development Minister Michaela Settle said restarting native forestry under a Coalition or One Nation government would cost Victorians. "Labor is backing forestry workers into new jobs, growing local plantation timber and keeping forestry skills and experience in our forests to reduce bushfire risk and support better forest management," she said. According to a 2026 Victorian Auditor-General's report, the Victorian government's decision to shut down the industry affected 1,000 workers and 200 businesses. It found the Victorian government spent $1.5 billion on transition arrangements and 87 per cent of workers had retired or found new jobs. But it found many had moved into part-time, casual or contract roles and it was "not clear if workers' new jobs meet their needs or are sustainable". Ms Bath said a revived industry would "look different to what the Labor government shut down in 2024" and would need to overcome challenges, such as rebuilding the workforce. Orbost District Chamber of Commerce and Industry secretary Garry Squires said any move to revive the forestry sector would be well received in the regions. Garry Squires says rural towns like Orbost would love to see a return of native forest logging. ( ABC Gippsland: Natasha Schapova ) "The reality is you can't just start big harvesting operations right across Victoria in a hurry, but start off slowly with thinning operations," he said. "We've got this great resource of eucalypt forests across Victoria. Victoria has more than 380,000 hectares of plantation forest, totalling more than 20 per cent of Australia's plantations. Victoria also produces about one-quarter of Australia's plantation-grown wood, at a gross value of about $550 million each year.

events.title: Christa Pike survived lethal injection. How your state carries out executions
events.summary: Data: Death Penalty Information Center ; Note: New Hampshire abolished the death penalty but retains one prisoner on death row; Map: Erin Davis/Axios Christa Pike 's survival after two lethal injection doses has put state execution protocols nationwide under new scrutiny. The big picture: How prisoners are executed varies by state , with lethal injection, electrocution, lethal gas and firing squads among the methods authorized. Lethal injections are the most common U.S. execution method , accounting for roughly 89% of the 1,683 executions carried out since 1976, per the Death Penalty Information Center . By the numbers: More than two dozen states have lethal injection as a primary method. Lethal gas is authorized in Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Oklahoma and Wyoming. Electrocution is allowed in Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Tennessee. Firing squad is allowed in Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah. Idaho is the only state where it is the primary method. Context: Some states let prisoners choose among the different execution methods. Zoom out: The Supreme Court requires states to keep the death penalty only for the most heinous murders. Pike , convicted of killing a classmate three decades ago, survived two rounds of lethal injection drugs earlier this week in what would have been the first execution of a woman in Tennessee in 200 years. Pike was still alive as of Friday, remaining on a ventilator and unconscious, AP reports.

events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at the UC Berkeley and FuriosaAI published a technical paper titled “Characterizing High Bandwidth Flash for LLM Serving.” “Large language model (LLM) serving requires substantial memory to store model weights and KV caches. As models grow larger and contexts become longer, memory capacity and bandwidth increasingly become bottlenecks for serving performance. Agentic workloads compound this pressure through repeated interactions over growing contexts, making it increasingly important to retain KV state for reuse. High-bandwidth flash (HBF) offers a way to expand accelerator memory capacity for large language model (LLM) serving, but its access costs and limited write endurance complicate its use. We evaluate HBF for high-throughput agentic serving across system design and scheduling choices to understand when additional capacity improves serving performance and energy efficiency. We introduce an HBM-HBF-host hierarchical storage system and buffered cache-aware scheduling, and use trace-driven simulations to analyze their effects on performance, energy consumption, and HBF write lifetime. Across the evaluated workloads, the fastest HBF-augmented systems reduce completion time by 36.1-87.0% relative to HBM-only systems. Modeled energy savings reach 55.8%, although HBF increases energy consumption on some light workloads. Buffered cache-aware scheduling extends estimated HBF write lifetime from 4.77 to 14.82 years in the evaluated configuration. These results demonstrate the importance of coordinating data placement and scheduling to improve serving efficiency while sustaining a practical HBF write lifetime.” Find the technical paper here . events.title: Google hearts Apple's Swift so much it's pumping out server-side support
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters After a decade of false starts, Swift is showing backend appeal KDE turns 30 with Plasma 6.8, but the X11 session isn't invited 4 days ago OpenAI tries disarming AI angst with cute graphics and always-on agents 5 days ago Open source tool distills Jev so you can run it locally 5 days ago Dutch government turns to NixOS for a sovereign desktop 6 days ago New software dependency validation process increases speeds by 54x 9 days ago After evolving from an Apple-made, client-side language and years of false starts, Swift could finally make it on the server. Google has taken note and has just rolled out Google Cloud API Client Libraries for Swift , evidently convinced Swift has a backend role thanks to its performance and ease of use. The GCP Swift libraries target Swift 6.2+ and take advantage of SwiftNIO's asynchronous event loops, HTTP/2 multiplexing, gRPC transport, and data race safety compiler flags. "For years, Swift was perceived mainly as a UI language tied to Apple client devices," said Karl Weinmeister, director of developer relations, and Carlos O'Ryan, software engineer, in a blog post . "With Swift 6 and strict concurrency checking, it has matured into a viable systems and cloud language, pairing Rust-like data-race safety with predictable, reference-counted performance." Weinmeister and O'Ryan argue that Swift manages to be both developer-friendly and suitable for low-level control over resources, which tends not to be the case for challenging systems languages like C++ or Rust. They voice appreciation for the language's lightweight runtime and Automatic Reference Counting (ARC), alongside its expressive syntax. And they approve of Swift's compile-time concurrency checking. "Data races are caught in your editor before a binary ever compiles or reaches production," they note. The Googlers argue that the Server Side Cloud Swift SDK is well-suited for servers, containers, and DevOps environments, pointing to its utility for building capable microservices using Swift web frameworks like Hummingbird or Vapor. "With google-cloud-swift, server-side Swift developers can write end-to-end cloud infrastructure with compile-time race safety, native async/await ergonomic APIs, and zero OS thread congestion," they declare. It's been quite a journey. Apple open-sourced the Swift programming language all the way back in 2015 and in the years that followed, developers started looking at Swift on the server. IBM in 2016 made Swift available on its Bluemix cloud and a few months later the Swift team announced a server API working group. The first server-side Swift conference was announced in late 2017. And Apple's work on the async SwiftNIO framework in 2018 advanced the case for backend Swift. Swift's popularity peaked in January 2020, according to the TIOBE index , when it ranked as the 9th most popular programming language. It currently ranks 18th. Stack Overflow's 2025 developer survey has Swift ranked 20th. Even so, server-side adoption of Swift has been slow. IBM reversed course in 2019, backing away from its Swift commitment. And Amazon hasn't really done much with its Smoke Framework for server-side Swift in the past few years. Still, the Swift community has kept at it. The Swift Server Workgroup launched in 2018 and, by 2024, the release of Swift 6 with data race safety checks made the language more interesting for backend applications. Swift may be more approachable than languages like Rust or C++, but it's unclear how much that will matter in the years to come as developers become more and more dependent on AI coding agents. Certainly, Swift code is readable, a benefit for those maintaining applications, but language ergonomics and approachability matter less when AI is reading and writing most of the code.

events.title: Australia's power supply forecasts have never been rosier. Experts are worried
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts The 'fantasy' underpinning Australia's rosy power supply forecasts Experts fear the way Australia's energy operator assesses future power reliability obscures problems. ( ABC News ) In the chaos and complexity of energy in Australia, one topic has always cut through the noise: blackouts. Or, more precisely, the need to avoid blackouts at seemingly any cost, so untenable are the political consequences. It is for this reason that so much of Australia's energy planning goes towards making sure there is always enough capacity to keep the lights on. "When people say, 'Oh, we've breached the reliability standard, therefore blackouts', the reliability standard that we have is incredibly, incredibly tight," Tristan Edis of Green Energy Markets says. Powerlines are a much bigger source of outages than lack of energy. ( ABC News: Keana Naughton ) To be exact, Australia's "reliability standard" prescribes that consumers should expect their electricity needs to be met 99.998 per cent of the time. In other, albeit simplified, words, no more than 0.002 per cent — or 10 minutes — of their demand should go unserved across an entire year. This does not include power lost because of outages on the poles-and-wires network, a much more common occurrence. For more than two decades now, one document has been central to ensuring Australia's onerous reliability standards are maintained. It's called the "electricity statement of opportunities" and it's handled by the body that runs the country's biggest electricity system — the Australian Energy Market Operator. Dylan McConnell from the University of New South Wales says it's called a statement of opportunities for a reason. He says it shows where there are likely to be supply gaps in the decade ahead, thereby signalling where new energy projects would be most needed. "It says everything will be fine if we do these things," McConnell says. "It's essentially supposed to provide guidance to the market on where reliability issues may emerge in the future. The cost of building wind projects has ballooned in the past five years. ( ABC News: Daniel Mercer ) There's just one problem, according to McConnell, Edis and several other respected energy market observers canvassed by the ABC. The statement of opportunities is now counting on projects that may not be built on time. Many, they say, may never be built at all. And they warn that fundamental changes to the way the reliability assessment is carried out are hiding major problems with Australia's energy transition. "At the moment, it's probably the case that we're downplaying some pretty significant risks and challenges ahead of us, and that has consequences," McConnell says. Among those consequences, he says, are higher wholesale energy costs in the event forecast generation and storage does not arrive in time or is simply not built. Partly, he says this is a function of supply and demand. If there's less supply than was forecast by the end of the decade, McConnell says prices will inevitably increase to reflect that scarcity. Equally, he says the market operator will turn to emergency measures to ensure supply is sufficient. These measures could include paying big energy users a premium to turn down or turn off their use at times of stress on the system. Or it could be shelling out small fortunes to the operators of diesel-fired generators to provide critical back-up power. Either way, McConnell says, the measures are not cheap. On top of this, he says governments themselves would step into the breach to stave off any shortfalls in supply. The lever most likely to be pulled would be the extension of ageing coal-fired power plants such as Yallourn in Victoria and Eraring in New South Wales. "At the end of the day, blackouts and unreliable electricity is politically untenable," he says. AEMO did not always publish such a rose-tinted view of reliability. If anything, Edis of Green Energy Markets says the agency used to take a much harder line that was arguably too conservative in its assumptions. He says it effectively underestimated forecast supply because of "silly rules". The next coal-fired domino to fall will be Victoria's Yallourn in 2028. ( ABC News: Freya Michie ) "And now it's probably gone too far the other way," Edis says. Key to the change is the way AEMO includes projects in the reliability outlook. Historically, he says it was only those projects which were either existing or committed that got a guernsey. Put another way, the plants had to be in the ground already or under construction to be used in the forecast.

events.title: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil in bid to curb soaring prices
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts G7 countries to release 100 million barrels of diesel and oil to curb fuel prices The G7 talks were convened by Emmanuel Macron after a conversation with US President Donald Trump. ( Reuters: Axel Schmidt ) G7 countries are set to release up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil reserves. It comes amid soaring fuel prices and after clashes between European leaders and Donald Trump. The US president is under political pressure in America over rising energy costs, which have been sparked by the US-Israeli war with Iran. G7 countries have agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from their reserves over four months to ease global energy supply concerns. The leaders also pledged not to impose export restrictions on energy products. The announcement came after G7 leaders held a video conference, chaired by French President Emmanuel Macron, as the United States stepped up pressure on Europe to release strategic reserves and threatened a diesel export ban. The talks, convened by Mr Macron after a conversation with US President Donald Trump, focused on coordinating a response to soaring fuel prices among the other G7 economies of Britain, Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States. The US-Israeli war with Iran has sent energy prices skyrocketing, coming back to bite Mr Trump at home with high fuel costs that have become a key issue ahead of midterm congressional elections in a month. Analyst warns diesel prices could top $4 a litre Analyst warns export ban the most worrying development since the Middle East conflict began. Mr Trump has floated the possibility of banning US exports of diesel, which is used in farming machinery, trucks and other hauling vehicles, an alarming prospect for the EU, which relies heavily on fossil fuel imports. The seven countries agreed to a coordinated release through the International Energy Agency (IEA) of 100 million barrels "to begin immediately over four months, including a front-loaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days", the leaders said in a statement released by Mr Macron's office. Emmanuel Macron, flanked by two French ministers, spoke after convening the G7 meeting. ( Reuters: Ludovic Marin. ) They also said there would be no ban on diesel exports between them. "We reaffirm our commitment to refrain from export restrictions on energy and energy products between G7 countries and call on all producers to refrain from imposing bans that could exacerbate market tensions," the leaders said. Mr Trump said European countries had agreed to release a "massive amount" of diesel from their reserves. "The process will begin immediately," he posted on his Truth Social network. Earlier the EU pushed back hard against US threats to impose a diesel export ban, something Mr Macron also warned against during his conversation with Mr Trump. A taxi driver says he is driving 12 hours a day to make ends meet amid rising fuel prices. "We fully reject any ban on diesel," European Commission spokeswoman Anna-Kaisa Itkonen said, warning it would "undermine our trust in the United States as a reliable partner". The flurry of diplomatic activity came a day after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent cranked up the pressure on European nations. The 32 members of the IEA agreed last March to unlock 400 million barrels of oil from reserves, their largest release ever.

events.title: Shut up and take our money: Amazon plows $1B+ into quashing datacenter dissent
events.summary: Faced with growing opposition to datacenters from residents who don't want the bit barns in their backyards, Amazon plans to invest more than $1 billion over the next five years to indoctrinate the public. The company announced the investment in a whataboutism-packed blog post aimed at convincing readers datacenters are not as bad as they've been led to believe, and that if the common folk don't get in line and support their development, the nation could be left in the dust. The program aims to invest in education, job training, local infrastructure improvements, and sustainability initiatives in communities home to Amazon datacenters. "This build out is so important geopolitically that there are widespread reports of various countries intentionally seeding misinformation in the US about datacenters to trick us into slowing down," the e-tailer turned cloud titan wrote. "Right now there are over 100 datacenter moratoriums being considered across the country. If these measures are enacted, the US could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations." If Jeff Bezos's cash cow is to be believed, datacenters will transform the US economy much like the buildout of the highway system did in the '50s. But that can't happen, Amazon argues, if Americans block the development of these bit barns over misguided fears. The blog post highlights four such datacenter fears, which Amazon claims are "myths," despite plenty of reporting to suggest otherwise. Who needs water? The first "myth" is the fact that datacenters consume an excessive share of water. Bit barns commonly employ evaporative coolers which use water to reject heat generated by the facility into the atmosphere. These cooling towers use less energy than dry coolers or refrigerant-based systems but remove water from local watersheds as a consequence. According to Amazon, citizens should really be more worried about the water consumed by golf courses, which it claims use 200x more water than all of Amazon's datacenters. That argument might be more convincing if people didn't like golf courses. But they do and the whole lesser of two evils argument works a lot better when one of those evils isn't extremely popular. Amazon also attempted to dispel claims that a typical datacenter consumes five million gallons a day, arguing that its facilities are much more efficient using just 13,000 gallons a day, the equivalent of 42 US households. But this leaves out an important detail. It is possible to build datacenters that don't consume large quantities of water, but these facilities often consume large sums of power as a consequence. Most gas, nuclear, coal, and anything else that uses steam to turn a turbine also consumes water. In other words, nearly every large-scale power-generation method uses water either directly or indirectly. And despite Amazon's attempts to downplay the impact of datacenters, there's good reason for those living nearby to be worried. Earlier this year, it was reported that a datacenter, which we'll note was not operated by Amazon, has quietly sucked up nearly 30 million gallons of water and the only reason anyone discovered the issue was that local residents started complaining of unusually low water pressure. We totally won't let datacenters drive up your power bill or poison your air Amazon also attempted to dispel fears that datacenters could leave neighboring residents picking up the tab for their massive power consumption. The company argues that rates are going up because the US grid is old, and that responsible bit barn builders are working with utilities to ensure they're paying their fair share for the additional capacity and infrastructure upgrades required to support them. What wasn't addressed is why folks might be worried about rising rates. One of the reasons that utilities and plant operators are so conservative is that they've been burned by speculative markets before. If new power plants are built to meet demand that never materializes, ratepayers could get stuck with the bill. Amazon and others agreeing to pay higher rates might help, but only if they're consuming an appreciable amount of the capacity they convinced utilities to build. An empty datacenter doesn't pull a lot of juice. Speaking of power, Amazon also attempted to downplay the impact of datacenters on air quality due to their reliance on diesel backup generators. "The truth is the datacenter generators almost never run," the company wrote. Amazon also argued that these generators are subject to stringent permitting requirements which dictate how long they can run for. That might be more reassuring if datacenters in power constrained regions weren't getting permission after the fact to exceed those limits. And, as we saw with Elon Musk's Colossus supercomputer, temporary gas turbines can be deployed when the local grid can't support the load. That hasn't sat well with residents of Boxtown, Tennessee, while the NAACP is suing xAI over allegedly unpermitted turbines in Mississippi. Amazon can argue it's got a better track record than most, but that doesn't mean the community's concerns are misplaced. But think of the taxes Finally, Amazon argues that folks don't realize how big of an economic impact datacenters have on their community. "Datacenter operators are often the single largest taxpayer in a community, with upfront payments routinely exceeding entire annual municipal budgets in the first year of construction," the company claimed. "For example, in St. Joseph County, Indiana, the taxes Amazon will pay to the county are estimated to exceed $3 billion." The subtext is that, by enacting datacenter moratoriums, communities are walking away from billions in tax dollars. Then again, if the tax revenue from these facilities is so great, it raises the question why Amazon needs to spend more than $1 billion over five years sweetening the deal for communities hosting its bit barns. ® Updated Oct 3 at 1447 GMT to reflect the fact that Amazon actually said it would spend more than $1 billion.

events.title: Formal Automotive Security Analysis Of CAN XL (Georgia Tech, QCRI, Purdue)
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at Georgia Institute of Technology, Qatar Computing Research Institute, and Purdue University published a technical paper titled “A Formal Security Analysis of CAN XL.” “For decades, the Controller Area Network (CAN) has been the backbone of in-vehicle communication. As modern vehicles integrate cameras, LiDARs, and AI components, classic CAN (CAN CC) faces growing limitations in bandwidth, functionality, and security. To fill these gaps, CAN XL was introduced as the next generation of CAN, aiming to offer longer payloads, higher bandwidth, and enhanced security. CAN XL makes significant standard-level changes across multiple stack layers. It also introduces several security features, but it is unclear whether these are mere add-on extensions or whether the standard redesign itself tackles CAN’s chronic security weakness: the MAC sub-layer. This sub-layer governs frame formats and error handling and has historically enabled many CAN CC attacks. As the industry transitions to CAN XL, the security posture of its yet-unexplored MAC sub-layer must be understood before widespread deployment. This paper presents the first security analysis of the CAN XL standard, focusing on its MAC sub-layer. We develop a bit-precise CAN XL formal model and release it to facilitate future research. We design a formal analysis workflow guided by CAN XL’s field-oriented structure to uncover vulnerabilities. Contrary to expectations, our analysis shows that CAN XL remains vulnerable to all known CAN CC MAC sub-layer issues while introducing seven new vulnerabilities, arguably worsening security. We validate them using commercial CAN XL controllers and demonstrate exploitability via two multi-stage attacks on a testbed simulating real vehicle traffic. Finally, we propose mitigations including formally verifying standard revisions that could prevent several attacks.” Find the technical paper here . August 2026. Tang, Zhaozhou, Khaled Serag, Z.
